# A 1,000-Year Flood on a River That Had Passed 10 Feet Only Once: the Toccoa and Ocoee Record of November 5, 2026

**Published**: 2026-11-09  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/toccoa-ocoee-river-record-flood-november-2026-georgia-tennessee  
**Summary**: Eleven inches of rain in 12 hours sent the Toccoa and Ocoee to a record 18.05 feet at Copperhill. Every warning, storm report and gauge reading on one map, with radar rainfall, FEMA flood zones and DisasterAWARE exposure as layers you can switch on.

_DisasterAWARE Weekly Intelligence Brief -- October 29 to November 7, 2026_

**In the early hours of November 5 the Toccoa River rose about 15 feet in nine hours and went past a record that had stood since 1990.** A mesonet site near Blue Ridge, Georgia measured 11.19 inches of rain in 12 hours, 10.28 of them in six, and NWS Atlanta said both totals exceeded the 1-in-1,000-year values in NOAA's rainfall atlas. The National Weather Service gauge at Copperhill, Tennessee, where the Toccoa becomes the Ocoee, crested at **18.05 feet at 11:00 UTC** (6:00 a.m. Eastern), 4 feet above major flood stage and above the 17.75-foot record of February 1990. Every other crest in that gauge's history is under 10 feet. The Atlanta and Morristown forecast offices issued **five flash flood warnings and one river flood warning** for the storm, and raised three of them to **flash flood emergencies** , the first at 03:47 UTC, nearly five hours before the river reached major stage. One woman died when her car was swept away in Murray County, and state emergency officials counted about 100 rescues, nearly all in Fannin County.

The same system then ran up the Atlantic coast. Elsewhere this week: a flash flood emergency each for Pearl River County, Mississippi and Brevard County, Florida, 51 flash-flood reports in Arizona, Brazil's Paraná under a thunderstorm warning covering 38.5 million people as an F2 tornado cut power to more than 85,000 homes in Maringá, and a magnitude 6.1 earthquake off Japan's Pacific coast.

**How to read every number in this brief.** We keep two kinds of numbers apart. _Alert-tier_ numbers are products an agency issued (warnings, watches, advisories): a forecast with a defined area and, in DisasterAWARE, an estimated population inside that footprint. _Observed-tier_ numbers are measurements and reports of what happened: gauge readings, NWS Local Storm Reports, damage surveys. Where we compare them, the question is always the same: at the time and place of each impact, what warning was in force?

## Top Risks This Week

  1. **North Georgia and southeast Tennessee flash flood, November 4 to 5.** Record crests on the Toccoa/Ocoee at Copperhill (18.05 ft) and on Mountaintown Creek near Ellijay (14.9 ft against a 10.03-foot record from 2015). One death, about 100 rescues in Georgia and 68 in Polk County, Tennessee, a state of emergency in Georgia.
  2. **The rest of the system.** Flash flood emergencies in Pearl River County, Mississippi (November 1) and Brevard County, Florida (November 2); 23 flash-flood reports each in Florida and Louisiana; a river flood warning for Florida's Treasure Coast with 906,000 people inside its footprint.
  3. **The Southwest's long tail.** 51 flash-flood reports in Arizona and 45 river-flood reports in New Mexico as the October pattern ended; NWS Flagstaff issued 17 flash flood warnings, the most of any office this week.
  4. **Southern Brazil.** INMET thunderstorm warnings for the South and Southeast through the window, the largest on November 2 covering 38.5 million people and $2.19 trillion of infrastructure; an F2 tornado through Maringá in the early hours of the same day.
  5. **A 6.1 off Japan.** 144 km southeast of Hasaki at 29 km depth on November 6; no tsunami warning or advisory, only a forecast of slight sea-level change.



## The Week in Numbers

_Alert tier (products issued, complete NWS record via the Iowa Environmental Mesonet, October 29 to November 7):_

  * **135** flash flood warnings nationwide, **5** of them flash flood emergencies (three for the Toccoa/Ocoee basin, one each for Pearl River County MS and Brevard County FL)
  * **55** river flood warnings (Albuquerque 14, the most of any office)
  * **24** tornado warnings (Shreveport 7) and **95** severe thunderstorm warnings (Norman 42)
  * **4,535** alert-tier records filtered out of the DisasterAWARE weekly bundle as formal alerts, forecasts or excluded types



_Observed tier (NWS Local Storm Reports via IEM, same window):_

  * **165** flash flood reports (Arizona 51, Florida 23, Louisiana 23, Georgia 15) and **95** flood reports (New Mexico 45)
  * **17** tornado reports (Texas 9), which are spotter reports, not confirmed tornado counts
  * **18.05 ft** at Copperhill and **14.9 ft** on Mountaintown Creek: two record crests in one night



_DisasterAWARE record:_ 266 active and 1,655 expired actual-event hazard records in the window after the weekly filter, with 11,482 Enterprise products attached.

## The Map: Every Layer, Warned vs. Observed

The map replays the night hour by hour. Drag the slider or press Play: warnings appear when they were issued and fade when they expired, storm reports appear when they were filed, and the two gauge markers change colour as the rivers climb through action, minor, moderate and major stage. The hydrographs on the right show the Copperhill and Mountaintown Creek readings against their flood categories and their previous records. The red band along the river through McCaysville and Copperhill is the National Weather Service's modelled inundation extent for the Copperhill gauge (the stage-based CatFIM library, mapped at one-foot stage intervals); it follows the gauge as you replay, growing from the 6-foot action band to the 18-foot band at the crest, and stays at the highest stage reached. It is a modelled extent, and the map labels it that way. At the crest a second layer appears on top of it: modelled flood depth in 10-metre cells, from a preview record built by the DisasterAWARE flood enhancer for this brief using the same NWS CatFIM library and the Copperhill crest. Through the centre of McCaysville and Copperhill it maps depths of two to six feet between the river and the main streets, which agrees with the storm report of two to three feet at Tennessee Avenue and Blue Ridge Drive; the deepest class is mostly the river channel. It is a model, not a measurement, and the map says so on every hover.

[Open map full screen ↗](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/maps/2026-11-07-weekly-hazards.html>)

**Explore the map.** The modelled depth at the crest, the CatFIM inundation, warnings, storm reports, fatality and two main gauges are on by default. Five more layers are off so the picture stays readable. Open the layer switcher at the top right and turn on:

  * **MRMS 24-h radar rainfall** : NOAA's radar-estimated totals ending 12:00 UTC November 5, with the 10-plus-inch band lying along the Fannin and Gilmer county line, exactly where the reports cluster.
  * **FEMA flood hazard zones (NFHL)** : the National Flood Hazard Layer, live from FEMA. Switch to the Esri satellite basemap and zoom to McCaysville and Copperhill to see how much of both towns sits outside the mapped 1% zone.
  * **DisasterAWARE warning records & exposure**: the platform's alert footprints for the three products it ingested, with the population, households and infrastructure inside each.
  * **All nearby river gauges** : the Toccoa above Blue Ridge Lake peaked at 3.22 feet (minor stage is 12). The record at Copperhill came from the creeks that join the river below the dam, not from the upper Toccoa.
  * **Esri satellite** basemap: the valley floor the river filled.



Every feature has a hover label and a click popup naming its source and tier. Deep links work: `#t=2026-11-05T09:00Z` jumps the clock, `#layers=mrms,nfhl` turns layers on.

## What Happened

Rain began over the Blue Ridge on the evening of November 4 and fell at its heaviest between about 8 p.m. and 2 a.m. Eastern, according to a mesonet report from Mineral Bluff. The first storm report came from McCaysville at 02:45 UTC (10:45 p.m.): "flooding reported". By 03:15 UTC roads near Mountaintown were under water; at 04:06 UTC water was in a home on Old CCC Camp Road in Murray County; at 04:27 and 04:38 UTC homes near Cherry Log were flooding and Boardtown Road was blocked by a mudslide; at 04:35 UTC swift water was approaching businesses on Blue Ridge Drive; at 04:47 UTC a water rescue was under way near Epworth. At 07:00 UTC (2:00 a.m.) a mesonet site two miles northwest of Blue Ridge reported **11.19 inches** ; a second site near Nottely Dam reported a storm total of 6.24 inches. NWS Atlanta's own statement put the Blue Ridge totals at 11.19 inches in 12 hours and 10.28 inches in six, and said both exceeded the 1-in-1,000-year rainfall values in NOAA Atlas 14, the Weather Service's national rainfall-frequency atlas.

The creeks answered first. Mountaintown Creek near Ellijay reached its record 14.9 feet at 06:30 UTC, nearly five feet above the 10.03-foot record set in December 2015 and just short of moderate stage. The Toccoa/Ocoee at Copperhill crossed major stage (14 feet) at 08:30 UTC, crested at 18.05 feet at 11:00 UTC and was still at 17.84 feet at 12:00 UTC; the gauge then reported nothing for three and a half hours and was at 12.43 feet when readings resumed at 15:30 UTC, so the timing of the recession is not known. Even so it is a flash-flood hydrograph on a reach that normally behaves like a mountain stream. The upper Toccoa near Dial, above Blue Ridge Lake, peaked at only 3.22 feet: the flood came from the tributaries below the dam, draining the ridges where the radar put the heaviest rain.

Downstream, McCaysville and Copperhill, two towns that share a state line and a river, took the crest through their centres: at 11:00 UTC, the hour of the crest, a storm report from McCaysville put water an estimated two to three feet deep near the intersection of Tennessee Avenue and Blue Ridge Drive, the one observed depth in the record. Cleanup reports on November 6 described businesses and homes along the river gutted by water and mud. Georgia's governor declared a state of emergency and the city of McCaysville declared its own.

## Warned vs. Observed

**The warnings came early and escalated in step with the water.** NWS Peachtree City (Atlanta) issued its first flash flood warning for the area at 01:55 UTC, fifty minutes before the first storm report. At 02:30 UTC (9:30 p.m.) it issued a second warning for northwest Fannin and north-central Gilmer counties, and at 03:47 UTC (10:47 p.m.) upgraded it to a flash flood emergency, the NWS's highest flood product, reserved for severe threats to life and catastrophic damage. A river flood warning for Mountaintown Creek followed at 06:27 UTC, reporting 14.5 feet against the 2015 record of 10.0 feet. NWS Morristown warned Polk County, Tennessee and Cherokee County, North Carolina at 07:19 UTC and issued a separate flash flood emergency for the Copperhill area at 08:58 UTC, half an hour after the gauge crossed major stage; Atlanta issued a third emergency for Fannin at 10:08 UTC, an hour before the crest. In DisasterAWARE the first two products arrived within minutes as warning-grain records with exposure: the combined Morristown and Peachtree City flash flood warning record, covering the basin from 01:55 to 14:15 UTC, held an estimated **4,890 people, 1,960 households and $380 million of infrastructure** ; the Gilmer County river warning 3,940 people and $179 million. A third record, for the Fannin County extension issued at 13:57 UTC, held 3,150 people and $251 million.

**The death.** Julie Barrs, 56, of Ellijay, died when her car was swept away on Old CCC Camp Road in Murray County; the county medical examiner identified her on November 6, and the sheriff's incident report, cited by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, puts the time shortly before 10 p.m. Eastern on November 4 (about 02:50 UTC), with her body found about noon the next day two miles downstream. Checked against the warning polygons, the location (the map places it at the 04:06 UTC storm report on the same block, so it is approximate) was **inside the 01:55 UTC flash flood warning** , issued 55 minutes earlier, and inside the DisasterAWARE alert footprint for the event. It was **outside all three emergency polygons** , which covered Fannin, Gilmer and Polk counties to the east; the nearest, the Fannin and Gilmer emergency, began about 2 km to the east and did not exist until an hour after she was swept away. That pattern, a fatal crossing inside a warning but outside the emergency upgrade, is the same one we found twice in New Mexico in October: the flood that kills is often the one on the small creek at the edge of the warned area, not the one on the river making the headlines.

**The rescues.** Georgia's emergency management director put the count at 100 rescues in Georgia, 97 of them in Fannin County, which was under an emergency from 03:47 UTC. Tennessee's emergency agency told WSMV that 68 people were rescued in Polk County. The one rescue in the storm-report record (Epworth at 04:47 UTC) falls inside the emergency polygon in force at that time.

**What the gauges add.** A flash flood emergency is an alert-tier product; the 18.05-foot reading is observed, and it settles the argument about scale. The Copperhill gauge's crest record goes back to the 1940s with only one crest above 10 feet before this week, the 17.75 feet of February 16, 1990. Thursday's crest beat it by 0.3 feet on a single night's rain.

## Elsewhere on the Board

**The same storm, farther south and east.** NWS New Orleans issued a flash flood emergency for Pearl River County, Mississippi at 02:47 UTC on November 1, and NWS Melbourne one for Brevard County, Florida at 12:56 UTC on November 2 as the system crossed the Gulf coast and the peninsula. Florida and Louisiana each logged 23 flash-flood reports. The river flood warning for Florida's Treasure Coast on November 3 carried the largest US flood-warning footprint of the week in DisasterAWARE: an estimated 906,000 people and $98 billion of infrastructure.

**Arizona and New Mexico, the long tail.** The October pattern that produced our last brief ended with 51 flash-flood reports in Arizona and 45 river-flood reports in New Mexico in this window. NWS Flagstaff issued 17 flash flood warnings, the most of any office nationwide, and a central Arizona flash flood warning on October 31 covered an estimated 419,000 people.

**Southern Brazil.** INMET kept thunderstorm warnings over the South and Southeast through the window. The largest, issued November 2 for Paraná, São Paulo and Mato Grosso do Sul, covered 38.5 million people, 13.9 million households and $2.19 trillion of infrastructure. In the early hours of that day a tornado crossed Maringá: the state meteorological service Simepar classified it on November 3 as an F2 with a 15 km track and winds of 180 to 250 km/h, per the Paraná state news agency. About 85,000 to 88,000 homes lost power, the city declared a state of public calamity and the fire department's headquarters lost its roof.

**Japan.** A magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck 144 km southeast of Hasaki, Chiba Prefecture at 10:39 UTC on November 6 at a depth of 29 km, per the USGS's revised location. The Japan Meteorological Agency issued no tsunami warning or advisory, only a forecast of slight sea-level change, and no immediate damage was reported.

**Also this week.** Syria's emergency ministry had a flash flood warning covering 14 governorates and the Jazira region, 17.3 million people, from October 27 to 30. The Mekong River Commission kept riverine flood watches in force for My Thuan and Can Tho in Vietnam, 19.5 million people in the footprint. A heat warning for the Sahel issued November 5 covers 118 million people for the coming week. Heavy snow of 20 to 50 cm was forecast for Tajikistan, eastern Afghanistan and northern Pakistan.

## On the Horizon (forecast)

  * **Southern Appalachians.** Saturated soils and debris-choked channels mean the next ordinary rain floods faster. Mudslide-blocked roads in Fannin and Gilmer counties and damaged crossings are the near-term risk.
  * **Brazil.** INMET's warnings for the South and Southeast continue through the weekend of November 7 to 8, with the Misiones, Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná footprint at 23.6 million people.
  * **Florida.** River flood warnings for the St. Johns River (DeLand, Cocoa, Geneva and Sanford) and the Peace River at Arcadia remain in force until further notice; the Treasure Coast warning ended November 4.



## What We're Watching Next

  1. NWS Atlanta's post-event summary, including the formal return-period analysis behind its 1-in-1,000-year statement and any revision of the rainfall totals.
  2. USGS high-water marks for the Toccoa, Ocoee and Mountaintown Creek reaches, which would turn the modelled depth on this map into a measured one; the enhancer's preview record gains them once USGS opens an event.
  3. A consolidated damage count for McCaysville and Copperhill and whether Georgia or Tennessee request a federal declaration.
  4. A consolidated damage and injury count for the Maringá tornado from Paraná's civil defence.



## How DisasterAWARE Delivers This

Every product in this brief, from a 30-minute flash flood warning for one county to an INMET warning covering 38.5 million people, arrives in DisasterAWARE as a geocoded record with its footprint, the population, households and infrastructure inside it, and the issuing agency's text. For the Toccoa flood that meant warning records with exposure estimates within minutes of the first two products, which is what an emergency manager or an insurer with assets in Fannin County needed at 9:30 p.m. The observed layer, gauges, storm reports and the rainfall field, is what this brief adds afterwards, and it is the layer that tells you which warnings verified.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How high did the Toccoa River get at McCaysville?**  
The NWS gauge at Copperhill, Tennessee, just across the state line from McCaysville, crested at 18.05 feet at 11:00 UTC (6:00 a.m. Eastern) on November 5, 2026. Major flood stage there is 14 feet. The previous record was 17.75 feet on February 16, 1990.

**Was the November 2026 Georgia flood really a 1,000-year event?**  
NWS Atlanta said the Blue Ridge rainfall, 11.19 inches in 12 hours and 10.28 inches in six, exceeded the 1-in-1,000-year values in NOAA Atlas 14, which means rainfall with roughly a 0.1 percent chance of occurring in any given year at that location, not something that happens once a millennium. The measured facts are those totals and a river crest above a 36-year-old record.

**Were people warned before the Toccoa flooded?**  
Yes. NWS Peachtree City issued a flash flood warning at 01:55 UTC, before the first storm report, and upgraded its Fannin and Gilmer warning to a flash flood emergency at 03:47 UTC, nearly five hours before the river at Copperhill reached major flood stage. The one death, in Murray County at about 02:50 UTC, occurred inside the 01:55 UTC warning area, before any emergency existed and outside the emergency polygons issued later for the counties to the east.

**What is the difference between a flash flood warning and a flash flood emergency?**  
Both are alert-tier NWS products. A flash flood warning means flash flooding is imminent or occurring in the warned area. A flash flood emergency is an upgrade the forecast office adds when it has reports of a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage; it is rare, and five were issued nationwide this week.

# The Southwest's October Flood: Three Deaths in New Mexico, a Santa Fe Tornado and 416 US Flash Flood Warnings in One Month

**Published**: 2026-11-03  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/southwest-october-2026-floods-tornadoes-new-mexico-arizona  
**Summary**: Ten days of flash floods and tornadoes across New Mexico, Arizona, West Texas and Nevada, checked warning by warning against what NWS storm reports say happened. Plus two cyclones in six days on India's east coast.

_DisasterAWARE Weekly Intelligence Brief -- October 23 to November 2, 2026_

**For ten days the desert Southwest had the weather of a Gulf Coast spring.** Between October 23 and November 2 the National Weather Service offices in El Paso, Albuquerque, Midland, Flagstaff, Phoenix, Tucson and Las Vegas issued **120 flash flood warnings** between them, 15 tornado warnings went out nationwide, 11 of them in New Mexico, West Texas and the Texas Panhandle, and Albuquerque and El Paso alone issued **140 severe thunderstorm warnings**. On the ground, NWS storm reports from six states record **204 flash-flood and flood reports, 10 tornado reports and three people swept away and killed in New Mexico** , a confirmed EF1 tornado in the city of Santa Fe, an estimated 1,500 homes and buildings affected by the San Juan River at Farmington, 150 to 200 homes flooded at Rimrock and Lake Montezuma in Arizona, and swift-water rescues from Las Vegas to Tucson. For October as a whole, the NWS issued **416 flash flood warnings nationwide, against 156 in October 2025** , and the seven Southwest offices issued 27 tornado warnings in a month that has never produced more than three in any year since 2020.

Half a world away, India's Andhra Pradesh coast took **two cyclone landfalls in six days** : Arnab on October 28 and Murasu, a Category 2 equivalent at landfall, in the early hours of November 3 with 11.9 million people inside its forecast wind footprint. This brief covers both, with Typhoon In-fa still at sea in the western Pacific.

**How to read every number in this brief.** We keep two kinds of numbers apart. _Alert-tier_ numbers are products the National Weather Service or another agency issued (warnings, advisories, watches): forecasts with a defined area and, in DisasterAWARE, an estimated population inside that footprint. _Observed-tier_ numbers are reports of something that happened: NWS Local Storm Reports, damage surveys, river gauges and official statements. A warning is not an event, and a footprint population is not a count of people affected. We label each figure by its tier.

## Top Risks This Week

  * **Flood and flash-flood threat, New Mexico and Arizona (observed and alert).** Three deaths in New Mexico and two suspected flood deaths in Flagstaff, a federal emergency declaration for four New Mexico counties and five tribal areas, an Arizona state emergency on November 2 for parts of seven counties and five tribal nations, and flood warnings along the San Juan River and the Four Corners running to November 6 and 7. More rain is forecast into this week.
  * **Cyclone Murasu, Andhra Pradesh (observed, landfall November 3).** Second landfall on the same coast in six days. Forecast footprint 11.9 million people. Early reports: two deaths, 12,230 in shelters, crops damaged across 52,459 hectares.
  * **Cyclone Arnab aftermath, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha (observed).** Six dead in Odisha with ten missing after landslides in Kandhamal and Ganjam districts; seven dead in Andhra Pradesh per the state's chief minister.
  * **Typhoon In-fa, western Pacific (alert).** A Category 1 equivalent on November 3, forecast to strengthen, no major landmass in its 72-hour track.
  * **Haiti and the Dominican Republic (observed).** A week of heavy rain to October 29 left at least 8 dead and 5 missing in Haiti, per the Pan American Health Organization's monitoring report, with flooding in 27 municipalities.



## The Week in Numbers

**Observed tier (reports, surveys and measurements, October 23 to November 2):**

  * 1,775 unique NWS Local Storm Reports across Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Nevada, Utah and Colorado, 1,454 of them rain totals.
  * 204 flash-flood and flood reports: 108 flash flood, 96 flood.
  * 3 flood deaths, all in New Mexico, each a person swept away in a vehicle at a crossing.
  * 10 tornado reports and 1 landspout; one tornado surveyed so far: Santa Fe, EF1, 110 mph, 1.48 miles, 10 homes damaged.
  * 23 hail reports, the largest 2 inches (egg-sized) southeast of Kent, Texas on October 27, and 1.75 inches (golf balls) in El Paso on October 23.
  * Heaviest reported rain: 4.85 inches north of Vallecito, Colorado (November 2) and 4.80 inches northwest of Los Pinos, Colorado (October 23).
  * NOAA river gauges with NWS flood categories, six states: 20 reached major flood stage, 12 moderate and 23 minor between October 22 and November 2 (NOAA NWPS observations, provisional). Eighteen of them peaked above every historic crest NOAA lists for the site, among them the San Juan River at Farmington (14.07 ft on October 23 against a 12.3 ft record from 1909) and at Shiprock (21.22 ft against 14.5), the Verde River near Camp Verde (24.65 ft against 19.67 in 2023), Oak Creek at Page Springs near Cornville (21.2 ft against 19.15 in 1993), the Little Colorado River near Winslow (25.29 ft against 22.12 in 2023) and the Gila River near Solomon (26.86 ft against 20.8 in 1983).



**Alert tier (NWS products issued, complete record via the Iowa Environmental Mesonet VTEC archive):**

  * 170 flash flood warnings nationwide, 120 of them from the seven Southwest offices: El Paso 38, Albuquerque 25, Midland 19, Flagstaff 16, Phoenix 9, Tucson 8, Las Vegas 5.
  * 15 tornado warnings: El Paso 5, Albuquerque 3, Amarillo 3, and one each from Austin/San Antonio, Minneapolis, Duluth and Norman.
  * 205 severe thunderstorm warnings: Albuquerque 74, El Paso 66, Norman 23.
  * October 2026 in full: 416 flash flood warnings nationwide (156 in October 2025; 74 to 245 in the Octobers of 2020 to 2024) and 101 tornado warnings (50 in October 2025). The seven Southwest offices: 149 flash flood warnings (67 last October) and 27 tornado warnings (one last October; the previous October high since 2020 was three).
  * DisasterAWARE's own feed carried 107 of these US products with footprint populations. The largest single footprints: the Phoenix flash flood warning of the evening of October 30 (419,000 people), the Albuquerque-area severe thunderstorm warning of October 23 (345,000), the multi-office Southwestern flood warning issued October 31 and running to November 7 (191,000), and the Four Corners flood warning of November 1 to 6 (129,000). Footprints overlap and are never summed.



[Open map full screen ↗](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/maps/2026-11-02-weekly-hazards.html>)

_Explore the map. It opens on the Four Corners, El Paso and Phoenix, and every layer is labelled by tier. Observed: the 55 NOAA river gauges that reached flood stage, coloured by category (dark red major, red moderate, amber minor), with each gauge's peak, thresholds and historic crests in its popup; the 11 confirmed tornado reports with the Santa Fe path drawn; and the three flood deaths. Modeled: the NWS's experimental flood-depth bands at the stage each of 8 gauges reached (1-foot steps, from the Rio Puerco at Bernardo to the San Juan at Farmington and Pagosa Springs), and the National Water Model's 9,449 stream reaches that peaked at a 20-year-or-rarer flow in the past 14 days (blue to purple as the flow gets rarer). Alert: the actual polygons of all 170 flash flood and flood warnings and all 15 tornado warnings issued in the window. Off by default: the 205 severe thunderstorm warning polygons, 127 rain reports of 2 inches or more, the 202 individual flood reports and 14 hail reports. Zoom out to the Bay of Bengal for the JTWC tracks and forecast cones of Cyclones Arnab and Murasu, coloured by category, and to the Pacific for Typhoon In-fa._

## What Happened

A slow-moving upper-level low sat over the Southwest from October 22, drawing subtropical moisture north, and what made it dangerous was that it stayed. Round after round of thunderstorms fell on northern New Mexico, the Four Corners and the Rio Grande valley, then on West Texas, then, on October 30 to November 1, on Nevada and central Arizona. The result was a stacking of hazards the region sees in monsoon season, not in the last week of October: river flooding on the San Juan, the Animas and the Rio Grande tributaries, flash floods in the arroyos of Albuquerque, Santa Fe and El Paso, and tornadoes on three days.

**New Mexico, October 23 to 26.** The San Juan River flooded Farmington on October 23. NWS Albuquerque's storm report that morning estimated as many as 1,500 homes and buildings impacted, with multiple evacuations under way, and the West Chaco bridge over the Animas in Aztec was overtopped later that morning; the next day the Highway 64 bridge at Shiprock closed as the river passed 21 feet. In the Rio Grande valley, Interstate 40 closed in both directions near Laguna Pueblo on October 24 as the Rio San Jose crossed it, and the Sky City Casino's first floor flooded, sending guests to the second floor. On October 25 to 26 the Rio Puerco took out a bridge near Belen and closed US 60 at Bernardo, where fifteen people needed water rescue and, in the early hours of October 26, a woman was swept away in a truck and found that afternoon. A levee breach in Socorro County forced the evacuation of the Escondida and Pueblito communities on the night of October 27. Earlier, late on the night of October 23, a man was swept away in a truck at a low-water crossing south of Pagosa Junction in northern New Mexico, and on the night of October 25 a car with three people was swept from a crossing north of Agua Fria near Santa Fe: the man and an infant were rescued, the woman died. Those are the three deaths in the NWS record. The Associated Press, reporting on October 27, counted "at least two" in New Mexico and quoted Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham estimating the state's damage at as much as $300 million. A federal emergency declaration (EM-3660-NM) dated October 26 covers Cibola, Rio Arriba, Sandoval and San Juan counties and five tribal areas, with 75 percent federal funding for emergency protective measures. San Juan County's spokesperson told AP that 200 to 300 people had been rescued in the county.

**The Santa Fe tornado, October 24.** At 7:00 PM on Saturday evening a tornado formed in the Via Caballero neighbourhood just north of I-25 and ran 1.48 miles north to the College of Santa Fe campus, lifting at 7:08 PM. NWS Albuquerque's survey, completed October 26, rated it **EF1 with peak winds of 110 mph** and a maximum width of 100 yards: broken power poles, uprooted trees, ten homes damaged, one of them with most of its roof removed and a wall collapsed, no injuries. Local reporting says the city had not seen a tornado inside its limits since 1971. It was one of four tornadoes reported in New Mexico that weekend: near Alto on the evening of October 24 (minor damage to a house, a garage door blown in), and two brief ones over open land on October 25, near Table Mesa and northeast of McAlister, both with no damage. Reported tornadoes are observed; the warnings around them are alerts, and the Santa Fe timeline shows how tight the margin was. NWS Albuquerque's severe thunderstorm warning for the city went out at 6:58 PM, two minutes before the tornado formed; its tornado warning was issued at 7:01 PM, one minute after, and the tornado lifted at 7:08 PM (IEM archive of the warning polygons, checked against the survey's start point). El Paso had issued the week's first two tornado warnings on October 23 for southwestern New Mexico, including Sierra County, and Albuquerque's October 25 warning for Quay County covered the McAlister tornado.

**El Paso and West Texas, October 23 to 30.** Golf-ball hail on October 23 ruined a golf course's greens south of Fort Bliss and covered a Costco parking lot. Flash floods on the night of October 25 to 26 put water into homes and apartments in east El Paso and left vehicles stuck in the Montana Vista and Sparks areas; on the evening of October 26, nine homes in Horizon City were evacuated for a suspected dam breach. In the Permian Basin, Midland issued 19 flash flood warnings in the window and its storm reports on October 30 record water over Interstate 20, Highway 158 and streets across Stanton. Near Uvalde on the evening of October 29, NWS Austin/San Antonio confirmed a tornado from video, over open ranch land, with EF0 damage to vegetation.

**Las Vegas, October 30.** The system's push west brought the valley its own afternoon: hail to 1.5 inches (ping-pong balls) near Sahara and Maryland Parkway, and six swift-water rescues logged by NWS Las Vegas between 1:15 and 1:47 PM, in Henderson, east of downtown and in North Las Vegas, plus road closures at Lake Mead, Overton and Laughlin. The flash flood warning NWS Las Vegas issued at 12:43 PM for the Arizona-Nevada border reached a footprint of 78,600 people in DisasterAWARE's record. Four adults were hurt when lightning struck near a bus stop in El Mirage, Arizona that morning.

**Arizona, October 31 to November 2.** Phoenix came first: on the evening of October 30, local time, six people were pulled from four vehicles in a wash near Paradise Valley and Camelback Road ran with water across two lanes. Then Sunday, November 1, was the worst single day of the week. Arizona logged 44 flash-flood and flood reports that day by local time, most of them from the Flagstaff and Tucson offices: Interstate 17 closed at Munds Park, where an estimated 100 properties flooded, with further closures northbound near Rimrock and southbound near Flagstaff; Oak Creek flooded Sedona and Cornville, and Lake Montezuma flooded too, with Yavapai County officials reporting floodwaters overrunning homes in Lake Montezuma and the Flagstaff office's storm report estimating 150 to 200 homes flooded in Rimrock and Lake Montezuma by Sunday night; the state Department of Public Safety rescued 18 people from the Oak Creek area, per Arizona's Family; Camp Verde ordered everyone near the Verde River, West Clear Creek and Wet Beaver Creek out; Highway 73 closed on the White Mountain Apache lands and the Show Low area saw widespread flooding; and Tucson's fire crews ran swift-water rescue after swift-water rescue across the city from 10:20 AM, with Sabino Canyon in minor flood and the Nogales Wash at bankfull. By Monday morning, November 2, Arizona's Family listed "GO" evacuation orders still in force at Winslow, on the San Carlos Apache and White Mountain Apache lands, at Cornville, Cottonwood, Camp Verde and Queen Valley, with Clifton's overnight evacuation lifted at 5 AM. That afternoon Governor Katie Hobbs declared a state of emergency for parts of Apache, Coconino, Gila, Greenlee, Navajo, Pinal and Yavapai counties and the Hopi, Navajo, San Carlos Apache, San Juan Southern Paiute and White Mountain Apache nations, with $200,000 in state funds, three days after a separate emergency for Navajo and Coconino counties over the three tornadoes of October 20 to 22 (an EF1 with 110 mph winds that ran more than nine miles through Heber-Overgaard, a 105 mph tornado near Prescott on October 21, and a third north of Bellemont the same morning). Arizona may also have its own flood deaths: Flagstaff police reported a 73-year-old swept away on the evening of November 1 and found dead the next day, and a second body found in a stormwater drainage on November 2, per KNAU and Arizona's Family. Neither is in the NWS storm-report record yet, so our observed-tier count stays at three.

**Colorado and Utah.** The first days of the window were the Four Corners' worst: the Park Creek bridge on US 160 washed away near South Fork on the night of October 22 to 23 with evacuations from Wolf Creek Ranch to Fun Valley, a house on the Rio Blanco near Pagosa Springs was swept away, and the Paria River in Utah ran three flood waves, the largest 3,150 cubic feet per second early on October 23. AP reported that in Bluff, Utah, a town of 250, 17 homes and five businesses had flooded by October 27.

**The rivers, by the gauges.** NOAA's river gauges turn the storm reports into a measured record. Of the gauges in Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Nevada and West Texas that carry NWS flood categories, 20 reached major flood stage between October 22 and November 2, 12 reached moderate and 23 minor (observed tier: NOAA NWPS provisional readings, checked against each site's published thresholds). The first wave was the San Juan basin's: the San Juan at Farmington peaked at 14.07 feet late on the morning of October 23, two feet above major stage and above the 12.3-foot crest of September 1909 that tops NOAA's list for the site; at Shiprock it reached 21.22 feet the next morning against a listed high of 14.5; the Rio Chama above Abiquiu hit 13.64 feet (major; listed high 10.76) and the South Fork Rio Grande at South Fork 9.03 feet (major, second only to 1911). The Rio Puerco near Bernardo, where the woman died on October 26, crested at 24.29 feet late that afternoon, moderate stage, second only to the 27.9-foot crest of September 1941 in NOAA's list for the site. The second wave was Arizona's: on November 1 and 2 the Verde River near Camp Verde reached 24.65 feet (major; listed high 19.67 in March 2023), Oak Creek at Page Springs near Cornville 21.2 feet (major; 19.15 in 1993), Wet Beaver Creek near Rimrock 13.56 feet (major), the Little Colorado near Winslow 25.29 feet (major; 22.12 in 2023), the San Carlos River above Peridot 16.59 feet (major) and the Gila near Solomon 26.86 feet (major; 20.8 in October 1983). In all, 18 gauges peaked above every historic crest NOAA lists for them. Two more (Carrizo Creek near Show Low and the Little Colorado above Lyman Lake) report values so far above their own thresholds that we treat them as suspect until NOAA reviews them. The map draws the NWS's experimental modeled inundation for eight of these gauges at the stage they reached, in one-foot bands.

See every warning next to what it verified

DisasterAWARE puts issued warnings and observed impacts on one map -- with the people, infrastructure and assets inside each footprint.

## Warned vs. Observed

Did the warnings match the water? We took the time and place of each major impact from the NWS storm reports and checked which storm-based warning polygons were in force there at that moment, using the Iowa Environmental Mesonet's archive. For the big, slow floods the answer is yes, and in the right order. Farmington on October 23 sat inside an Albuquerque river flood warning issued at 8 PM the night before, on top of a flood advisory issued that same morning, October 22. The Sky City Casino and the I-40 closure at Laguna on October 24 were inside both an areal flood warning from October 23 and a flash flood warning issued four hours earlier. Bernardo's rescues and its death on October 26 were inside the Rio Puerco river flood warning issued on the evening of October 24. Henderson's swift-water rescues on October 30 fell inside a Las Vegas flash flood warning issued 32 minutes before the first one; the Paradise Valley rescues on the evening of October 30 were inside a Phoenix flash flood warning issued an hour before; Rimrock's flooded homes on November 1 were inside a Flagstaff flood warning from that morning.

The two other deaths are the exception, and the lesson. The truck swept from a low-water crossing south of Pagosa Junction late on October 23, and the car swept from a crossing north of Agua Fria on the night of October 25, were both outside every storm-based warning polygon in force at the time the NWS recorded for them (the nearest flood warning to the Agua Fria crossing was about 10 miles away). A county-wide flash flood watch may well have been in effect; watches are not polygon products and we did not check them. Both reports carry approximate times. But on the record as it stands, two of this week's three deaths happened at crossings no warning polygon covered, in a week when the Albuquerque office issued 25 flash flood warnings and 74 severe thunderstorm warnings. The volume of warnings is not the problem; low-water crossings at night are, and no warning product draws a polygon around every arroyo.

For tornadoes the picture is thinner. Fifteen tornado warnings in the window, ten tornado reports, one survey published. The Santa Fe tornado is the clearest example of the gap between the two tiers: the tornado warning came one minute after it formed, it did EF1 damage in a city that had no tornado in living memory, and it was rated two days later. DisasterAWARE's own feed carried 8 of the 15 tornado warnings, and not the Santa Fe one, which is one reason this brief counts from the complete archive. On the map, the warnings (alert) and the 11 reports (observed) are separate layers.

**A note on the platform's numbers.** DisasterAWARE's feed carried 107 of these US products with footprint populations; the complete NWS record is larger because the feed folds re-issued and continued products into one hazard. We use our records for exposure and the complete record for counts, and we say which is which.

## India's Coast: Two Cyclones in Six Days

**Cyclone Arnab (observed, landfall October 28).** Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast near Narsapur on the morning of October 28. In DisasterAWARE's record, built from Joint Typhoon Warning Center advisories, the storm was over land near the coast with sustained winds of 102 km/h (63 mph) at the 09:00 UTC advisory that day; the India Meteorological Department had tracked it as a very severe cyclonic storm with gusts to 150 km/h before landfall. The Associated Press reported at least three deaths in Andhra Pradesh on the day of landfall and tens of thousands evacuated; by October 30 Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu put the state's toll at seven. The worse toll came later and inland: rain from the weakening system set off landslides in Odisha's Kandhamal and Ganjam districts on the night of October 29 to 30, and by November 1 Odisha's toll stood at six with ten still missing, per Indian press reports citing state officials, with more than 23,000 people in relief camps as of October 30. The state announced a relief package on November 1, with a central assessment team due in Odisha the next day.

**Cyclone Murasu (observed, landfall November 3).** Murasu formed over the Bay of Bengal on November 1 and came ashore on the south Andhra coast near Ongole in the early hours of November 3: the landfall process began around 1 AM local time, and the IMD put the centre's crossing between 3:30 and 5:30 AM. At the 03:00 UTC JTWC advisory, with the centre 15 km from the coast, DisasterAWARE recorded sustained winds of 157 km/h (98 mph), gusts to 194 km/h, a Category 2 equivalent, and estimated **11.9 million people, 2.90 million households and $55.6 billion of infrastructure** inside the forecast area exposed to moderate to severe damaging winds (alert tier: a footprint estimate, not a count of people affected). The IMD forecast a storm surge of 1.0 to 1.5 metres above the astronomical tide for low-lying parts of south coastal Andhra Pradesh. Preparations were larger than for Arnab: red alerts for the south coastal districts, 11 NDRF and 13 SDRF teams, 725 medical teams and 171 relief camps (PTI, November 3), schools closed in several districts and in Chennai, and at least 19 domestic flights cancelled at Vijayawada, Tirupati and Visakhapatnam. First reports on November 3 put the toll at two deaths, 12,230 people in cyclone shelters, crops damaged across 52,459 hectares in 15 districts (Krishna, Bapatla and Nandyal worst hit) and around 2,750 electricity poles down, with a preliminary damage estimate of Rs 344 crore. These are first-day figures and will change. Readers in the region can check the live status for [Chennai](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/hurricane-risk/chennai-india/>).

**Typhoon In-fa (alert).** In-fa passed near or over the sparsely populated northern islands of the Northern Marianas, well north of Saipan, on October 30 to 31, the fifth typhoon to affect the Marianas this year by AccuWeather's count, after Super Typhoon Champi's Category 5 peak and its pass over Taiwan and southern Japan on October 22 to 24. At the November 3 03:00 UTC advisory In-fa was a Category 1 equivalent (130 km/h sustained), heading west at 11 km/h and forecast to strengthen, with no major landmass in its 48 to 72 hour track. The Japan Meteorological Agency declared Champi extratropical over the East China Sea on October 25, and its remnant crossed Kyushu the next day.

## Elsewhere on the Board

  * **Haiti and the Dominican Republic (observed).** The Pan American Health Organization's October 29 monitoring report relayed Haiti's Civil Protection figures from a week of rain: at least 8 dead, 40 injured, 5 missing and flooding in 27 municipalities; 30 communities were reported cut off in the Dominican Republic on October 28.
  * **Minnesota, October 28 (alert).** A tornado watch and a tornado warning from NWS Twin Cities for southeast Minnesota and west-central Wisconsin, plus severe thunderstorm warnings, late in the season for the Upper Midwest. No survey found.
  * **Eastern New Mexico and the Panhandles, November 1 to 2 (alert).** Albuquerque's late-evening tornado warning for Quay County on November 1, three from Amarillo for the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles overnight, one from Norman for southwest Oklahoma on the evening of November 2, and 30 severe thunderstorm warnings on November 2 as the next system moved in.
  * **The global board, from DisasterAWARE's records for the window:** 2,525 hazard records after de-duplication, 1,872 of them wildfire (286 warning-level incidents and 1,520 satellite detections), 100 flood, 97 earthquake (3 at warning level), 61 conflict, 32 volcano (14 warning-level), 11 tropical cyclone.



## On the Horizon (forecast)

  * **The Southwest.** Flood warnings for the San Juan River and the Four Corners run to November 6 and 7, and the multi-office Southwestern flood warning issued October 31 runs to November 7. Saturated ground across northern Arizona and New Mexico means any further rain floods faster than the first round did.
  * **Murasu inland.** The IMD expected Murasu to weaken to a cyclonic storm by midday November 3 and to bring heavy rain to Telangana (six districts on orange alert) and south Odisha, where Arnab's landslide search is still under way.
  * **In-fa.** Strengthening forecast over the next 24 hours; track to be watched for Japan's Ogasawara Islands.



## What We're Watching Next

  1. NWS damage surveys for the remaining New Mexico and Texas tornado reports, and whether the Santa Fe tornado's rating changes (the Albuquerque Journal reported some damage could have supported EF2).
  2. A consolidated death toll for the Southwest flood from New Mexico's Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, and confirmation of the two Flagstaff deaths reported by local police on November 2 (not yet in the NWS storm-report record).
  3. Murasu's final toll and the IMD's post-landfall assessment, and whether a third system follows in the Bay of Bengal.
  4. The FEMA declaration's upgrade from emergency to major disaster for New Mexico, and whether Arizona's November 2 state emergency becomes a federal request.



## How DisasterAWARE Delivers This

Every product in this brief, from a 30-minute severe thunderstorm warning for one New Mexico county to a cyclone forecast with 11.9 million people in its path, arrives in DisasterAWARE as a geocoded record with its footprint, the population, households and infrastructure inside it, and the issuing agency's own text. Observed impacts, from NWS storm reports to damage surveys, sit alongside the alerts rather than being mixed into them. For operations teams that means a site screen that answers two questions separately: is my facility inside an active warning, and has anything been reported there? The [live flood board](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/floods/>) and the [live tornado board](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/current/tornadoes/>) on Explore show the same feed for the public, by city: [Albuquerque](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/flood-risk/albuquerque-nm/>), [El Paso](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/tornado-risk/el-paso-tx/>), [Phoenix](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/flood-risk/phoenix-az/>), [Tucson](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/flood-risk/tucson-az/>) and [Las Vegas](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/flood-risk/las-vegas-nv/>) all had live warnings this week.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Was there a tornado in Santa Fe in October 2026?**  
Yes. The National Weather Service in Albuquerque confirmed an EF1 tornado with peak winds of 110 mph in the city of Santa Fe on the evening of October 24, 2026. It travelled 1.48 miles from the Via Caballero neighbourhood to the College of Santa Fe campus, damaged ten homes and injured no one.

**How many people died in the New Mexico floods?**  
NWS Albuquerque's storm reports record three deaths between October 23 and 26, 2026, each a person swept away in a vehicle at a flooded crossing: south of Pagosa Junction in Rio Arriba County, north of Agua Fria near Santa Fe, and at Bernardo in Socorro County. The Associated Press reported "at least two" on October 27. Official state totals may differ.

**How unusual were 416 flash flood warnings in October?**  
Very. The NWS issued 416 flash flood warnings nationwide in October 2026, against 156 in October 2025 and between 74 and 245 in each October from 2020 to 2024, per the Iowa Environmental Mesonet's archive of NWS products. The seven Southwest offices issued 149 of them; their previous October high in that period was 68, in 2022.

**What is the difference between a warning and a flood report in this brief?**  
A warning is an alert-tier product: the NWS's forecast that flooding is imminent or occurring in a defined area. A flood report is observed-tier: a Local Storm Report of water over a road, a rescue, a flooded home, filed by spotters, emergency managers and officials. We count and map them separately.

**Did Cyclone Murasu hit the same place as Cyclone Arnab?**  
Nearly. Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast near Narsapur on October 28, 2026; Murasu came ashore about 200 km further south near Ongole in the early hours of November 3, with its forecast wind footprint overlapping the districts Arnab had already soaked.

# Hail and Severe Wind, Live: Two New DisasterAWARE API Endpoints Built From Warnings, Radar and Ground Reports

**Published**: 2026-10-24  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/hail-wind-api  
**Summary**: Two new DisasterAWARE V2 API endpoints, /hail and /wind, deliver every active hail and severe wind hazard as one record: the NWS warning and its versions, the radar hail swath by size band, the ground reports, and an evidence-labelled assessment.

**DisasterAWARE's V2 API now serves live hail and severe wind hazards on two new endpoints,`/hail` and `/wind`.** Each hazard is one record that carries the National Weather Service warning and every version of it, the radar hail swath growing by size band, the spotter and measured reports as they arrive, and an assessment that says plainly what the evidence was: a warning tag alone, a radar signature, or hail on the ground.

A severe thunderstorm is three things to the people who have to act on it: a warning that says what might happen, radar that shows where it is happening, and reports that confirm what did happen. Until now those lived in three feeds with three clocks. The new endpoints join them into a single hazard that changes as the storm does and closes into a record you can query the next day.

## What the endpoints deliver

Hail hazards are DisasterAWARE hazards of type `STORM` with a sub-type of `HAIL`; severe wind hazards carry the sub-type `WIND`. Each is built from the NWS severe thunderstorm warnings carrying a hail tag (or a wind tag or damage threat), the MRMS radar hail swaths, and the ground reports that belong to the same storm. A hazard passes through three stages, and the record shows which one it is in.

  * **Stage 1, the warning arrives.** NWS issues a Severe Thunderstorm Warning with a polygon and tags: expected hail size, wind speed, damage threat. Every version is kept as it is issued, from the original through each continuation to the cancellation or expiry, so the record shows the polygon and the tags as forecasters updated them. A hazard usually opens on the first warning and, at this stage, rests on the warning alone; a hazard can also open on radar alone, and the basis says so.
  * **Stage 2, the storm is observed.** Radar takes over within minutes. MRMS estimates hail size every two minutes, and the record builds the swath of where radar estimates hail of each size has fallen, growing as the storm moves, in six cumulative bands from 1 inch to 2.5 inches. Then the first reports arrive, each with size, place, time and whether the hail was measured or estimated. For wind, the measured gusts and damage reports arrive the same way and build a report footprint.
  * **Stage 3, the record is complete.** When the last warning has expired and radar and reports have gone quiet, the hazard closes. The warning polygons stay as the alert geometry, the observed footprint by hail size becomes the exposure areas, and the assessment states what the evidence was. The next day, once late reports are in, the history record is finalised.



## What is in a record

Every record has the standard V2 hazard fields, with `type` STORM, `severity` WARNING and `category` EVENT. Two GeoJSON collections carry the geometry. `alertGeometry` holds one Feature per linked NWS warning at that warning's current polygon. `exposureAreas` holds where the hazard was actually observed, each Feature labelled with an exposure level: for hail, levels 1 to 6 are the cumulative radar swaths for 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2 and 2.5 inches, and for wind a single level 1 is the footprint of the damage reports and gusts of 58 mph or more. A warning-only hazard has nothing observed yet, and its `exposureAreas` is an empty object rather than null.

Each hail record then carries two blocks:

  * **`hailAssessment`** , the summary: the largest warning hail tag, the largest reported and largest measured hail, the largest swath threshold the radar reached and the radar peak, a best estimate with its source (report or radar, whichever is larger), how long radar saw hail, the counts of reports and of measured reports, the exposure-level scale, why the hazard ended, which sources were consulted and what each observed, and the **hail basis** : `report` when at least one ground report exists, `radar` for a radar signature of 1 inch or more, `warning` when only a tagged warning exists, and `radar_brief` for a radar-only signature that lasted under 10 minutes, published but labelled as unconfirmed.
  * **`hailDetails`** , the evidence: the swath outline and area per size threshold, the radar timeline frame by frame, the swath growth at 10-minute steps showing when each threshold first appeared, every hail report, and every linked warning with its VTEC code, tags, damage threat, current polygon and every version.



Wind records mirror that with `windAssessment` and `windDetails`: the largest warning wind tag, the highest NWS damage threat across the linked warnings (`base`, `considerable` or `destructive`, and null when no warning carries a tag, which is not the same as no threat), the strongest measured gust and the strongest gust of any kind, counts of damage, gust and measured reports, the report timeline, and the **wind basis** : `gust_measured` for a measured gust of 58 mph or more, `damage_reported` for damage reports or an estimated gust at that threshold, and `forecast_only` for a warning with no observed evidence yet.

While a hazard is active its end time is a projection and the record says so. When it ends, the end time becomes the last part's end and `end_basis` says why: the warnings expired, radar went quiet for 30 minutes, reports went quiet, or the hazard was merged into another, in which case the record names the survivor.

## How to query

Both endpoints serve a file rather than a query result. A call with no parameters returns a redirect to the current gzipped NDJSON file with every active hazard, one per line. With parameters, the redirect points at a filtered file and an `X-Match-Count` header says how many hazards it holds. Every redirect carries the time the file was last written, so a client can pass that back as `updated_since` and receive only what changed. The file is rewritten when something changes, at most every two minutes, and if the feed's heartbeat is more than 15 minutes old the endpoint returns a 503 rather than serving stale data.

Filters combine with AND, lists mean "any of", and a misspelled parameter or an unknown value returns a 400 that names the problem rather than an empty file. The common filters are the ones you know from the active hazards endpoint: `uuid`, `type`, `severity`, `category`, `country`, `state`, `name`, time bounds on `started_at`, `created_at` and `updated_at` (on or after) and `ended_at` (on or before), and a `latitude`/`longitude` range. On top of those:
    
    
    # hail confirmed on the ground in Arizona or New Mexico
    GET /hail?hail_basis=report&state=AZ,NM
    
    # any hazard whose best estimate is 1.5 inches or more, changed since your last poll
    GET /hail?min_hail_in=1.5&updated_since=2026-10-21T22:00:00Z
    
    # wind hazards with observed evidence under a considerable or destructive damage threat
    GET /wind?wind_basis=gust_measured,damage_reported&damage_threat=considerable,destructive
    
    # measured gusts of 70 mph or more
    GET /wind?min_gust_mph=70
    

`min_reported_hail_in` filters on ground reports alone, ignoring radar. `scope=active` is the only scope today; the historical scope, which will serve the finalised records, returns a 501 that names the scopes available until it ships.

Get live hail and wind hazards into your systems

The /hail and /wind endpoints deliver each hazard with its warnings, radar swaths, ground reports and an evidence-labelled assessment, refreshed as the storm evolves.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/sign-up?intent=free-trial&source=mid-article-cta&article=hail-wind-api>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=hail-wind-api>)

## One convective day, one record

Take one convective day, 21 October 2026, across the Southwest. Between noon UTC that day and noon the next, the feeds carried 75 hail hazards and 20 severe wind hazards across Arizona, California, Maine, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah: 90 NWS warnings in 245 versions, 529 radar frames, 140 swath polygons covering about 3,450 km² of hail of 1 inch or more, 35 hail reports of which 19 were measured, and 9 wind reports. Of the hail hazards, 9 rested on ground reports, 21 on a persistent radar signature, 10 on a brief one, and 35 on a warning tag alone, which is the honest shape of a hail day: most warnings never get a confirmed stone.

The richest record was the Phoenix storm. It opened at 22:04 UTC on a Phoenix-office warning, and over the next 3 hours 39 minutes six warnings from the Phoenix and Flagstaff offices, in 19 versions, followed it north-east past Payson. Radar first saw 1-inch hail at 22:18 UTC; the first ground report followed within seven minutes. By the time the last warning expired at 01:43 UTC the record held 68 radar frames, a swath of 628 km² at 1 inch narrowing to 5 km² at 2.5 inches, and 18 reports, nine of them measured. The assessment reads like this: largest warning tag 2.75 inches, radar peak 2.98 inches, largest reported 2 inches, largest measured 1.5 inches, best estimate 2.98 inches from radar, basis `report`, ended because the warning expired.

_The Phoenix hail hazard three minutes before its last warning expired: the radar swath by size band, every hail report (dark rings are measured), and the last warning polygon still in force. Rendered from the record's own geometry._

The wind side of the same day looked different, as it usually does. Of the 20 wind hazards, 11 rested on a warning alone, 6 on damage reports and 3 on a measured gust. The strongest gust was 72 mph, measured. The record below, near Safford in Graham County, shows what a wind hazard carries: a Tucson-office warning tagged for 70 mph winds with a destructive damage threat, a measured 61 mph gust inside it, and the small level-1 footprint of that evidence.

_A severe wind hazard near Safford, Arizona: the warning polygon, the measured gust that confirmed it, and the report footprint that becomes the hazard's exposure area._

## Who it is for

  * **Insurance and claims teams** get, for each storm, the warning that triggered coverage questions, the radar-estimated swath of hail by size, and the reports that confirm it, with every number labelled measured, reported or radar-estimated.
  * **Supply chain and facilities teams** can screen sites against the warning polygons while the storm is live and against the observed footprint afterwards, and tell the two apart.
  * **Model validation teams** get the full evidence chain: every warning version, every radar frame, the swath growth in 10-minute steps, and the reports, so a hail model can be scored against what was observed rather than what was warned.
  * **Emergency managers** see which warnings have been confirmed on the ground and which have not, and when each hazard actually ended.



## How to get access

The hail and wind feeds need their own access on your DisasterAWARE API credential; a token that works on the other hazard endpoints will not necessarily work here. Contact your sales contact or support@disasteraware.com to have it added, or to talk about hail and wind data if you do not have API access today. The [hail](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-hail>) and [wind](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-wind>) documentation pages carry the full parameter reference, the lifecycle rules and a complete sample record for each feed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What do the /hail and /wind endpoints return?**  
Every active hail or severe wind hazard DisasterAWARE is tracking, one record per hazard, as gzipped NDJSON. Each record carries the linked NWS warnings with every version, the radar hail swath by size band (hail), the ground reports, the observed footprint as exposure areas, and an assessment block that labels the evidence.

**How do I know whether a hazard is confirmed?**  
Read the basis. For hail, `hail_basis` is `report` when hail was reported on the ground, `radar` for a radar signature of 1 inch or more, `warning` when only a tagged warning exists, and `radar_brief` for a short radar-only signature that is published but labelled unconfirmed. For wind, `wind_basis` is `gust_measured`, `damage_reported` or `forecast_only`.

**How fresh is the feed?**  
The file is rewritten when something changes, at most every two minutes, and every redirect carries the time it was last written. If the feed's heartbeat is more than 15 minutes old the endpoint returns a 503 rather than stale data.

**What happens when a hazard ends?**  
It leaves the active file on the first write after it ends and moves to the history archive. Its final record states why it ended and, the next day, is finalised once late reports have arrived. A historical scope for those records is planned; until it ships, a client that needs to detect endings compares successive files.

**Are DisasterAWARE's existing STORM and TORNADO records included?**  
No. The two feeds return only hazards of type STORM with the HAIL or WIND sub-type. The general active hazards endpoint is unchanged.

**Do I need new credentials?**  
You need the hail or wind feed access added to your existing DisasterAWARE API credential. Contact your sales contact or support@disasteraware.com to have it added.

## Related Reading

  * [Requesting Hail Hazards](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-hail>) and [Requesting Wind Hazards](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-wind>)
  * [Hail Sample](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/hazard-samples/hail-sample>) and [Severe Wind Sample](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/hazard-samples/wind-sample>)
  * [Severe Convective Storm Data](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/severe-convective-storm-data>)
  * [Ask What Is Happening Right Now: DisasterAWARE's Live Hazards MCP Server](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/live-hazards-mcp-server>)

# TornadoAWARE Is Live: A Free Morning Report on Tornado Risk at the Places You Care About

**Published**: 2026-10-23  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/tornadoaware-launch  
**Summary**: TornadoAWARE is a free email service from DisasterAWARE. Add up to five places and get a morning report on what tornado and severe-weather activity touched them, with the history of what has hit there before. Launched 23 October 2026.

**TornadoAWARE is a free email service from DisasterAWARE for individuals. Add up to five places, and each morning something happens there you get a report on what tornado and severe-weather activity touched them, with the history of what has hit there before.** It launched today at [explore.disasteraware.com/tornadoaware](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/tornadoaware/?utm_source=explore&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=launch-announcement>).

Most people with a parent in Tulsa, a student in Norman and a house in Moore find out what happened at those places the same way everyone else does: a news alert about somewhere nearby, a group text, a search the next morning. TornadoAWARE answers the narrower question you actually have: did a warning cover _my_ places, how close did it come, and what has this town seen before?

## What you get

  * **A morning report, by 7 am your time.** Which of your places sit inside an active tornado warning, severe thunderstorm warning or watch, how far the hazard edge is from each, and what changed since yesterday. By default it arrives only when something is happening or has changed at your places; tick one option at sign-up and you get it on quiet days too, when it takes one glance: one status chip per place.
  * **The map and the official detail.** Each active hazard comes with the National Weather Service polygon drawn on a map with your place marked, the distance in miles to the hazard edge rather than "near", and whether NWS called the tornado radar-indicated or observed.
  * **Your places' history.** How many tornado warnings have covered each place since 2014, the nearest surveyed damage path, the strongest rating, and the months it happens. Plainly written, so "does my town get tornadoes?" has an answer.
  * **Five places, free.** Home, work, school, a parent's house. A city or a landmark works as well as a street address; the service only needs a point to measure from, and for a city it treats the whole city as your place.
  * **Control in every email.** A one-click unsubscribe link and a manage link where you can change places, pause, or delete your data. Nothing is saved until you confirm your email.



## What a report looks like

The landing page shows a real one, built from the NWS Tornado Warning that covered Moore, Oklahoma, on 10 March 2026, for a place labelled "Home". The subject line reads "Tue Mar 10: Tornado Warning — Home (Moore, OK)". The report says that Home was inside the warning polygon, not nearby, that NWS called the tornado radar-indicated, and that the warning was new since the day before. The map is the NWS polygon with the place marked on it. The report closes with one line of history: 16 tornado warnings within 15 miles of that place since 2014.

The full sample, with each element explained, is on the landing page under "See a sample report".

## Context, not a siren

This part matters, so here it is in the service's own words: "TornadoAWARE is context, not a siren. Wireless Emergency Alerts, NOAA Weather Radio and local sirens are the official warnings and are faster in the first minutes — we are typically a few minutes behind the National Weather Service."

Keep your phone's emergency alerts on. TornadoAWARE is the report that tells you, the next morning, what those warnings meant for the places you named.

Get your morning tornado report, free

Add up to five places, confirm your email, and TornadoAWARE tells you each morning something happens what tornado and severe-weather activity touched them.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/sign-up?intent=free-trial&source=mid-article-cta&article=tornadoaware-launch>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=tornadoaware-launch>)

## Where the data comes from

TornadoAWARE runs on the DisasterAWARE platform, the hazard-intelligence system built by DisasterIQ and used by Pacific Disaster Center, emergency managers and enterprises worldwide. The warnings, watches and history come from the National Weather Service, NOAA's Storm Prediction Center, the NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit and USGS. The same platform powers our [tornado data](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/tornado-data>) and [tornado intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/tornado-intelligence>) pages. On launch day the landing page's live counter stood at more than 1,800 tornado warnings issued in the United States so far in 2026.

Your places are used only to match hazards to them.

## How to sign up

  1. Go to [explore.disasteraware.com/tornadoaware](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/tornadoaware/?utm_source=explore&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=launch-announcement>) and choose "Get my daily report — free".
  2. Enter your email and up to five places: a city, an address, a postal code or a landmark.
  3. Confirm your email from the message that arrives. Nothing is saved until you click the link.



Reports then arrive every morning something is active or has changed at your places, or every morning if you tick that option. Everything you need to change places, pause or stop is in the footer of every email.

## What is coming

Alerts are next: when a warning newly covers one of your places, escalates or clears, one email, bundled and capped, and quiet overnight unless it is a tornado warning. That is being built now and is coming this season. Until it is live, the morning report carries everything that happened at your places.

TornadoAWARE is the first of a family. FloodAWARE, the same morning report for flash floods, coastal floods and high surf, is the next one planned.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is TornadoAWARE?**  
A free email service from DisasterAWARE. You add up to five places, confirm your email, and by 7 am your time you get a report on what tornado and severe-weather activity touched those places, with the history of what has hit there since 2014. It arrives on mornings when something is active or has changed, or every morning if you choose.

**Is TornadoAWARE an official warning service?**  
No. It is context, not a siren. Wireless Emergency Alerts, NOAA Weather Radio and local sirens are the official warnings and are faster in the first minutes; TornadoAWARE is typically a few minutes behind the National Weather Service.

**Do I need to give a street address?**  
No. A city, a neighbourhood, a landmark or a postal code works. For a city, the whole city is treated as your place, so you are covered if any part of it is in a warning.

**Does TornadoAWARE send alerts during a storm?**  
Not yet. Alerts when a warning newly covers one of your places are coming this season. Today the service is the morning report.

**Is it really free?**  
Yes, for up to five places. A paid plan for more places is being considered, and the sign-up form asks whether you would use one.

**How do I stop the emails?**  
Every email has a one-click unsubscribe link and a manage link where you can change places, pause, or delete your data.
