# Ask What Is Happening Right Now: DisasterAWARE's Live Hazards MCP Server

**Published**: 2026-10-23  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/live-hazards-mcp-server  
**Summary**: DisasterAWARE's Live Hazards MCP server connects AI assistants to the live hazard feed: about 1,000 active hazards worldwide with official warning text, footprints and exposure. Ask what is happening now, screen your own sites, and see what changed.

**DisasterAWARE's Live Hazards MCP server connects the AI assistant you already use to DisasterAWARE's live hazard feed: every active hazard worldwide, with its official warning text, its footprint, and the people, hospitals, schools and capital exposed inside it.** You ask in plain language: "Which of our twelve ports are inside an active hazard right now, worst first?" The assistant screens your list against every live footprint, ranks what it finds and tells you exactly how fresh the picture is.

It is the live companion of the [Historical Hazards MCP server](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-hazards-mcp-server>) we introduced earlier this month. Connect both and one conversation can answer "what is happening now" and "what happened here before".

## What an MCP server is

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to outside data and tools. An MCP server tells the assistant what it can look up and how; the assistant decides which lookups a question needs, runs them and reads the results before it answers.

The Live Hazards MCP server gives an assistant six purpose-built tools over the live feed: one that describes what the feed holds right now and how fresh it is, one that finds and ranks active hazards by type, severity, country, state or province, map window, distance from a point, time or people exposed, one that screens your own sites, routes or areas against every active footprint, one that opens a single hazard with its official text and exposure, one that reports what is new and what changed since a time, and one for counts and exposure totals by type, severity, country, state, urgency, certainty or issuer. You never call these yourself. Knowing they exist simply helps you ask better questions.

## What the assistant can reach

The live feed holds **every active hazard DisasterAWARE tracks, worldwide: about 1,000 at any moment across some 20 hazard types.** Floods, wildfires, tropical cyclones, severe weather, high wind, winter storms, extreme temperatures, earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides, drought, marine and surf hazards, disease outbreaks and smoke, and security incidents.

For each hazard the assistant can read:

  * **The official alert.** The headline, description and instruction as the issuing agency wrote them, who issued it, how urgent and how certain it is, when it started, when it was last updated, and when it is expected to end or expire.
  * **The footprint.** The official alert polygon for almost every record, which is what your sites, routes and areas are screened against.
  * **The exposure inside it.** Modelled population by age group, households, hospitals, schools and capital value, by country and administrative area, and the states, provinces or regions the footprint touches.
  * **The clock.** The feed is regenerated every few minutes. Every answer states the time of the feed it came from and says so plainly if that feed is older than it should be.



What it does not hold: hazards that have ended, which leave the feed and live on in the [historical archive](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-hazard-data-enhancements>), and the measurements gathered after an event, such as gauge crests, damage surveys and burned acres, which arrive with the historical enhancement.

## What makes it different

  * **It answers "right now", with a timestamp.** Every answer carries the time of the feed generation it came from. If the feed is stale, the assistant says so instead of pretending.
  * **It screens your assets, not just the map.** Paste a list of sites with coordinates, or a route or area as GeoJSON, add a buffer if you want one, and the assistant returns the hazards intersecting each location, worst first, or the distance to the nearest active footprint.
  * **It quotes the official instruction.** Ask what the warning covering a city says you should do and you get the issuing agency's own instruction text, not a paraphrase.
  * **It counts people and assets, by country and state.** Rankings by people, hospitals, schools or capital exposed, grouped the way you ask.
  * **It is honest about what a record is.** Records are alerts, so one storm can produce several of them, and the assistant says so when it counts.
  * **It pairs with the archive.** With both servers connected, the assistant can take a hazard that is active now and ask the historical archive what that place has seen before.
  * **Setup is documented for the assistants you already use,** and sign-in is through your DisasterAWARE account in the browser. You never paste a password or key into the assistant.



## Example questions and answers

Every answer below was produced from one generation of the live feed, timestamped 20:32 UTC on 23 October 2026, and checked independently against the DisasterAWARE Active Hazards API. The feed changes every few minutes, so the same questions give different answers today. That is the point.

### 1\. The world right now

**Q: What is happening in the world right now, by hazard type and severity?**

**A:** The feed holds 1,077 active hazard records of 20 types touching 177 countries. Wildfire records lead with 439, then floods 195, high wind 113, severe weather 102, severe thunderstorms 44, landslides 39 and extreme temperatures 28, down to five tropical cyclones and four earthquakes. By severity: 224 Warnings, 176 Watches, 572 Advisories and 105 Information records. Almost every record carries an official footprint, 973 were updated in the last 24 hours and more than 300 in the last hour.

_Why it matters:_ a duty officer or analyst gets the shape of the whole day in one answer, with the feed time attached, before drilling into any of it.

### 2\. Where the Warnings are

**Q: Which countries have the most active Warnings?**

**A:** The United States with 88 active Warning records, then Ecuador and Kazakhstan with 15 each, Russia with 10, and Peru, the United Kingdom and Canada with 9 each. These are alert records, often one per forecast office or region, so they describe how heavily a country is being warned rather than how many events it has.

_Why it matters:_ corporate security and travel-risk teams see at a glance where official agencies are issuing the most warnings right now.

### 3\. Twelve ports, worst first

**Q: Which of these ports are inside an active hazard right now, worst first?** (Shanghai, Singapore, Rotterdam, Los Angeles, Houston, Manila, Mumbai, Santos, Durban, Tokyo, Kaohsiung and Miami, with coordinates.)

**A:** Nine of the twelve sit inside at least one active footprint. Shanghai, Tokyo and Kaohsiung are all inside the alert area of Typhoon Champi. Santos is inside five overlapping severe thunderstorm records from Brazil's national weather service, two of them Warnings: one in force now, the others issued for the next two days. Manila lies inside the warning footprint for Taal volcano, from a Tokyo Volcanic Ash Advisory Centre report of 21 October. Los Angeles is inside a coastal flood advisory for the central and northern California coast that takes effect on 24 October and runs through 29 October. Rotterdam is under a Dutch coastal wind advisory. Houston, Miami and Rotterdam also sit inside continent-scale drought monitor records, which the assistant lists but ranks below the weather warnings. Singapore, Mumbai and Durban are clear. With a 50 km buffer, Singapore picks up a severe weather warning for Peninsular Malaysia whose edge is 29 km away, and Miami picks up four coastal records, among them a coastal flood warning for the Upper Keys and a gale watch for the Florida east coast. Mumbai stays clear: the nearest active footprint, a flood watch in Gujarat, is more than 500 km away.

_Why it matters:_ a logistics control tower or supply-chain team screens its own network against the live picture in seconds, and the "five records at Santos" result shows why the assistant reports alerts rather than counting storms.

### 4\. What the official warning says

**Q: What does the official warning covering Santos say I should do?**

**A:** Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology (INMET) issued a Severe Thunderstorm Warning for southern and south-eastern Brazil at 14:58 UTC on 23 October. Urgency Future, certainty Likely, in force from 03:00 UTC on 24 October (just after midnight local time) until 02:59 UTC on 25 October. The record describes very heavy rain of 30 to 60 mm per hour, winds of 60 to 100 km/h and hail, with power outages, crop and structural damage, downed trees and localised flooding expected. Its instruction tells people not to shelter under trees during gusts, to avoid parking near transmission towers or large billboards, to switch off appliances and the main power panel if possible, and gives the civil defence and fire brigade numbers. About 48.9 million people live inside the warning area.

_Why it matters:_ operations and HR teams get the agency's own guidance, with its validity window, for the place they are responsible for, without hunting for the bulletin.

### 5\. Every active tropical cyclone

**Q: List every active tropical cyclone and the countries it exposes.**

**A:** Five. Typhoon Champi, north-east of Taiwan, the equivalent of a Category 3 hurricane in the Joint Typhoon Warning Center's forecast issued at 15:00 UTC, with sustained winds of 185 km/h (115 mph) and gusts to 232 km/h (144 mph): about 10.2 million people exposed, almost all in Taiwan and about 55,000 in Japan, with 168 hospitals and 287 schools inside the alert area. Hurricane Vance in the eastern Pacific off Mexico, with a few hundred people in its area. Tropical Storm In-Fa under a Warning near the Marshall Islands, with a few hundred people exposed. Tropical Cyclone Agueda over open ocean in the south-west Indian Ocean, exposing no one. And Post-Tropical Cyclone Josephine off Canada, whose record was minutes from expiring.

_Why it matters:_ insurers, shippers and travel-risk teams get the live storm list with exposure attached, down to the hospitals and schools inside a typhoon's alert area.

Put the live hazard picture in your AI assistant

The Live Hazards MCP server answers what is happening right now, anywhere, from DisasterAWARE's live feed, and screens your own sites and routes against every active footprint.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/sign-up?intent=free-trial&source=mid-article-cta&article=live-hazards-mcp-server>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=live-hazards-mcp-server>)

### 6\. What changed since this morning

**Q: What changed in the last six hours?**

**A:** 230 new hazard records and 400 updated ones. The new records were led by wildfire advisories (96), landslide advisories (24), wildfire warnings (23), high wind advisories (15) and severe weather advisories and watches (23 together), plus six new flood warnings. The biggest by people exposed were a new wind alert covering multiple districts of Germany (about 66 million people), a new heavy rain advisory for Tamil Nadu and Karaikal in India (about 41 million) and an updated wind advisory across French departments (about 39 million). The assistant also says what it cannot see: hazards that ended in those six hours have already left the feed, so it does not list them yet.

_Why it matters:_ a duty officer coming on shift gets the delta, not the whole board, and knows which part of the delta the feed cannot show.

### 7\. People under flood warnings, by country

**Q: How many people are under flood warnings right now, by country?**

**A:** Colombia leads with about 18.8 million people inside one flood warning covering the north-west of the country, an area holding 1,044 hospitals. A single Central American flood warning exposes about 14.6 million people, almost all of them in Guatemala, with small areas of Honduras and Mexico inside its footprint. The Dominican Republic has about 10.7 million people under a flood warning and Bolivia about 7.8 million. The United States has eight flood warning records from National Weather Service offices, from the Yukon Delta coast to the Florida Keys, exposing about 3 million people between them, most of them under a coastal flood warning for the Southern California coast.

_Why it matters:_ humanitarian, insurance and public-sector teams see where flood warnings touch the most people right now, and can open any record for the agency text and the exposure by administrative area.

### 8\. Live and history in one conversation

**Q: Any earthquake or volcano activity in the last 24 hours, and has that area seen this before?** (both servers connected)

**A:** From the live feed: a Warning for Krakatau in Indonesia, an Advisory for Manam in Papua New Guinea, a magnitude 5.7 earthquake under a Watch 61 km west-north-west of Leni in Italy's Aeolian Islands, a magnitude 5.2 nearby off Malfa with about 14,400 people in its area, and a magnitude 5.1 off Noda in Japan with about 39,900 people and two hospitals. From the historical archive: within 100 km of today's Aeolian epicentre there have been four earthquakes of magnitude 5 or greater since 2000, the strongest a magnitude 6.0 in September 2002 north of Santa Flavia and a 5.8 off Ustica in October 2016. Today's 5.7 is the third strongest in that stretch of the Tyrrhenian in a quarter century.

_Why it matters:_ the live server gives the event, the historical server gives the context, and the assistant combines them without you switching tools.

## How it is best used

  * **Duty officers and security operations centres:** the picture at shift start, every new Warning in a region since a time, and the official instruction for the places you are responsible for.
  * **Supply chain, logistics and control towers:** screen supplier sites, ports, routes and lanes against every active footprint, with a buffer, worst first.
  * **Insurance and claims:** which insured locations are inside an active hazard now, how many people and assets are exposed, and, with the historical server, what that place has seen before.
  * **Travel risk, HR and facilities:** what is active around an office, a plant or a traveller, who issued it, and when it expires.
  * **Analysts and journalists:** rankings and counts by country, state, type and severity, with the feed time attached.



A few habits get the best answers:

  * **Start with coverage.** "What is in the live feed right now?" tells the assistant what it is working with and how fresh it is.
  * **Give coordinates for your sites.** A list of names with latitude and longitude, or a GeoJSON line or polygon, is screened exactly. A place name alone is matched against the feed's country and region names.
  * **Remember that records are alerts.** One real storm can produce several records, one per office or region. Ask for "the biggest" or "the worst" rather than "how many storms".
  * **Exposure is modelled.** People, hospital and capital figures are estimates for the footprint, not observed impacts.
  * **Ask about the ones that are missing.** If a hazard you expect is not there, it may have ended; ask the Historical Hazards server.



The MCP server is built for answering questions. To bring the live records themselves into your own systems, use the [Active Hazards API](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-active-hazards>), which serves the same feed, or have updates pushed to you by webhook.

## How to get started

  1. **Add the MCP access permission to your DisasterAWARE account.** It is separate from DisasterAWARE web or API access, and the same permission covers the Live and the Historical server. Ask your DisasterAWARE administrator or your PDC account representative to add it.
  2. **Add the server to your assistant.** Follow the setup steps in the [Live Hazards MCP documentation](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/mcp-server/live-hazards-mcp>), then sign in with your DisasterAWARE account when the sign-in page opens.
  3. **Ask a question.** Start with "What is in the live feed right now?" and go from there.



The documentation has setup steps for Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT and Cursor, the full list of example questions, and tips for accurate answers.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the DisasterAWARE Live Hazards MCP server?**  
It is a Model Context Protocol server that connects AI assistants to DisasterAWARE's live hazard feed: about 1,000 active hazards worldwide across some 20 hazard types, each with its official warning text, footprint and modelled exposure. You ask in plain language and the assistant finds, ranks, screens and summarises the live picture, and tells you how fresh it is.

**How current is the data?**  
The feed is regenerated every few minutes, and every answer states the time of the feed generation it came from. If the feed is older than it should be, the assistant says so.

**Can I screen my own sites or routes?**  
Yes. Paste a list of sites with coordinates, or a route or area as GeoJSON, and optionally a buffer distance. The assistant returns the hazards whose footprint intersects each location, worst first, or the distance to the nearest active footprint when none does.

**How is it different from the Historical Hazards MCP server?**  
The live server holds what is active right now and nothing that has ended. The historical server holds the archive of past hazards with the measurements gathered after each event. The same access permission covers both, and with both connected the assistant can answer live and historical questions in one conversation.

**Which AI assistants can I use with it?**  
The documentation has setup steps for Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT and Cursor. Other assistants that support remote MCP servers with OAuth sign-in can also connect.

**Are the exposure numbers observed impacts?**  
No. Population, household, hospital, school and capital figures are modelled estimates for what lies inside each hazard's footprint. They tell you what is exposed, not what has been damaged.

# Ask Decades of Hazard History in Plain Language: DisasterAWARE's Historical Hazards MCP Server

**Published**: 2026-10-19  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-hazards-mcp-server  
**Summary**: DisasterAWARE's Historical Hazards MCP server connects AI assistants to nearly 680,000 hazard records. Ask in plain language and get counts, rankings and the gauge, station or survey behind each number.

**DisasterAWARE's Historical Hazards MCP server connects the AI assistant you already use to DisasterAWARE's historical hazard archive.** You ask a question in plain language: "Which flood rose highest during Hurricane Harvey, and at which gauge?" The assistant runs the searches, counts, rankings and lookups against the archive and explains the answer, including where each number comes from.

There is no query language to learn and no GIS to run. The assistant works out which filters, places, dates and measures your question needs, and you can keep asking follow-ups until you have what you came for.

## What an MCP server is

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to outside data and tools. An MCP server tells the assistant what it can look up and how; the assistant decides which lookups a question needs, runs them and reads the results before it answers.

The Historical Hazards MCP server gives an assistant a set of purpose-built tools over the archive: one that describes what the archive contains, one that lists the measurements available for each hazard type, one that finds and sorts events by any filter or measurement, one for counts, totals, averages, percentiles and rankings, one that builds a hazard history for a place, and two that open a single event and the evidence behind its numbers. You never call these yourself. Knowing they exist simply helps you ask better questions.

## What the assistant can reach

The archive holds **nearly 680,000 historical hazard records across about 30 hazard types** : earthquakes, floods, wildfires, tropical cyclones, tornadoes, severe storms, winter storms, extreme temperatures, volcanoes, tsunamis, landslides, smoke and more.

Hundreds of thousands of those records are **enhanced** with what was measured and reported after the event, from NOAA, the National Weather Service, USGS, FEMA, NIFC and other agencies, satellites and monitoring networks:

  * **Floods:** river gauge peaks above flood stage and the NWS flood category reached, surveyed high-water marks and depths, NOAA Storm Events deaths and damage.
  * **Wildfires:** final burned acres, fire duration, biggest one-day growth, structures threatened and destroyed, suppression cost, evacuations, and the smoke each fire produced.
  * **Tornadoes, hail and wind:** NWS damage-survey paths and EF ratings, deaths and injuries, measured, reported and radar-estimated hail, and measured and estimated gusts.
  * **Tropical cyclones:** peak wind and lowest pressure, track length, landfalls, and, for storms that affected the United States or its territories from 2023, post-storm station measurements of storm tide, rainfall and gusts.
  * **Earthquakes:** USGS ShakeMap intensity and shaking footprint, and deaths, injuries and damage where NOAA records them.
  * **Smoke:** nearly 35,000 smoke events with their density and duration and, where monitors exist, ground air-quality readings (preliminary EPA AirNow data).



Nearly every tornado record and about two thirds of flood and severe thunderstorm records are enhanced, every wildfire record states what kind of evidence it rests on, and modeled population and economic exposure is available on about 260,000 records. Coverage differs by hazard: tornado, hail, wind and flood enhancements come from US agency data, while earthquake and tropical cyclone enhancements are worldwide (cyclone station reports cover the United States and its territories). For the hazard-by-hazard detail, see [What's Inside DisasterAWARE's Enhanced Historical Hazard Data](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-hazard-data-enhancements>).

## What makes it different

  * **Plain-language questions over a deep, sourced archive.** Ask the way you would ask a colleague. The assistant handles place codes, date windows and thresholds.
  * **It answers the "where" behind a number.** Ask for the highest flood and you get the river gauge that recorded it; ask for the strongest gust and you get the station.
  * **It shows provenance.** Every figure can be traced to its source: a NOAA Storm Events entry, an NWS damage survey, a USGS gauge, a post-storm station report. Hail and gust values say whether they were measured, reported or estimated from radar.
  * **Totals are honest.** One storm often produces several overlapping warnings. When the assistant adds up losses, deaths or insurance payments, each item of evidence is counted once, so a storm with five warnings is not counted five times.
  * **Setup is documented for the assistants you already use.** The documentation has setup steps for Claude (claude.ai and the Claude desktop app), Claude Code, ChatGPT and Cursor.
  * **Access is secure.** You sign in with your DisasterAWARE account on a DisasterAWARE sign-in page in your browser. You never paste a password or key into the assistant.



## Example questions and answers

Every answer below was produced from the archive and checked against the DisasterAWARE Historical Hazards API in October 2026. The archive is rebuilt periodically and enhancement continues after each event, so later answers can differ slightly.

### 1\. One question, a whole disaster's footprint

**Q: Everything that happened in Texas during Hurricane Harvey, August 25 to September 5, 2017, by hazard type.**

**A:** The archive holds 299 flood records, 63 tornado records, 16 marine warning records and one smoke event that began in Texas in that window. Each flood and tornado record is an alert, such as a flash flood warning or a tornado warning, so the counts describe how the event was warned rather than a count of separate floods or tornadoes.

_Why it matters:_ emergency managers and analysts get the full shape of a past disaster in seconds, as a starting point for after-action reviews and comparisons with the next event.

### 2\. The gauge behind the headline

**Q: During Harvey, which Texas flood rose highest above flood stage, and at which gauge?**

**A:** The San Bernard River near Boling. The gauge crested at 43.79 feet late on August 31, 2017 (local time), 25.79 feet above its 18-foot flood stage, in the Major flood category. It is the highest crest in the NWS crest history for that gauge, above the previous record of 42.61 feet from October 1998.

_Why it matters:_ insurance and risk teams can tie a loss to a specific measured peak at a specific place, and see how it ranks against that gauge's own history.

### 3\. Two sources, one tornado

**Q: How many people did the Greenfield, Iowa, tornado of May 21, 2024, kill, and where does that figure come from?**

**A:** Five deaths and 35 injuries, according to the NWS damage survey, which maps one continuous EF4 path 43 miles long and up to 1,600 yards wide. NOAA's Storm Events database splits the same tornado into four county segments. Two are short entries in Page and Taylor counties, under two miles together. The other two carry the toll: an EF3 segment in Adams County (24.8 miles, one death) and an EF4 segment in Adair County, which includes Greenfield (15.7 miles, four deaths, 35 injuries and $30 million in property damage). The sources agree on the toll and slice the path differently, and the archive record carries both.

_Why it matters:_ underwriters and analysts can see which source a casualty, rating or damage figure comes from before they compare events or attribute losses by county.

### 4\. A storm that never made landfall, measured station by station

**Q: Hurricane Lee did not make a tropical landfall in the United States in 2023. What did the NWS post-storm station network record?**

**A:** Reports from three NWS forecast offices in New England list a highest gust of 58 knots (67 mph) at Matinicus Rock, Maine; a water level 1.62 feet above the normal high-tide line at Chatham, Massachusetts; 6.5 inches of rain near Steuben, Maine; and a lowest measured station pressure of 981.9 mb at Plum Island, Massachusetts (Eastport, Maine, logged an estimated 981.3 mb).

_Why it matters:_ supply chain and facilities teams see what a passing storm actually did at the coast and inland, even when the landfall headline was elsewhere.

### 5\. Rankings, with the right unit

**Q: Which states had the most tornado alert records in 2024?**

**A:** Texas with 272, Florida 200, Oklahoma 170, Missouri 154 and Illinois 141. These are tornado records, mostly NWS tornado warnings and the confirmed touchdowns under them, so one tornado can appear on several records and a warning can be issued for a tornado that never touched down.

_Why it matters:_ corporate security and site-selection teams get a quick read on where tornado warnings disrupt operations most often, without mistaking alerts for tornadoes.

Put decades of hazard history in your AI assistant

The Historical Hazards MCP server answers questions about floods, storms, fires, earthquakes and cyclones from DisasterAWARE's enhanced archive, with the source behind every number.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/sign-up?intent=free-trial&source=mid-article-cta&article=historical-hazards-mcp-server>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=historical-hazards-mcp-server>)

### 6\. Money questions, counted once

**Q: Rank the top states by FEMA flood insurance building payments for 2017 floods.**

**A:** Texas, about $6.86 billion; Florida, about $615 million; Louisiana, about $77 million, counting the payments the archive ties to each state's 2017 flood records. These totals are de-duplicated: a flood insurance claim that falls under several overlapping flood warnings is counted once. Adding up every warning's claims without that step would give Texas more than $339 billion, roughly fifty times the real figure. Payments the archive cannot tie to a flood record are left out, so these are not FEMA's own state totals.

_Why it matters:_ insurance and public-sector analysts get loss rankings they can rely on, and a clear demonstration of why counting overlapping alerts naively goes wrong.

### 7\. Smoke and air quality, down to the monitor

**Q: What was the worst smoke event by air quality in California in 2020, and which monitoring station recorded it?**

**A:** Seven California smoke events in 2020 reached the top of the US Air Quality Index scale (500, Hazardous) on preliminary EPA AirNow readings. The highest daily (24-hour) fine-particle reading at a California monitor was 487.4 µg/m³ of PM2.5, at Mammoth Lakes on October 17, 2020, in smoke observed from October 14 to 22.

_Why it matters:_ health, facilities and business-continuity planners can find the worst air-quality days for a region and the monitor behind each one.

### 8\. Hazard history for a site

**Q: How many hazard records of each type fall within 50 km of the Port of Houston since 2014, and in which months do floods peak?**

**A:** Floods dominate, with 733 flood records since 2014, concentrated in August and May, followed by September. There are 70 tornado records, 27 of them in 2017, the year of Harvey, and 72 severe thunderstorm records, most of them in May.

_Tip:_ tornado records begin in 2014, and record counts reflect how often warnings were issued, so a window starting in 2014 compares like with like across hazard types.

_Why it matters:_ site-selection, logistics and insurance teams get a defensible first look at a facility's hazard history and seasonality before they commission deeper work.

## How it is best used

  * **Insurance and risk teams:** loss history and hazard climatology for a location or portfolio region. "What's the worst that has happened here, and how often?"
  * **Corporate security, supply chain and site selection:** hazard profiles for facilities and routes, and the months that matter where.
  * **Emergency managers and planners:** after-action context ("how did this event compare with past ones?"), recurring patterns, and the population and capital exposed.
  * **Analysts, researchers and journalists:** fast answers with the evidence attached, ready to check.



A few habits get the best answers:

  * **Start broad, then narrow.** Ask what the archive contains, or for a hazard profile of a place, then narrow by place, time window and measure.
  * **Ask where a number came from.** At any point, ask for the source of a death toll, a damage figure or a maximum, and for the list behind it: the gauges, stations or survey paths.
  * **Count fires as confirmed fires.** Wildfire records include satellite detections and fire-weather alerts, so ask for confirmed fires when you want to know how many fires there were.
  * **Remember that records are alerts.** One real storm can produce several records. Totals of damage, deaths and payments are already de-duplicated; counts of records describe alerting.



The MCP server is built for answering questions. To bring the records themselves into your own systems or analysis pipelines, use the [Historical Hazards API](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-historical-hazards>), which serves the same archive with every enhancement.

  1. **Add the MCP access permission to your DisasterAWARE account.** It is separate from DisasterAWARE web or API access. Ask your DisasterAWARE administrator or your PDC account representative to add it.
  2. **Add the server to your assistant.** Follow the setup steps for your assistant in the [Historical Hazards MCP documentation](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/mcp-server/historical-hazards-mcp>), then sign in with your DisasterAWARE account when the sign-in page opens.
  3. **Ask a question.** Start with "What does the historical hazards archive contain?" and go from there.

# What's Inside DisasterAWARE's Enhanced Historical Hazard Data, Hazard by Hazard

**Published**: 2026-10-19  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/historical-hazard-data-enhancements  
**Summary**: A hazard-by-hazard guide to the enhancements in DisasterAWARE's historical hazard archive: what each record carries, where it comes from, where it applies, and how far back it goes.

**DisasterAWARE's historical hazard archive holds nearly 680,000 records across about 30 hazard types** , from earthquakes and floods to wildfires, tornadoes and tropical cyclones. Every record carries the basics: what happened, where, when, how severe the alert was and, for most, the alert footprint. For the hazards where authoritative post-event data exists, records also carry an **enhancement** : the surveys, gauges, radar, claims and agency records that describe what actually happened on the ground.

This guide walks through those enhancements one hazard at a time: what each one contains, which source it comes from, where in the world it applies, and how far back it goes. The short version: tornado, hail, wind and flood enhancements come from US agency data and apply to the United States; earthquake and tropical cyclone enhancements come from global catalogs and apply worldwide; wildfire burned-area detail is almost entirely US, while every wildfire record worldwide states what kind of evidence it rests on.

## What "enhanced" means

A hazard record starts life as an alert: a National Weather Service warning, a USGS earthquake notice, a satellite fire detection, a tropical cyclone advisory. Enhancement adds structured blocks of evidence to that record after the event. Each block is attached to the record it describes, so a single tornado warning can carry its damage survey, its hail and wind reports and its storm classification together.

Three conventions hold across every enhancement:

  * **Each block names its sources and what they returned.** A source can have data for the event, have nothing for it, or be unavailable, and the record says which. "No damage survey found" and "no survey exists for this period" are different answers, and the record tells you which one you are looking at.
  * **Missing means null, never zero.** An unreported damage figure, an unmeasured hail size or a blank wind radius is null, so averages are not dragged down by invented zeros.
  * **Shared evidence is counted once.** One damage survey or storm report often touches several warning records. Every record lists the evidence that touches it, and exactly one record "owns" each item, so totals summed across records do not double-count.



## Tornado

**Coverage: United States. Tornado records from 2014; damage-survey evidence mainly from 2017 onward.**

The archive holds about 22,500 tornado records, and 98% of them carry the tornado enhancement. These are warning-grain records, mostly NWS tornado warnings and the confirmed touchdowns under them, so one tornado can appear on several records; they are not a list of distinct tornadoes. Each enhanced record carries:

  * **NWS damage survey paths and points** from the Damage Assessment Toolkit: path start and end, length, width, EF rating, the surveyors' estimated peak wind, injuries and deaths, and survey comments, plus the individual damage points along the track.
  * **NOAA Storm Events rows** for the tornado: rating, length, width, direct and indirect deaths and injuries, and property and crop damage.
  * **Storm reports** : NWS Local Storm Reports and Storm Prediction Center reports, with SPC copies of NWS reports flagged so each report counts once.
  * **Path length with its source** (survey geometry, survey attribute or the SPC track), on more than 12,600 records.
  * **Touchdown status** , separating confirmed touchdowns from warnings with no confirmed tornado. Confirmed tornadoes that no NWS tornado warning covered are named that way rather than folded into a warning.



_Example:_ the warning records for the Greenfield, Iowa tornado of May 21, 2024 carry the NWS survey path for the EF4: 43 miles long, up to 1,600 yards wide, surveyors' estimated peak wind 180 mph, 5 deaths and 35 injuries. The same path is listed on each warning it touched, and one record owns it for counting.

## Hail, damaging wind and severe storms

**Coverage: United States. Radar hail swaths from late 2019; storm reports and warnings across the enhanced years.**

Severe thunderstorm records (more than 98,000 storm records in all) and tornado records share three enhancement blocks, carried by nearly 64,000 storm records and almost every tornado record:

  * **Hail:** ground reports with size, measured or estimated qualifier and reporter; **NOAA MRMS MESH radar hail swaths** as polygons at the 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2 and 2.5 inch thresholds insurers use; the radar-estimated size at the record's location; the hail size forecast in the warning; and a single best estimate that says whether it is a measured report, an estimated report or a radar value.
  * **Wind:** gust reports labelled measured or estimated, damage reports, and **NWS damage-survey wind points** with damage indicator, degree of damage and the estimated wind. Survey winds are engineering estimates from damage, kept in their own field and never mixed with measured gusts.
  * **Severe convective storm classification:** whether hail of 1 inch or more, wind of 58 mph or more, or a tornado was actually observed, which sub-perils were present, and the source of each maximum. Warning tags are kept as forecast context and never count as observations.



Where radar or reports from the US network are used on an event just across the border, the record flags it as US-network evidence. Thousands of US marine warning records carry the same hail and wind blocks.

_Example:_ a severe thunderstorm record in southeastern Colorado on September 20, 2026 (local time) carries a measured 4.0-inch (softball-size) hail report near Chivington, measured 3.1-inch hail near Brandon, eight radar swath polygons at thresholds from 1 to 2 inches, and the warning that covered them.

## Flood

**Coverage: the United States and its territories. Flood enhancement from late 2007.**

About 84,800 of the archive's nearly 129,000 flood records carry the flood enhancement, more than 98% of them in the United States, and almost all the rest in US territories such as Puerto Rico. US flood records begin as NWS flood products (flash flood, areal, river and coastal warnings), so the enhancement adds what was measured and reported on the ground:

  * **River gauges:** USGS gauges in the warning area with peak stage, peak time, flood stage and NWS flood category. More than 78,000 records carry the greatest gauge height above flood stage, and nearly 12,000 reached Major flood category.
  * **Alert history:** every NWS alert that makes up the flood, with issue and expiry times.
  * **Storm reports and road closures** , with flood reports and heavy-rain reports counted separately.
  * **Measured water depth** from USGS high-water marks and storm-tide sensor peaks, as height above ground.
  * **Modeled water depth** from NWS inundation mapping libraries at river gauges, always labelled as modeled.
  * **NOAA tide gauges** for coastal flood and storm surge warnings, as height above high tide.
  * **NOAA Storm Events** deaths, injuries and property and crop damage for the matched events.
  * **FEMA flood insurance (NFIP) claims** in the area and dates of the flood, and **FEMA individual assistance** for the disaster declaration. Claims are located only to about 11 km by FEMA, and assistance figures are declaration-wide, and the record says both.



Outside the United States and its territories, flood records carry this enhancement only where a US flood alert reaches across the border; many carry a modeled exposure assessment instead (see below). The geometry on a flood record is the alert area, not a mapped flood extent.

_Example:_ a flash flood warning for Alleghany, Ashe, Watauga and Wilkes counties, North Carolina, during Hurricane Helene in September 2024 carries five river gauges, two of them at Major flood (the Watauga River near Sugar Grove crested 23.6 feet above flood stage), a USGS high-water mark showing 3.75 feet of water above ground, a modeled depth of 5.5 feet, three road closures and 322 NFIP flood insurance claims.

Every hazard record, with its evidence attached

DisasterAWARE Historical Event Intelligence delivers the archive by API and bulk extract, with each enhancement labelled by source and coverage.

[START FREE TRIAL ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/sign-up?intent=free-trial&source=mid-article-cta&article=historical-hazard-data-enhancements>)[TALK TO AN EXPERT ->](<https://www.disasteraware.com/talk-to-expert?source=mid-article-cta&article=historical-hazard-data-enhancements>)

## Tropical cyclones

**Coverage: worldwide, every basin. Enhancement from the 1998 season.**

Nearly 2,000 of the archive's roughly 3,000 tropical cyclone records are enhanced from **IBTrACS v04r01 (NOAA/NCEI)** , the international best-track archive. An enhanced storm carries:

  * **The full best track:** position, sustained wind, central pressure, storm nature and agency status at each point, with distance to land, and 34-, 50- and 64-knot wind radii by quadrant where the agencies published them.
  * **The wind averaging basis** for each wind value (1-minute or 10-minute, and which agency), so winds from different basins are not compared as if they were the same measure.
  * **Storm summary:** peak Saffir-Simpson category, peak wind, minimum pressure, duration, hours at hurricane and major-hurricane strength, and track length.
  * **Every tropical landfall** with time, position, wind, country and state. More than 950 enhanced records carry at least one landfall. Landfalls are derived from the track, so a crossing of a very small island can be missed and counts are a minimum.
  * **NWS post-storm station reports** for storms that affected the United States or its territories, from 2023: station rainfall totals, storm-tide water levels above high tide, peak gusts with anemometer height, and lowest station pressure.



_Example:_ Hurricane Helene (2024) carries its 45-point track, a Category 4 peak of 120 knots and 939 mb, its landfall in Florida at 120 knots, and the NWS post-storm reports from 12 forecast offices, including 30.78 inches of rain at Busick, North Carolina, and storm tide 9.3 feet above high tide at Cedar Key, Florida.

## Earthquake

**Coverage: worldwide. Records from 1999.**

The archive holds about 74,000 earthquake records worldwide. More than 12,700 of them, the events USGS processed with ShakeMap (95% of them magnitude 4.5 or above), carry the earthquake enhancement:

  * **USGS ShakeMap:** maximum Modified Mercalli intensity, the highest peak-ground-acceleration contour level, and the acceleration contour polygons, the shaking footprint rather than a point.
  * **The USGS authoritative event:** current epicentre, depth, time, magnitude and magnitude type, so a record created from a preliminary alert carries the revised USGS solution alongside.
  * **NOAA NCEI Significant Earthquake Database impacts** where NCEI lists the event: deaths, injuries, houses damaged and destroyed, damage in dollars, a link to any tsunami, and a flag when figures include secondary effects such as tsunami or landslides. More than 570 records carry a death toll from NCEI.
  * **The USGS PAGER alert level** where USGS issued one, kept as a modeled alert level, not a count.



_Example:_ the magnitude 7.8 earthquake north of Ende, Flores, Indonesia, in August 2026 carries its ShakeMap (maximum intensity 8.6, acceleration contours up to 0.5 g across 11 levels), PAGER alert orange, and NCEI's record of 156 deaths, 1,620 injuries and 5,099 houses destroyed.

## Wildfire

**Coverage: every wildfire record worldwide states its evidence basis; burned area and fire detail are almost entirely United States, from 1999.**

The archive holds nearly 130,000 wildfire records, and **every one says what it is based on** : an agency-confirmed fire incident, a satellite heat detection, a satellite burned-area product, an unconfirmed report, a prescribed burn, or a product that is not a fire at all (such as fire-weather alerts). Confirmed incidents and satellite detections make up the great majority. That matters, because a satellite detection is a potential fire, not a confirmed one.

More than 75,000 wildfire records, almost all of them US fires since 1999, carry the fire enhancement, joined to the US interagency fire record (NIFC/WFIGS and its predecessors). Depending on what the agencies reported for each fire, a record carries:

  * **Fire identity:** fire name and national incident ID, and how the record was matched to the fire, with a confidence score.
  * **Final burned size** in acres, with the source and date of the figure. Where the agency's reported size and the latest mapped perimeter disagree sharply, the record shows both.
  * **Perimeters:** the final mapped perimeter and, where available, the dated perimeters showing the fire's growth, with the largest one-day growth.
  * **Timeline:** discovery, containment and fire-out dates, fire-days, and cause.
  * **Incident reports (ICS-209):** structures destroyed and threatened, injuries and deaths, peak personnel, and suppression cost (kept separate from damage).
  * **NASA FIRMS satellite detections** inside the fire's area during the record's dates: daily counts, sensors and peak fire radiative power.
  * **Smoke linked to the fire:** the smoke events the fire fed, smoke days, peak density and the worst air-quality reading (preliminary AirNow data).



_Example:_ the 2026 Wildhorse fire in Idaho carries a final size of 107,563 acres from its mapped perimeter, dated perimeters through its growth (largest one-day growth 16,623 acres), 1,135 satellite detections, and 27 linked smoke events over 15 days, with air quality reaching Very Unhealthy on preliminary AirNow readings.

## Smoke

**Coverage: North America (mainly the United States, Canada and Mexico). From 2008.**

The archive holds nearly 35,000 smoke events. Each one is built from daily **NOAA Hazard Mapping System** satellite smoke outlines. Each carries its smoke density and dates, and, where available:

  * **Smoke density** (light, medium, heavy) by day, first and last observed date, and area-days.
  * **Ground air quality** from EPA AirNow monitors inside the smoke, on about 9,900 events, almost all from 2014 on: the highest 24-hour PM2.5 reading and its US EPA Air Quality Index category. AirNow readings are preliminary, unvalidated data. Ground readings decide the category where monitors exist.
  * **Source fires:** the wildfires feeding the smoke, with name, incident ID and size.



## Exposure, and the hazards without a dedicated enhancement

Many records across hazard types, worldwide, carry a **modeled exposure assessment** : estimated population, households, schools, hospitals and capital value inside the alert footprint. It is an estimate of what lay inside the alert area, not a count of observed impact, and a large precautionary warning yields a large figure.

Landslide, volcano, tsunami, winter storm, extreme temperature and drought records carry the core record and, where modeled, exposure, but no hazard-specific enhancement.

## Data quality built into the dataset

  * **Exercise and test records are withdrawn.** Drills and test messages are not presented as hazard events.
  * **Records describe ended events.** A hazard still active when the archive is built is held back until it has ended.
  * **Every measurement says what kind it is:** measured or estimated hail, measured or estimated gust, survey wind versus anemometer gust, modeled versus measured flood depth, 1-minute versus 10-minute cyclone wind.
  * **Alert area is not event area.** The area on a record is the alert footprint. Burned area, flood depth and shaking footprint live in their own enhancement fields.
  * **Records are alerts, not deduplicated events.** One flood or tornado can span several records; counts of records are never presented as counts of events.



## Enhancements at a glance

Hazard | Enhancement | Main sources | Where | From  
---|---|---|---|---  
Tornado | Damage-survey paths and points, Storm Events, storm reports, path length | NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit, NOAA Storm Events, NWS, SPC | US | 2014 (surveys mainly 2017+)  
Hail | Reports, radar hail swaths, best size estimate | NWS and SPC reports, NOAA MRMS MESH | US | Radar from late 2019  
Wind | Gusts, damage reports, survey wind points | NWS and SPC reports, NWS damage surveys | US | Enhanced years  
Severe storm | Observed hail, wind and tornado classification | Derived from the blocks above | US | Enhanced years  
Flood | Gauges, alert history, reports, measured and modeled depth, tides, Storm Events, flood insurance claims | USGS, NWS, NOAA, FEMA | US and territories | Late 2007  
Tropical cyclone | Best track, wind radii, landfalls, station reports | IBTrACS (NOAA/NCEI), NWS post-storm reports | Worldwide (station reports US and territories) | 1998 season (station reports 2023+)  
Earthquake | ShakeMap, USGS event, NCEI impacts, PAGER level | USGS, NOAA NCEI | Worldwide | 1999  
Wildfire | Evidence basis | Agency and satellite sources | Worldwide | All records  
Wildfire | Burned size, perimeters, timeline, incident reports, satellite detections, smoke links | NIFC/WFIGS and interagency records, ICS-209, NASA FIRMS | Almost entirely US | 1999  
Smoke | Daily smoke outlines, ground air quality, source fires | NOAA HMS, EPA AirNow (preliminary) | North America | 2008  
All types | Modeled exposure | DisasterAWARE exposure model | Worldwide, where modeled | Varies  
  
## How to access the data

The archive is served through the **Historical Hazards API** : filter by hazard type, date, country, state, county, radius or containment test, and by enhancement values such as EF rating, hail size, gauge category, landfall country, magnitude, intensity or final acres. Records come back as full records with every enhancement block or as a compact list for analysis. See the [API documentation](<https://api-v2-docs.disasteraware.com/hazards/requesting-historical-hazards>) for every parameter and field.

Licensed extracts are available through [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>), and the same archive can feed AI agents and analytics platforms through [AI & Analytics Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/ai-analytics-intelligence>). Free sample datasets for tornado, hail, tropical cyclone and earthquake are on the [sample datasets page](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>), and each hazard's data page has field-level detail: [tornado](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/tornado-data>), [severe convective storm](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/severe-convective-storm-data>), [flood](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/flood-data>), [hurricane](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/hurricane-data>), [earthquake](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/earthquake-data>) and [wildfire](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/wildfire-data>).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does "enhanced" mean in DisasterAWARE's historical hazard data?**  
An enhanced record carries structured post-event evidence on top of the original alert: damage surveys and storm reports for tornadoes, radar hail swaths and reports for hail, river gauges, high-water marks and flood insurance claims for floods, best tracks and landfalls for tropical cyclones, ShakeMap and impact records for earthquakes, and burned size, perimeters and incident reports for wildfires. Each block names its sources and whether they had data.

**Is the enhanced data global?**  
It depends on the hazard. Earthquake and tropical cyclone enhancements come from global catalogs (USGS, NOAA NCEI, IBTrACS) and apply worldwide. Tornado, hail, wind and flood enhancements come from US agency data and apply to the United States (flood also covers US territories). Wildfire burned-area detail is almost entirely US, while every wildfire record worldwide states its evidence basis. Smoke covers North America.

**How far back does the historical hazard data go?**  
Earthquake records run from 1999, tropical cyclone enhancement from the 1998 season, wildfire burned-area detail from 1999, flood enhancement from late 2007, smoke from 2008, and tornado records from 2014, with NWS damage-survey evidence mainly from 2017 onward and radar hail swaths from late 2019.

**Are the tornado records a count of tornadoes?**  
No. Tornado records are warning-grain: mostly NWS tornado warnings and the confirmed touchdowns under them, so one tornado can appear on several records. Each record carries the survey paths and reports that touch it, and exactly one record owns each piece of evidence, so totals summed across records count each path and report once.

**Does the flood data include flood depth?**  
Yes, labelled by method. Measured depth comes from USGS high-water marks and storm-tide sensors as height above ground; modeled depth comes from NWS inundation mapping libraries at river gauges and is always marked as modeled. The geometry on a flood record is the alert area, not a mapped flood extent.

**How do I get the data?**  
Through the Historical Hazards API, or as licensed extracts through Historical Event Intelligence. Free samples for tornado, hail, tropical cyclone and earthquake are on the sample datasets page.

# Largest Wildfires in US History by Acres — and the Biggest in Every Western State (Mapped)

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/largest-wildfires-us-history  
**Summary**: Every US wildfire of 500,000+ acres since 1950 in the national records, ranked by final size and mapped: Kateel River, Smokehouse Creek, Dixie, Morrill, Big Grass. Plus each western state's record, the pre-1950 giants, and the deadliest fires.

**What is the largest wildfire in US history? By the old estimates, either the "Big Burn" of August 1910, when hurricane-force winds fanned some 1,700 fires across about 3 million acres of Idaho and Montana, or the October 1871 Peshtigo fire, which NIFC's fire history puts at 3.78 million acres in Wisconsin and Michigan (NWS: about 1.5 million).** Both are estimates, listed separately below. Among fires with an official final size and a mapped perimeter, the largest is Alaska's **Kateel River #5 fire of 1957, at 1,161,200 acres**. The largest in the lower 48 states is the **Smokehouse Creek Fire** (Texas Panhandle, February 2024), at 1,054,153 acres in the national incident record (Texas A&M Forest Service's final update gave 1,058,482). Two 2026 fires have since joined the list: Nebraska's Morrill Fire and Oregon's Big Grass Fire, each now its state's record.

## How We Rank: Official Acres, Not Satellite Outlines

Fire size is counted three ways, and they disagree:

  * **Reported final size** : the acreage the managing agency records when the fire is out. We rank by this. Sources: the Alaska Interagency Coordination Center (AICC) fire history; the US Forest Service's fire occurrence record (FPA-FOD, 1992–2024); and the interagency WFIGS/IRWIN incident record (2014 onward).
  * **Mapped perimeter** : the GIS area inside the final perimeter, from NIFC's Interagency Fire Perimeter History. For older fires the two can differ widely: the 1950 Little Black River fire was reported at 892,900 acres, but its mapped perimeter encloses 1,366,799.
  * **Alert or satellite footprint** : the outline of a warning, or the area of satellite heat detections. These are not burned area, and we never rank by them.



Complexes, groups of fires managed as one incident, are listed separately. **OBSERVED** marks a measured or reported fire size, **ALERT** a product DisasterAWARE issued; loss figures are **estimates** from the sources cited.

## The Largest US Wildfires Since 1950

These are all the single US wildfires since 1950 with a reported final size of 500,000 acres or more in the national incident records (OBSERVED). In those records there are 19, and 11 are in Alaska.

#| Fire| Year| State| Reported acres| Mapped perimeter (GIS acres)  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Kateel River #5**|  1957| Alaska| 1,161,200| 1,130,020  
2| **Smokehouse Creek**|  2024| Texas, into Oklahoma| 1,054,153| 1,054,154  
3| **Dixie**|  2021| California| 963,309| 963,309  
4| Little Black River| 1950| Alaska| 892,900| 1,366,799  
5| Holanada Creek| 1969| Alaska| 803,470| 614,642  
6| **Starbuck**|  2017| Oklahoma, mostly in Kansas| 662,700| 656,868 (MTBS)  
7| Shageluk E| 1957| Alaska| 644,380| 705,214  
8| **Morrill**|  2026| Nebraska| 642,029| 642,029  
9| Inowak| 1997| Alaska| 606,945| 489,738  
10| **Doe** (August Complex)| 2020| California| 589,368| 589,835  
11| **Big Grass**|  2026| Oregon, mostly in Idaho| 578,637| 575,163  
12| Long Draw| 2012| Oregon| 558,198| 558,054  
13| Fire 832015 (unnamed)| 1988| Alaska| 541,231| 558,929  
14| **Wallow**|  2011| Arizona, into New Mexico| 538,049| 538,052  
15| Boundary| 2004| Alaska| 537,627| 538,652  
16| Schuman House–Porcupine River| 1950| Alaska| 529,900| 608,614  
17| Butte Creek| 1969| Alaska| 525,000| 469,185  
18| Minto Flats South| 2009| Alaska| 517,078| 534,912  
19| Buza| 1974| Alaska| 512,000| 354,010  
  
_Reported acres: AICC Alaska fire history (Alaska), FPA-FOD 2024 edition (Long Draw, Wallow), WFIGS/IRWIN incident record (2014 onward). Mapped acres: NIFC Interagency Fire Perimeter History and WFIGS perimeters; Starbuck from the MTBS burned-area boundary. State = where the fire started. Big Grass as of 2026-10-09. Before 1992 the national incident record covers only Alaska. The one earlier lower-48 fire known to exceed 500,000 acres is Yellowstone's 1988 North Fork Fire, which started in Idaho's Targhee National Forest and burned 504,025 acres (1988 interagency survey); it is not ranked here._

What stands out:

  * **Alaska dominates, and its old numbers are rough.** Eleven of the 19 are Alaskan, and the reported sizes of the 1950s and 1960s fires are pre-satellite estimates. Hence the gaps between mapped and reported acres for Little Black River, Holanada Creek and Buza; by mapped area, Little Black River would rank first.
  * **The lower 48's giants are recent.** All eight lower-48 fires in the table burned in 2011 or later, and three of them in 2024–2026. Smokehouse Creek, Starbuck and Morrill were Plains grass and rangeland fires.
  * **The August Complex is not one fire.** CAL FIRE's largest California wildfire, the 2020 August Complex (1,032,648 acres), was a group of lightning fires; its largest member, Doe, ranks 10th on its own.



## The Largest Fire Complexes

Some complexes merge, others never touch. These are all US complexes of 750,000 acres or more in the national records (OBSERVED, total of all member fires):

  1. **Taylor Complex** , Alaska, 2004: 1,303,356 acres (FPA-FOD, seven fire records).
  2. **August Complex** , California, 2020: 1,032,648 acres (CAL FIRE; WFIGS).
  3. **East Amarillo Complex** , Texas, 2006: 907,245 acres (FPA-FOD, two fire records).
  4. **Lime Complex** , Alaska, 2022: 865,625 acres (WFIGS).
  5. **Solstice Complex** , Alaska, 2004: 812,765 acres (FPA-FOD, 19 fire records).
  6. **NW Oklahoma Complex** , Oklahoma and Kansas, 2017: 779,292 acres, including Starbuck (WFIGS).



_FPA-FOD covers 1992–2024 and WFIGS 2014 onward; complexes before 1992 are not in either record._

## Before the Perimeter Era: The Great Fires of 1871–1941

Sizes of these pre-perimeter fires are estimates that vary widely by source, so they are listed by date, not ranked.

  * **Peshtigo Fire** , Wisconsin, October 8, 1871: about 1.5 million acres (NWS) to 3.78 million with the Michigan fires (NIFC); an estimated 1,200–2,400 deaths.
  * **Thumb Fire** , Michigan, September 4–6, 1881: well over 1 million acres; 282 deaths (MSU; NIFC: 169).
  * **Great Hinckley Fire** , Minnesota, September 1, 1894: 350,000 acres; at least 418 deaths.
  * **Yacolt Burn** , Washington, September 1902: nearly 239,000 acres; 38 deaths.
  * **Big Burn (Great Fire of 1910)** , Idaho and Montana, August 1910: about 3 million acres; about 85 deaths.
  * **Cloquet–Moose Lake fires** , Minnesota, October 12, 1918: from 250,000 acres (NWS) to 1,500 square miles (MNopedia); over 450 deaths.
  * **Ruby fire** , Alaska, 1940: 1,250,000 acres (AICC estimate).
  * **Unalakleet fire** , Alaska, 1941: 1,000,000 acres (AICC estimate).



_Sources: NWS Green Bay (Peshtigo); Michigan State University (Thumb); Minnesota DNR (Hinckley); Washington DNR (Yacolt); NWCG staff-ride library and Forest History Society (1910); NIFC fire history (Peshtigo, Thumb); NWS Duluth and MNopedia (1918); AICC fire history (Ruby, Unalakleet)._

The **Big Burn** is usually called the largest wildfire in US history, but it was some 1,736 fires, started by lightning and by people, that hurricane-force winds fanned into one blowup on August 20–21, 1910. It killed an estimated 85 people, firefighters and residents, and it shaped Forest Service fire policy for decades. **Peshtigo** burned the same night as the Great Chicago Fire and remains the deadliest wildfire in American history. Alaska's **Ruby fire of 1940** is the largest in AICC's records but predates mapped perimeters.

## Map: The Largest US Wildfires and Every State Record

The map shows the 19 ranked fires' final perimeters (Alaska's 1950s ones redrawn later), each state record's origin and, in violet, the 15 deadliest and most destructive fires named below (outlines where agencies mapped them, approximate markers for the oldest).

**Explore the map:** more layers are switched off when it opens. Turn them on with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: **fire growth** , dated perimeters for 9 fires since 2004; **satellite fire detections** (NASA FIRMS) and **burn severity** (MTBS), 2004–2024; **smoke** and **NWS red flag warnings** on each fire's key days (2009–2026); and **CAL FIRE damage inspections** , 45,326 damaged or destroyed structures at Dixie, August Complex, Camp, Tubbs, Eaton and Palisades.

## The Largest Wildfire in Each Western State

Each row is the largest fire in that state's own record, by reported final size (OBSERVED), listed under the state where it started.

State| Largest wildfire| Year| Acres| Notes  
---|---|---|---|---

**Idaho**|  Murphy Complex| 2007| 367,785| Its largest FPA-FOD record; the complex's five records total 655,000 acres in Idaho and Nevada. Larger: the 1910 Big Burn and the 1988 North Fork Fire (504,025 acres), which started in Idaho and burned mostly in Yellowstone.  
**Montana**|  Lodgepole Complex| 2017| 270,743| Fires that merged. The 1910 Big Burn was far larger.

_Acres: AICC (Alaska), FPA-FOD 1992–2024 (Wallow, Murphy, Holloway, Milford Flat), CAL FIRE and WFIGS (August Complex), WFIGS/IRWIN incident record (all others). Clover-Mist: NIFC perimeter history (mapped). Holloway: Central Nevada Interagency Dispatch Center 2012 annual report (215,541 acres in Nevada, 245,547 in Oregon)._

Nebraska also has a fire on the national list: the **Morrill Fire** of March 2026, which burned 642,029 acres of western Nebraska rangeland. Nebraska's governor said its cause was "electrical in nature with wind popping wires and sparks."

## The Deadliest US Wildfires

Acreage and deaths rank different fires.

  1. **Peshtigo** , Wisconsin, 1871: an estimated 1,200–2,400.
  2. **Cloquet–Moose Lake** , Minnesota, 1918: over 450.
  3. **Great Hinckley Fire** , Minnesota, 1894: at least 418.
  4. **Thumb Fire** , Michigan, 1881: 282.
  5. **Lahaina** , Hawaii, 2023: 102.
  6. **Big Burn** , Idaho and Montana, 1910: about 85; and the **Camp Fire** , California, 2018: 85.



_The October 1871 Michigan fires, on the same days as Peshtigo, likely killed more than 500 in all (NWS), across several separate fires. Sources: NWS Green Bay; MNopedia (NWS Duluth cites about 1,000 for 1918); Minnesota DNR; Michigan State University; Maui County via the Associated Press (Lahaina); NWCG; CAL FIRE._

**Lahaina** is the deadliest US wildfire in more than a century, and the **Camp Fire** is the deadliest in California's records. Next in CAL FIRE's table come Griffith Park (1933, 29 deaths), the Tunnel Fire in the Oakland Hills (1991, 25) and Tubbs (2017, 22). The January 2025 Los Angeles fires killed 19 in the Eaton Fire and 12 in the Palisades Fire.

## The Most Destructive US Wildfires

Measured by structures destroyed, these are the six most destructive wildfires in California's records (OBSERVED, CAL FIRE); the top five also lead the national list:

  1. **Camp Fire** (2018): 18,804 structures, on 153,336 acres.
  2. **Eaton Fire** (2025): 9,413 structures, on 14,021 acres.
  3. **Palisades Fire** (2025): 6,833 structures, on 23,707 acres.
  4. **Tubbs Fire** (2017): 5,636 structures, on 36,807 acres.
  5. **Tunnel Fire** , Oakland Hills (1991): 2,900 structures, on 1,600 acres.
  6. **Cedar Fire** (2003): 2,820 structures, on 273,246 acres.



Outside California, the most destructive are the **Chimney Tops 2** fire at Gatlinburg, Tennessee (2016; 2,545 structures lost with the fires it merged into), Oregon's **Almeda Drive Fire** (2020; 2,428 structures destroyed and 134 damaged, per the Ashland Police and Jackson County Sheriff) and **Lahaina** (2023; about 2,200 damaged or destroyed). None of the six burned even 300,000 acres.

## In the DisasterAWARE Archive

The DisasterAWARE historical hazard archive holds 130,061 wildfire records worldwide (pulled October 9, 2026). The archive is alert-grain, so one fire can have many records. Records matched to a fire carry a fire assessment linked to the incident record by IRWIN identifier: final acres, perimeters joined, cause, discovery and containment times. **Backfill** records were added later from NIFC history, not issued at the time; we count them separately.

Fires here with DisasterAWARE products issued as they burned (ALERT tier; times UTC):

Fire| Records| First DisasterAWARE product| Discovery in the incident record| Perimeters joined  
---|---|---|---|---  
**Smokehouse Creek** 2024| 9 (5 warnings)| Warning, Feb 27 17:19| Feb 26 20:16| 34  
**Dixie** 2021| 11 (1 warning, 1 watch, 4 advisories)| Warning, Jul 14 23:35| Jul 14 00:15| 656  
**Morrill** 2026| 7 (2 warnings)| Information, Mar 13 00:20| Mar 13 14:14| 25  
**Big Grass** 2026| 1 (warning)| Warning, Jul 23 22:15| Jul 23 20:30| 92  
Park 2024| 4 (3 warnings)| Information, Jul 25 12:29| Jul 24 21:52| 90  
**Camp** 2018| 1 (warning)| Warning, Nov 8 19:45| Nov 8 14:29| 31  
**Palisades** 2025| 2 (warnings)| Warning, Jan 8 00:09| Jan 7 18:30| 35  
**Eaton** 2025| 2 (warnings)| Warning, Jan 8 06:28| Jan 8 02:18| 35  
  
_Source: DisasterAWARE Historical Hazards API, queried 2026-10-09; discovery times from the WFIGS incident record._

A few things the archive shows:

  * **Incident discovery times can be wrong.** Morrill's incident record puts discovery 14 hours after DisasterAWARE's first product, though the fire started on March 12, local time.
  * **Alert-grain means duplicates.** The August Complex has two live warnings (the Doe and Hull fires) and 15 backfill records for its member fires and zones.
  * **Backfill fills the gaps.** Starbuck, Carlton and Tubbs are in the archive only as backfill from NIFC history. Starbuck's backfill record carries an early 150,000-acre incident report, and a separate 400,000-acre Kansas grassfire report covers the same days nearby. Even the national incident record holds partial reports, so we rank from each fire's final record (662,700 acres for Starbuck).



The archive also holds live products for Lahaina (a response-support product on August 9, 2023), Hermits Peak–Calf Canyon (filed under Calf Canyon), the Lime Complex's Koktuli River fire, Remington, House Draw, Cameron Peak, Bootleg, Mullen, Martin, Lodgepole, Woolsey, Marshall and Chimney Tops 2. It cannot yet tell an incident confirmed by NIFC from a satellite detection that may not be a fire, so we do not publish archive fire counts.

Every fire perimeter, every alert, one record

DisasterAWARE Historical Event Intelligence links fire perimeters, final acreage, cause and alerts into event-level records -- for every hazard, worldwide.

## For Insurers and Reinsurers: Acres Don't Drive Loss

The largest fires on this page burned tundra, sagebrush and grassland; the costliest burned neighborhoods. Wildfire loss is a question of **exposure in the wildland–urban interface (WUI)** and, increasingly, of **who started the fire**.

  * **Los Angeles, January 2025.** The Palisades Fire burned 23,707 acres and the Eaton Fire 14,021 (CAL FIRE): together less than 4% of Smokehouse Creek's area. Munich Re puts the overall loss at around US$53 billion, about US$40 billion of it insured: the most expensive wildfire disaster to date.
  * **Camp Fire, 2018.** On 153,336 acres, it destroyed 18,804 structures and killed 85 people. Munich Re puts the overall loss at US$16.5 billion, US$12.5 billion insured: the costliest natural catastrophe of 2018 worldwide.
  * **Tubbs and the 2017 fires.** Tubbs burned 36,807 acres in Napa and Sonoma counties and destroyed 5,636 structures. California's Department of Insurance counted more than US$11.79 billion in insured losses from the October and December 2017 wildfires, Tubbs among them.



**Utility liability.** The ignition source now shapes recovery and subrogation:

  * **Camp.** PG&E pleaded guilty to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter. Its bankruptcy plan put US$13.5 billion into the Fire Victim Trust, which covers the Camp Fire, the 2017 North Bay fires (Tubbs among them) and the 2015 Butte Fire.
  * **Dixie.** CAL FIRE lists its cause as power lines.
  * **Lahaina.** A US$4.037 billion global settlement (Maui County) resolved the 2023 Maui fire claims; Hawaiian Electric's share was US$1.99 billion, with no admission of liability.
  * **Smokehouse Creek.** Xcel Energy acknowledged that its facilities "appear to have been involved in an ignition" of the fire, while disputing negligence.
  * **Eaton.** The US Department of Justice sued Southern California Edison in September 2025, alleging that its equipment ignited the fire.
  * **Tubbs.** CAL FIRE found a private electrical system, not PG&E, caused it.



**The data question.** Underwriting and subrogation need event-level facts: origin, perimeter growth and cause. DisasterAWARE's [wildfire data](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/wildfire-data>) links each fire's alerts to its perimeters, final acres, cause, discovery and containment times. Smokehouse Creek alone has 34 perimeters joined and Dixie 656. [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>) licenses the archive across every hazard, and the [sample datasets](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>) show the record format with no signup.

Explore the historical record

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the largest wildfire in US history?**  
By the old estimates, the 1910 Big Burn (about 3 million acres in Idaho and Montana) or the 1871 Peshtigo fire (3.78 million acres in NIFC's history; 1.5 million by NWS). Among fires with an official final size and a mapped perimeter, it is Alaska's Kateel River #5 fire of 1957 (1,161,200 acres). In the lower 48 it is Texas's 2024 Smokehouse Creek Fire (1,054,153 acres).

**What is the largest wildfire in California history?**  
The August Complex of 2020, a group of lightning fires, at 1,032,648 acres (CAL FIRE). The largest single fire is the 2021 Dixie Fire, at 963,309 acres.

**What is the deadliest wildfire in modern US history?**  
The Lahaina fire on Maui, on August 8, 2023, which killed 102 people. The deadliest in American history is the 1871 Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin, with an estimated 1,200 to 2,400 deaths.

**What is the costliest wildfire in US history?**  
The January 2025 Los Angeles fires, Palisades and Eaton: around US$53 billion overall and about US$40 billion insured, by Munich Re's estimate, the most expensive wildfire disaster to date.

**What is the largest wildfire in Colorado history?**  
The Cameron Peak Fire of 2020, at 208,913 acres, ahead of the 2020 East Troublesome Fire (193,812 acres).
