# The Worst Tornadoes in US History: Deadliest, Widest, Longest-Tracked (Mapped)

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/worst-tornadoes-us-history  
**Summary**: The worst tornadoes in US history, ranked and mapped: the deadliest since 1840, the deadliest, widest and longest-tracked since records began in 1950, the worst tornado in 28 states, and what single tornadoes cost insurers.

**The worst tornado in US history is the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925, which killed 695 people across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.** Since official records began in 1950, the deadliest is the Joplin, Missouri tornado of May 22, 2011 (158 deaths); the widest is El Reno, Oklahoma on May 31, 2013 (2.6 miles); and the longest track in SPC's database since the 1973 Kansas–Nebraska track is the Western Kentucky tornado of December 10, 2021: 168.5 miles (165.6 on the National Weather Service damage survey), essentially tied with a 168.5-mile 1975 Florida–Georgia track. Below: the lists, the worst tornado in 28 states, and a map of every tornado named here.

How the lists are built: the 1950–2025 rankings come from the NOAA Storm Prediction Center (SPC) tornado database, downloaded October 9, 2026. One row is one tornado, so a tornado that crossed a state line is counted once. Dates are local (SPC logs Central Standard Time): Kissimmee, at 11:40 p.m. CST on February 22, 1998, is dated February 23. Deaths before 1950 come from SPC's list of the 25 deadliest US tornadoes. Where two official sources disagree, both figures are given.

## The Deadliest Tornadoes in US History

Eight of the ten deadliest US tornadoes struck before 1950, before formal damage surveys and official ratings; only Joplin and Flint–Beecher carry one. SPC cautions that "some of these events may have been composed of multiple tornadoes along a damage path," and that death counts from the 1800s and early 1900s "should be treated as estimates."

Rank| Date| Tornado| Deaths  
---|---|---|---  
1| March 18, 1925| Tri-State Tornado (Missouri, Illinois, Indiana)| **695**  
2| May 6, 1840| Natchez, Mississippi| 317  
3| May 27, 1896| St. Louis, Missouri| 255  
4| April 5, 1936| Tupelo, Mississippi| 216  
5| April 6, 1936| Gainesville, Georgia| 203  
6| April 9, 1947| Woodward, Oklahoma| 181  
7| May 22, 2011| Joplin, Missouri (EF5)| 158  
8| April 24, 1908| Amite, Louisiana – Purvis, Mississippi| 143  
9| June 12, 1899| New Richmond, Wisconsin| 117  
10| June 8, 1953| Flint–Beecher, Michigan (F5)| 116  
  
The Tri-State Tornado's toll is in a class of its own: more than twice the second-worst on the list. According to the National Weather Service office in Paducah, it touched down 3 miles north-northwest of Ellington, Missouri at 1:01 p.m., crossed southern Illinois — where more than 600 people died, 234 of them in Murphysboro alone — and dissipated about 3 miles southwest of Petersburg, Indiana, three and a half hours later; at least 71 died in southwest Indiana. It injured 2,027 people and is retrospectively regarded as an F5.

## The Deadliest Tornadoes Since 1950

Joplin's 158 deaths are 42 more than the next-worst, Flint–Beecher in 1953. Two years account for six of the ten: 1953, with three of the top four in 29 days, and 2011, with three.

Rank| Date| Tornado| Rating| Deaths| Injuries| Path (mi)  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| May 22, 2011| Joplin, Missouri| EF5| 158| 1,150| 21.6  
2| June 8, 1953| Flint–Beecher, Michigan| F5| 116| 844| 18.9  
3| May 11, 1953| Waco, Texas| F5| 114| 597| 20.9  
4| June 9, 1953| Worcester, Massachusetts| F4| 94| 1,228| 34.9  
5| May 25, 1955| Udall, Kansas| F5| 80| 273| 56.4  
6| April 27, 2011| Hackleburg–Phil Campbell, Alabama| EF5| 72| 145| 132.0  
7| April 27, 2011| Tuscaloosa–Birmingham, Alabama| EF4| 64| 1,500| 80.7  
8| February 21, 1971| Cary, Mississippi to near Middleton, Tennessee| F4| 58| 795| 202.1  
9| March 3, 1966| Candlestick Park (Jackson), Mississippi| F5| 58| 518| 202.5  
10| December 10, 2021| Western Kentucky (Mayfield)| EF4| 57| 515| 168.5  
  
Two caveats. The 1971 Cary–Middleton and 1966 Candlestick Park tornadoes tie at 58 deaths; they are ordered here by injuries. And SPC's own "25 deadliest" page lists Worcester with 90 deaths, while its database records 94. We rank by the database and show its figure.

No US tornado since Joplin has killed more than 57.

## Map: Every Tornado on This Page

[Open map full screen ↗](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/maps/evergreen-worst-tornadoes-us-history.html>)

**Explore the map:** switch on more layers with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: **NWS tornado warnings** (ALERT, 2002+); **NWS damage-survey points** (2011+; none for Joplin); **hail and wind reports** within 50 km (1955+); **radar reflectivity and velocity** (1995+); and **radar hail and rotation swaths** (MODELED, late 2019+).

The map draws all 45 tornadoes since 1950 named here, coloured by F- or EF-rating, plus the 17 pre-1950 tornadoes. Lines by era:

  * **2015 onward (six tornadoes):** our NWS damage-survey (DAT) path where it covers the whole track. Lee County, Alabama (2019): it covers 26.6 of 68.0 miles, so SPC's line is used.
  * **1950–2014:** straight SPC start-to-end lines, as in SPC's track file. Warner Robins, Larose and Ivy have only a start point (dots).
  * **Before 1950:** no surveyed track or official rating; a purple dot at or near the town SPC names. The Tri-State line (Ellington, Missouri to Petersburg, Indiana) is approximate.



EF contours (2011+; none for Joplin) and width envelopes are on at load.

## The Widest Tornadoes on Record

**The widest tornado ever recorded is the El Reno, Oklahoma tornado of May 31, 2013: 2.6 miles (4,576 yards) across.** The NWS office in Norman calls it "the widest known tornado on record." It was also "one of the most powerful tornadoes sampled by mobile radar," yet it is rated only EF3, because ratings come from damage, and over open country it hit little that could prove higher winds. It killed eight people, all motorists caught along Interstate 40 and nearby roads.

Rank| Date| Tornado| Rating| Max width| Deaths  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| May 31, 2013| El Reno, Oklahoma| EF3| 4,576 yd (2.6 mi)| 8  
2| May 22, 2004| Hallam, Nebraska| F4| 4,400 yd (2.5 mi)| 1  
3| April 12, 2020| Bassfield–Soso, Mississippi| EF4| 3,960 yd (2.25 mi)| 7 (SPC; NWS Jackson, MS: 8)  
4| May 4, 2007| Kiowa–Edwards counties, Kansas| EF3| 3,872 yd (2.2 mi)| 0  
5| June 7, 2008| Columbia County, Wisconsin| EF2| 3,520 yd (2.0 mi)| 0  
  
Width matters most for exposure: a wider path sweeps more buildings per mile. Three of the five widest have struck since 2008.

## The Longest Tornado Tracks: A Disputed Record

  * **The Tri-State Tornado (1925):** the NWS Paducah office gives a 219-mile path, "a record for a single tornado." A 2013 reanalysis it cites found that the 174 miles from central Madison County, Missouri to western Pike County, Indiana were likely continuous, and the 151 miles from central Bollinger County, Missouri the most likely to have been continuous.
  * **The SPC database (1950–2025):** the longest recorded track is a 234.7-mile F2 from Louisiana into Mississippi on March 22, 1953. The top seven all date from 1953 to 1973, before modern damage surveys. A 176-mile F1 from 1965 is recorded as 10 yards wide.
  * **The modern record:** the Western Kentucky tornado of December 10, 2021 has SPC's longest track since the 1973 Kansas–Nebraska track, by a hair: 168.53 miles vs 168.5 for a January 12, 1975 F2 from the Florida Panhandle into Georgia (recorded to a tenth of a mile); on either NWS figure below, the 1975 track is longer. By source: 168.5 miles in the SPC database; 165.6 miles on the NWS DAT surveyed path in our archive; and 165.7 miles on the NWS Paducah event page, which calls it the "ninth longest tornado path ever recorded in the U.S."

Rank| Date| Track| Rating| Length (mi)| Deaths  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| March 22, 1953| Louisiana – Mississippi (Vernon Parish to Washington Co.)| F2| 234.7| 2  
2| April 18, 1969| South Georgia (Seminole to Liberty counties)| F2| 217.8| 0  
3| March 3, 1966| Candlestick Park (Jackson), Mississippi| F5| 202.5| 58  
4| February 21, 1971| Cary, Mississippi to near Middleton, Tennessee| F4| 202.1| 58  
5| May 24, 1965| Buffalo County, Nebraska (recorded to near Yankton, SD)| F1| 176.4| 0  
6| April 29, 1970| Southwest to north-central Oklahoma| F2| 170.5| 0  
7| September 25, 1973| Kansas – Nebraska| F3| 169.7| 3  
8| December 10, 2021| Western Kentucky (Mayfield)| EF4| 168.5| 57  
  
## The Worst Tornado in Each State

The rule: every state whose deadliest tornado since 1950 killed at least six people there, untied. That gives 28 states (South Carolina's top two tie at 7). Deaths are those SPC records inside the state, so Udall, which touched down in Oklahoma, is under Kansas (80). The last column lists every pre-1950 tornado on SPC's 25-deadliest list that killed at least as many there.

By total tornado deaths since 1950, **Alabama leads with 682** , followed by Texas (593), Mississippi (533), Missouri (423) and Arkansas (415). ## In the DisasterAWARE Archive Since 2015

DisasterAWARE's archive holds 15,774 distinct tornadoes from January 3, 2015 to September 30, 2026 (UTC), each built from SPC, NCEI and/or NWS damage-survey records. Its tornado warnings are kept separate and never counted as tornadoes. These are the five deadliest, with the NWS damage-survey path stored on each tornado's record (OBSERVED tier):

Rank| Date| Tornado| Rating| Deaths| Track (mi)| NWS damage survey in our record (rating, length, max width, peak est. wind)  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| December 10, 2021| Western Kentucky (Mayfield)| EF4| 57| 168.5| EF4, 165.6 mi, 1,760 yd, 190 mph  
2| March 3, 2019| Lee County (Beauregard), Alabama| EF4| 23| 68.0| EF4, 26.6 mi, 1,600 yd, 170 mph  
3| March 3, 2020| Cookeville, Tennessee| EF4| 19| 8.4| EF4, 8.4 mi, 900 yd, 175 mph  
4| May 16, 2025| Somerset–London, Kentucky| EF4| 18| 60.1| EF4, 60.0 mi, 1,700 yd, 170 mph  
5| March 24, 2023| Rolling Fork, Mississippi| EF4| 17| 59.2| EF4, 59.4 mi, 1,320 yd, 195 mph  
  
Deaths and track lengths are from the SPC database. NWS Jackson, KY reports 19 Somerset–London deaths, one more than SPC's 18.

**Were they warned? (ALERT tier.)** For all five, an NWS tornado warning polygon covered the touchdown point when the tornado formed. Four were issued 12 to 41 minutes earlier: Rolling Fork 12, Somerset–London 22, Western Kentucky 26 and Lee County 41. Cookeville's (NWS Nashville) was issued at 1:48 a.m. CST, the same minute SPC records touchdown: no lead time. Source: NWS storm-based warnings (Iowa Environmental Mesonet VTEC archive), checked against each SPC start point and time. A warning is an issued product, not proof of what happened on the ground.

## For Insurers and Reinsurers

**Single tornadoes are small-footprint, high-severity losses.** Joplin's path was 21.6 miles long and at most 1,600 yards wide. Even taking the maximum width along the whole length, that is under 20 square miles, yet SPC's database records $2.8 billion in property damage for it (nominal dollars, a Storm Data estimate). An AP review a year later called it the costliest tornado since at least 1950, with insurance expected to cover most of the $2.8 billion.

**Why tornado sits inside severe convective storm (SCS).** The storms that produce tornadoes also produce hail and straight-line wind, so tornado is modelled, reinsured and reported as part of SCS. Swiss Re estimated $50 billion of global insured SCS losses in 2025, the third-highest year on record after 2023 and 2024, and said it is "observing a steady rise in losses from severe convective storms."

**What the record says about the view of risk.**

  * **The extremes are path events.** The deadliest and costliest tornadoes on these lists hit towns: Joplin, Tuscaloosa, Moore, Mayfield.
  * **The record is uneven by era.** Widths and lengths from the early decades were recorded without today's survey tools, and ratings moved from the Fujita to the Enhanced Fujita scale in February 2007. Any frequency-severity curve fitted to 1950s data inherits those limits.
  * **The modern data is path-level.** Of the 244 tornadoes rated EF3 or higher in our archive since 2019, 237 are linked to an NWS DAT surveyed path, with EF-rated segments and damage points. That supports the questions underwriters actually ask: which locations were inside the EF2+ segment, and how close did the EF4 core pass?



**What event-level data exists.** DisasterAWARE Historical Event Intelligence stores each tornado as one event, kept separate from the warnings issued for it. Each event carries its rating and, where linked, the NWS surveyed path, damage-survey points, related storm reports and the warning polygons that covered it. Surveyed paths are linked for most tornadoes since 2019 (few before 2017), so portfolios can be screened by path, not county counts, and the same records feed real-time alerting.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the worst tornado in US history?**  
The Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925. It killed 695 people and injured 2,027 across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana, according to the National Weather Service. Since official records began in 1950, the deadliest is the Joplin, Missouri EF5 of May 22, 2011, with 158 deaths.

**What was the widest tornado ever recorded?**  
The El Reno, Oklahoma tornado of May 31, 2013, at 2.6 miles (4,576 yards) wide. Second is the Hallam, Nebraska tornado of May 22, 2004, at 4,400 yards (2.5 miles).

**What is the longest tornado path ever recorded?**  
It is disputed. The 1925 Tri-State Tornado is traditionally given 219 miles, though a 2013 reanalysis found only about 174 miles likely continuous. SPC's database has a 234.7-mile track from 1953, recorded before modern damage surveys. The longest surveyed with modern methods is the Western Kentucky tornado of December 10, 2021: 165.6 miles on the NWS damage survey and 168.5 miles in the SPC database.

**What was the deadliest tornado since 1950?**  
Joplin, Missouri, May 22, 2011: an EF5 that killed 158 people and injured 1,150. It is the seventh-deadliest US tornado on record and the deadliest since the 1947 Woodward, Oklahoma tornado.

**Which state has had the most tornado deaths?**  
Alabama, with 682 tornado deaths from 1950 through 2025 in SPC's database. Texas (593) and Mississippi (533) follow. Alabama's deadliest was the Hackleburg–Phil Campbell EF5 of April 27, 2011, which killed 72.

# Deadliest Heat Waves in US History, Including the 2021 Pacific Northwest Heat Dome

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/deadliest-heat-waves-us-history  
**Summary**: The deadliest heat waves in US history: 1936, 1980, Chicago 1995, the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome and Phoenix 2023, with each death toll's basis stated, station records and maps of how far temperatures ran above normal.

_Two rankings and one rule: never compare a death count with an excess-mortality estimate without saying which is which. With station records and maps of how far temperatures ran above normal._

**What was the deadliest heat wave in US history? By the widest measure, the summer of 1980: NOAA's billion-dollar disaster record, now kept by Climate Central, estimates about 10,000 deaths when indirect deaths from heat stress (excess mortality) are included, and its own death count of 1,260 is higher than for any other heat wave since its record began in 1980.** The July 1936 heat wave killed about 5,000 people nationwide, according to the National Weather Service; no excess-mortality estimate exists for 1936, so the two cannot be ranked on one basis. The deadliest US city heat wave of modern times was Chicago's in July 1995: 739 more deaths than expected in one week. And the June 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, which drove Portland to 116°F and Seattle to 108°F, was the deadliest weather disaster in Washington State's history.

## Why Heat Death Tolls Disagree

Heat kills quietly, often indoors and disproportionately among older people, so there is no single death count for a heat wave. Published figures come in three kinds, and they can differ by a factor of ten for the same event:

  * **Heat-related deaths** are deaths that a medical examiner, coroner or death certificate attributes to heat. This is the narrowest count.
  * **Excess deaths** are all deaths above the number expected for that place and time of year. They capture the heart attacks, kidney failures and strokes that heat brings on but that are not certified as heat deaths. This is the widest count, and the one epidemiologists trust most for big events.
  * **Surveillance totals** are a county's or state's tally of heat deaths over a whole season or year, not one heat wave.



So the tables below keep the bases apart. The first ranks heat waves on a single basis. The second lists the deadliest heat waves on every basis that has been published, and says which is which.

## The Deadliest Heat Waves Since 1980 (One Basis)

Ranking rule: every event in Climate Central's billion-dollar disaster dataset with "heat wave" in its name, 1980 to 2026 (20 events), ranked by the deaths the dataset records. Climate Central took over the dataset from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) in 2025. Each event is a heat wave combined with drought, so its dates span a season and its cost is mostly crop losses.

#| Event (Climate Central name)| Period| Deaths| Cost, 2026 dollars  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Central/Eastern Drought/Heat Wave (**1980**)| Jun–Nov 1980| 1,260| $43.0 billion  
2| Central, Southern and Northeast Drought/Heat Wave (**Chicago 1995**)| Jul–Sep 1995| 872| $2.1 billion  
3| Eastern Drought/Heat Wave| Jun–Aug 1999| 502| $5.1 billion  
4| U.S. Drought/Heat Wave| Jun–Aug 1988| 454| $57.8 billion  
5| Southern/Midwestern Drought and Heatwave| Apr–Sep 2023| 247| $15.8 billion  
6| Western Drought and Heat Wave (**Pacific Northwest heat dome**)| 2021| 229| $10.8 billion  
7| Southern Drought and Heat Wave| Jun–Aug 1998| 200| $7.3 billion  
8| Western/Central/Southeast Drought/Heat Wave| Mar–Nov 2000| 140| $9.9 billion  
9=| Western/Central Drought and Heat Wave| 2022| 136| $24.9 billion  
9=| Southern/Eastern/Northwestern Drought and Heat Wave| 2024| 136| $5.7 billion  
  
_Source: Climate Central, U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters (events list read October 9, 2026). Common names in bold are ours. Next on the list: the 2012 drought and heat wave (123 deaths)._

The dataset's own summaries show how much the basis matters. For 1980, it records 1,260 deaths but notes that "combined direct and indirect deaths (i.e., excess mortality) due to heat stress" were "estimated at 10,000". For 1988, it records 454 deaths and estimates excess mortality at 5,000. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), counting death certificates, attributed 1,700 deaths to heat in 1980 and 454 in 1988. The 2026 heat waves are in the dataset too, but with no death count yet: Climate Central says a fatality count "will be included in our end-of-year reporting".

## The 2021 Pacific Northwest Heat Dome

For about a week at the end of June 2021, a ridge of high pressure parked over the Pacific Northwest and pushed temperatures to levels the region had never measured. The National Weather Service in Seattle described it as a long-duration, unprecedented heat wave from June 26 to July 2.

**Temperatures.** We checked every major weather station (NOAA GHCN-Daily "first-order" stations) in Washington, Oregon and Idaho with at least 30 years of data. Of the 43 we could evaluate, **24 set a new all-time high and 3 tied theirs** between June 25 and July 2:

Station| High, June 2021| Previous all-time high| Data since  
---|---|---|---  
Dallesport (The Dalles), WA| 118°F, Jun 28| 111°F (1998)| 1948  
Salem, OR| 117°F, Jun 28| 108°F (1981)| 1893  
Pendleton, OR| 117°F, Jun 29| 114°F (1928)| 1928  
**Portland International Airport, OR**| **116°F, Jun 28**|  107°F (1981)| 1938  
Walla Walla, WA| 116°F, Jun 29| 114°F (1975)| 1949  
Yakima, WA| 113°F, Jun 29| 110°F (1971)| 1946  
Quillayute (Olympic coast), WA| 110°F, Jun 28| 99°F (1981)| 1966  
Spokane International Airport, WA| 109°F, Jun 29| 108°F (1961)| 1889  
**Seattle-Tacoma Airport, WA**| **108°F, Jun 28**|  103°F (2009)| 1948  
  
_Source: NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily station records, read October 9, 2026 (°F converted from the archived tenths of a degree Celsius). "Previous all-time high" is the station's highest reading before June 25, 2021, with the last year it was reached. All 27 record stations are on the map below._

Portland's previous record was beaten by 9°F and Salem's by 9°F; Quillayute, on the Pacific coast, beat its old record by 11°F. The University of Washington's Climate Impacts Group, with the Washington State Department of Health, counts 128 all-time high temperature records set across Washington, using every station in the state, not just the major ones.

**Deaths.** Washington's official estimate is 126 heat-related deaths; the Department of Health's final report counts 100 between June 26 and July 2 alone. The Oregon Health Authority counts 102 deaths caused by the heat dome. In Multnomah County, which includes Portland, 69 of the county's 72 heat deaths of 2021 came from the heat of the last week of June, against zero in a typical year; 68 of the 72 died in their own homes. Counting excess deaths instead, a 2023 report by the University of Washington's Climate Impacts Group and the Department of Health found **441 more deaths than expected between June 27 and July 3** , after removing COVID-19 deaths. The same report calls the heat dome the deadliest weather-related disaster in Washington's history.

## Chicago, July 1995: The Deadliest Modern Heat Wave in a US City

From July 12 to 16, 1995, daily highs in Chicago ranged from 93°F to 104°F, and on July 13 the heat index peaked at 119°F, a record for the city (CDC). The National Weather Service recorded 106°F at Midway Airport and 104°F at O'Hare, which tied O'Hare's all-time high from June 1988. The Cook County Medical Examiner certified 465 deaths as heat-related between July 11 and 27. From July 13 to 21, 1,177 people died in Chicago from all causes, 85% more than in the same days of 1994. A later study counted 739 excess deaths in the worst week alone, July 14 to 20. The NWS called it Chicago's worst weather-related disaster. In Milwaukee, the same heat wave killed 85.

## The 1980 Heat Wave

The 1980 heat wave was long rather than sharp. In NOAA's gridded temperature analysis, daily highs across much of Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and north Texas averaged 5°F to more than 10°F above normal for the whole of July. Of 120 major weather stations with 30 years of data in the 13 affected states we checked, 19 set and 10 tied their all-time highs between June 20 and July 31, 1980, among them **117°F at Wichita Falls, Texas** (June 28), 112°F at Dallas Love Field, 109°F at Little Rock, 108°F at Memphis and 105°F at Atlanta (records at the time; some have since been beaten). A 1982 study in _JAMA_ found that deaths from all causes in July 1980 rose 57% in St. Louis and 64% in Kansas City compared with the two previous Julys, but only 10% in rural Missouri: heat waves kill most in cities.

## Phoenix and the Longest Heat Waves

Arizona's heat waves are measured in weeks. At Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport, the high reached 110°F or more on **31 consecutive days, June 30 to July 30, 2023** , by far the longest run in Phoenix's official record, which goes back to the 1890s; the next longest was 18 days in 1974. Maricopa County counted **645 heat-related deaths in 2023** , the most it has ever recorded, then 608 in 2024 (a year with 70 days of 110°F or more at Sky Harbor) and 430 in 2025. These are calendar-year totals of deaths where heat was a cause or a contributing factor, not single heat waves, which is why they sit apart from the tables above.

## Is 2026 One of the Worst?

By temperature, yes. In NOAA's Climate at a Glance national series, **summer 2026 (June to August) was the hottest on record for the contiguous United States, at 74.37°F** , ahead of 1936 and 2021 (both 73.98°F). By average _daily high_ , 1936 still leads (87.89°F against 87.02°F in 2026), so the Dust Bowl summer of 1936 still has the highest average daily high on record.

In early July, a heat dome over the eastern half of the country set or tied all-time highs at 12 of the 226 major weather stations we checked from Illinois to New England and the Carolinas (June 28 to July 6), including **106°F at Langley Air Force Base, Virginia** , a new record, and 106°F at Atlantic City International Airport, New Jersey, which tied the airport's record from 1969. These 2026 readings are preliminary until NOAA finishes its quality control. In Texas, the ERCOT grid set an unofficial all-time demand record of 91,089 megawatts on July 22, 2026. Phoenix reached 110°F on 39 days so far (preliminary).

By deaths, it is too early to say. No official national count exists yet, and Climate Central will add one at the end of the year. 2026 will join the rankings above when it does.

## Map: How Hot It Got, and Where the Deaths Were Counted

The map shows how far daily highs ran above normal in three of the deadliest heat waves: the 2021 heat dome (June 25 to July 2), Chicago 1995 (July 11 to 16) and July 1980 (switch between them in the layer menu). Each is NOAA's gridded daily maximum temperature, averaged over those days, minus the 1991–2020 normal for the same days. The dots are the all-time station records from each event, and teal markers show where the death counts above were made.

[Open map full screen ↗](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/maps/evergreen-deadliest-heat-waves-us-history.html>)

**Explore the map:** switch on more layers with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: **daily highs above normal** for Chicago 1995 and July 1980; the **highest temperature at every station** during the 1936, 1980, 1995, 2021 and 2026 heat waves; the **heat index at airports** at one afternoon hour on a peak day in 1995, 2021 and 2026; **NWS heat warnings and advisories** by forecast zone for California 2006, the 2021 heat dome, Phoenix 2023 and July 2026, and **DisasterAWARE heat alert records** (both ALERT tier: issued products, not measurements); and **outlines of the areas** behind the local death counts (all but Milwaukee's).

**What the map can show, by era.** NOAA's gridded daily temperatures (NClimGrid) start in 1951, so every heat wave since then can be mapped this way; for 1936, only station records exist. NWS heat warnings survive in the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive from 2005 (called extreme heat warnings since 2025), so there are none to map for 1936, 1980 or 1995. Station all-time records depend on each station's length of record, so they are clearest for long-running airport stations. Death counts are reported by city, county or state, so they appear as one marker per place, not as a map of where people died.

## In the DisasterAWARE Archive Since 2014

DisasterAWARE's historical hazard archive holds 677 US heat records from August 2014 to September 2026 (pulled October 9, 2026): 244 warnings, 64 watches and 369 advisories. They are **alerts** , issued products, not temperature measurements or deaths. Since 2025 most of these records are issued per forecast area (111 in 2025 and 432 in 2026), so counts across years are not comparable. Here is what it recorded for the recent events above:

Event| DisasterAWARE archive (alerts)  
---|---

Portland's ran from June 26 to June 28, Seattle's from June 25 to June 29, and Spokane's from June 25 to July 2 (local time).  
Phoenix, summer 2023| ALERT: an "Extreme Heat – Western United States" warning record covering Phoenix, June 29 – July 31, 2023. NWS Phoenix's excessive heat warning for central Phoenix ran from July 1 to July 29 (IEM VTEC), covering 29 of the run's 31 days.

The population figures attached to alerts measure who lived inside the alert area, not who was affected, so we never rank heat waves by them.

## For Insurers and Reinsurers: Heat Is a Mortality, Power and Productivity Peril

Heat rarely damages buildings, so it barely registers in property catastrophe models. Its losses fall on other lines.

  * **Mortality and health.** Heat deaths land on life, health and long-term care books, concentrated among older people and people who live alone. In Multnomah County in 2021, 68 of the 72 heat deaths happened at home. Excess deaths can be several times the certified count (441 against 126 in Washington in 2021), so pricing from certified deaths alone understates the peril.
  * **Crops and drought.** The losses in Climate Central's dataset are large because the heat waves came with drought: $57.8 billion for 1988, $44.1 billion for 2012, $43.0 billion for 1980, and $15.8 billion for 2023 (2026 dollars).
  * **Power demand and the grid.** Heat drives peak electricity demand. ERCOT's all-time records are summer heat records: 85,508 MW on August 10, 2023, and an unofficial 91,089 MW on July 22, 2026. A heat wave that coincides with a generation shortfall turns into an outage, and an outage turns heat into business interruption, spoilage and more deaths.
  * **Labour productivity.** A 2021 report from the Atlantic Council's Adrienne Arsht–Rockefeller Foundation Resilience Center estimated that heat already costs the US economy about $100 billion a year in lost labour productivity.
  * **Parametric covers.** Because heat is measured, not inspected, it suits parametric triggers. In India in 2024, a heat-triggered income cover run by the Self-Employed Women's Association, with the insurer ICICI Lombard delivering the payouts, paid out about $350,859 to women working in the informal sector, more than 46,000 of them across 22 districts. Each region has its own trigger: in Ahmedabad, a daytime high above 43.6°C for two consecutive days. A trigger like that needs a defensible daily temperature record for the insured place, and a history of how often it has been crossed.



**What event-level data exists.** For a heat portfolio, the useful record is temperature, duration and footprint: NOAA's gridded daily temperatures go back to 1951 and station records further, and city, county and state health departments publish death counts on the bases described above. DisasterAWARE's archive adds the alerts themselves since 2014, each with its area and the population inside it: who was warned, where and when. [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>) licenses that archive across every hazard for back-testing, accumulation studies and event sets. The [sample datasets](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>) show the record format with no signup.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What was the deadliest heat wave in US history?**  
By the widest measure, the 1980 heat wave and drought: NOAA's billion-dollar disaster record, now kept by Climate Central, estimates about 10,000 deaths including indirect deaths, and its own death count, 1,260, is the most of any heat wave since 1980. The July 1936 heat wave killed about 5,000 people, according to the National Weather Service, but on a basis that cannot be compared directly.

**How many people died in the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome?**  
Officially, 126 heat-related deaths in Washington (100 of them between June 26 and July 2, Washington State Department of Health) and 102 in Oregon (Oregon Health Authority). Counting excess deaths, Washington had 441 more deaths than expected between June 27 and July 3, 2021.

**How many people died in the 1995 Chicago heat wave?**  
The Cook County Medical Examiner certified 465 heat-related deaths between July 11 and 27, 1995. A 1997 study counted 739 excess deaths in the week of July 14 to 20.

**What was the hottest heat wave in US history?**  
By average daily high temperature across the contiguous US, the summer of 1936 (87.89°F, NOAA). By average temperature, summer 2026 is now the hottest on record, at 74.37°F, ahead of 1936 and 2021.

**What is the longest heat wave in US history?**  
The longest run of 110°F days in a major US city is Phoenix's 31 consecutive days, from June 30 to July 30, 2023, at Sky Harbor Airport; the next longest there was 18 days in 1974.

# Worst Hurricanes to Hit Florida, Texas, Louisiana and North Carolina

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/worst-hurricanes-florida-texas-louisiana-north-carolina  
**Summary**: State by state, the strongest, deadliest and costliest hurricanes on record in Florida, Texas, Louisiana and North Carolina, with every track mapped, peak storm surge since 2017 and how early DisasterAWARE was tracking each recent landfall.

_The strongest, deadliest and costliest hurricanes on record in the four most hurricane-struck states, ranked from NOAA records and mapped._

**The worst hurricane to hit Florida was the 1928 Okeechobee hurricane, which killed at least 2,500 people; the strongest was the 1935 Labor Day hurricane and the costliest was Ian in 2022. In Texas, the Galveston hurricane of 1900 killed at least 8,000 people, more than any other US hurricane, and Harvey (2017) is the costliest. Louisiana's deadliest was the Cheniere Caminada hurricane of 1893 and its costliest was Katrina (2005). In North Carolina, Helene (2024) is the deadliest hurricane on record, and Hazel (1954) the strongest.**

NOAA's state-by-state table of continental US hurricane impacts records 128 hurricanes in Florida from 1851 through 2025, 67 in Texas, 65 in Louisiana and 60 in North Carolina, more than in any other state. Each state gets three lists below: strongest by wind, deadliest and costliest. Every storm on them is drawn on the map. For the hurricanes since 2014 we add what DisasterAWARE's archive recorded, and for the major landfalls since 2017 the peak storm surge.

## How These Lists Are Ranked

  * **Strongest.** Every hurricane that NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory (AOML) rates at Category 4 or 5 in the state, or Category 3 or higher in North Carolina, which has had only one Category 4. AOML rates each state separately from the estimated maximum sustained winds there. Storms are ordered by that category, then by the wind at landfall in the state from NHC's HURDAT2 best track, then by lower central pressure.
  * **Deadliest.** Deaths as the National Hurricane Center (NHC) or a National Weather Service (NWS) office report them for the state. For recent storms we rank the direct deaths (drowning, wind, surge) that NHC's Tropical Cyclone Reports give for the state. Older figures come from NOAA's list of US tropical cyclones that caused 25 or more deaths, where it names only this state. Where NOAA gives only a total for several states, the storm is not ranked; such totals of 50 or more are noted below the list.
  * **Costliest.** NOAA's billion-dollar disaster estimates, now maintained by Climate Central, which cover 1980 onward and are adjusted for inflation to 2026 dollars. These are whole-storm US costs, so each hurricane is counted once, for the state of its strongest US landfall.



## The Map: Every Listed Storm, Its Landfall and the Peak Surge

The map draws the NHC best track of every storm on the 12 lists, coloured by category at each 6-hourly fix, with a dot at each state landfall. Blue dots mark peak surge in NHC's post-storm analyses for 2017–2024 major landfalls and Florence (2018).

[Open map full screen ↗](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/maps/evergreen-worst-hurricanes-florida-texas-louisiana-north-carolina.html>)

**Explore the map:** switch on more layers with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: the **2014–2025 landfalls** below, as DisasterAWARE first recorded them; **wind swaths** and **wind radii** (2004 on); **NHC and NWS warnings** (ALERT, 2008 on); **aircraft recon fixes** (2008 on); **USGS high-water marks** (zoom in), **tide gauges** and **storm-total rainfall** ; and **satellite and radar** at landfall, one storm at a time (1980 on).

**Missing dots.** Camille (1969) came ashore in Mississippi, so it has no Louisiana dot; Helene (1958), Emily (1993) and Matthew (2016) kept their centres off the North Carolina coast. Helene (2024) has no North Carolina dot because it made landfall in Florida, and Allen (1980) has no Texas dot because HURDAT2 does not yet mark landfall points for 1976 to 1982. 

## Florida

Florida has been hit by more hurricanes than any other state, and by three of the four Category 5 landfalls on record in the continental US (see our [list of every Category 5 landfall](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/category-5-hurricanes-us-landfall>)).

### Strongest hurricanes to hit Florida

Rank| Hurricane| Florida landfall (UTC)| Category in Florida| Wind at landfall| Pressure  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Labor Day hurricane** 1935| Sep 3, 1935| 5| 160 kt (185 mph)| 892 mb  
2| **Andrew** 1992| Aug 24, 1992| 5| 145 kt (165 mph)| 922 mb  
3| **Michael** 2018| Oct 10, 2018| 5| 140 kt (160 mph)| 919 mb  
4| Florida Keys hurricane 1919| Sep 10, 1919| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 927 mb  
5 (tie)| Charley 2004| Aug 13, 2004| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 941 mb  
5 (tie)| Ian 2022| Sep 28, 2022| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 941 mb  
7| Okeechobee hurricane 1928| Sep 17, 1928| 4| 125 kt (145 mph)| 929 mb  
8 (tie)| Great Miami hurricane 1926| Sep 18, 1926| 4| 125 kt (145 mph)| 930 mb  
8 (tie)| Donna 1960| Sep 10, 1960| 4| 125 kt (145 mph)| 930 mb  
10| Helene 2024| Sep 27, 2024| 4| 120 kt (140 mph)| 939 mb

_Category: AOML state impact table. Wind and pressure: the storm's strongest Florida landfall record in NHC HURDAT2; landfall dates are UTC (the Labor Day hurricane came ashore on the evening of September 2 local time). Rows 12–16, in order: September 1948 (940 mb), September 1947 (943 mb), September 1945 (949 mb), August 1949 (954 mb) and King, October 1950 (955 mb)._

Sixteen hurricanes have hit Florida at Category 4 or 5, five of them since 2004. Charley and Ian came ashore at the same strength, 130 knots and 941 mb, at Cayo Costa on Florida's southwest coast, 18 years apart.

### Deadliest hurricanes to hit Florida

  1. **Okeechobee hurricane, 1928: at least 2,500 deaths** , and possibly as many as 3,000 (NHC). Thousands drowned when the storm pushed Lake Okeechobee over its levee (NWS Miami).
  2. **Labor Day hurricane, 1935: 408** , in the Florida Keys.
  3. **October 1906 hurricane: 164** , in southeast Florida and the Keys.
  4. **Ian, 2022: 66 direct deaths, 150 in all.** Every one of Ian's 66 direct US deaths was in Florida, and storm surge caused 41 of them; another 84 Floridians died of indirect causes, according to NHC.
  5. **October 1910 hurricane: 30** , in southwest Florida.



_Not ranked, because NOAA gives only a total for several states: the Great Miami hurricane of 1926 (372, the Red Cross count reported by NWS Miami), the September 1906 hurricane (134, Mississippi, Alabama and Pensacola), the September 1896 hurricane (130, with Georgia and South Carolina), Agnes in 1972 (122, Florida and the Northeast), Betsy in 1965 (75, with Louisiana), the September 1947 hurricane (51, with Louisiana and Mississippi) and Donna in 1960 (50, Florida and the eastern US). The 1919 Florida Keys hurricane's deaths are counted under Texas, where most of them occurred._

### Costliest hurricanes to hit Florida

  1. **Ian, 2022: $126.3 billion**
  2. **Helene, 2024: $83.4 billion**
  3. **Irma, 2017: $67.5 billion**
  4. **Andrew, 1992: $64.0 billion**
  5. **Milton, 2024: $36.3 billion**



_Whole-storm US cost, adjusted to 2026 dollars (Climate Central billion-dollar disaster database, continuing NOAA's). Michael (2018) is sixth at $33.0 billion._

## Texas

**No Category 5 hurricane has ever hit Texas.** Eight have struck at Category 4.

### Strongest hurricanes to hit Texas

Rank| Hurricane| Texas landfall (UTC)| Category in Texas| Wind at landfall| Pressure  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Indianola hurricane** 1886| Aug 20, 1886| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 925 mb  
2| **Freeport hurricane** 1932| Aug 14, 1932| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 935 mb  
3| **Carla** 1961| Sep 11, 1961| 4| 125 kt (145 mph)| 931 mb  
4| Galveston hurricane 1900| Sep 9, 1900| 4| 120 kt (140 mph)| 936 mb  
5| Celia 1970| Aug 3, 1970| 4| 120 kt (140 mph)| 944 mb  
6| Unnamed 1916| Aug 18, 1916| 4| 115 kt (130 mph)| 932 mb  
7| Harvey 2017| Aug 26, 2017| 4| 115 kt (130 mph)| 937 mb  
8| Galveston hurricane 1915| Aug 17, 1915| 4| 115 kt (130 mph)| 940 mb  
  
_Category: AOML. Wind and pressure: NHC HURDAT2 Texas landfall record. Dates are UTC._

### Deadliest hurricanes to hit Texas

  1. **Galveston hurricane, 1900: at least 8,000 deaths** , and possibly as many as 12,000 (NHC).
  2. **1919 Florida Keys hurricane: 284** , the official toll in Corpus Christi, where the NWS office there says the true number was more likely 600 to 1,000. The storm surge there reached 16 feet.
  3. **Galveston hurricane, 1915: 275.**
  4. **September 1875 hurricane: 176.**
  5. **Indianola hurricane, 1886: 150.** Harvey (2017) is next, with 68 direct deaths, all in Texas, and about 35 indirect; all but three of the direct deaths were from freshwater flooding. NHC calls Harvey the deadliest hurricane to hit Texas since 1919.



_Not ranked, because NOAA gives only a total for several states: Audrey in 1957 (416, southwest Louisiana and north Texas)._

### Costliest hurricanes to hit Texas

  1. **Harvey, 2017: $168.8 billion**
  2. **Ike, 2008: $45.9 billion**
  3. **Alicia, 1983: $10.0 billion**
  4. **Beryl, 2024: $7.7 billion**
  5. **Allen, 1980: $2.4 billion**



_Whole-storm US cost in 2026 dollars (Climate Central). Tropical Storm Allison (2001, $16.0 billion) would rank third but was never a hurricane._

Harvey alone cost more than twice as much as the other seven Texas-landfall hurricanes in the database combined. Its losses were driven by rain: NHC's report records more than 60 inches over southeastern Texas, and TDI found that most insured losses came from flood and commercial property claims.

## Louisiana

Louisiana's worst hurricanes are water disasters. Its deadliest struck low coastal settlements, and its costliest, Katrina, left about 80% of New Orleans flooded, according to NHC.

### Strongest hurricanes to hit Louisiana

Rank| Hurricane| Louisiana landfall (UTC)| Category in Louisiana| Wind at landfall| Pressure  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Camille** 1969| Landfall in Mississippi| 5| 150 kt (175 mph) *| 900 mb *  
2| **Ida** 2021| Aug 29, 2021| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 931 mb  
3| **Last Island hurricane** 1856| Aug 10, 1856| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 934 mb  
4| Laura 2020| Aug 27, 2020| 4| 130 kt (150 mph)| 939 mb  
5| Betsy 1965| Sep 10, 1965| 4| 115 kt (130 mph)| 946 mb  
6| Cheniere Caminada hurricane 1893| Oct 2, 1893| 4| 115 kt (130 mph)| 948 mb  
  
_Category: AOML. Wind and pressure: NHC HURDAT2 Louisiana landfall record. *Camille's centre came ashore near Waveland, Mississippi; AOML rates its winds in Louisiana at Category 5, and the values shown are AOML's for the US coast._

Katrina is not on this list: it came ashore in southeast Louisiana in 2005 as a Category 3, with 110-knot winds, although its 920 mb pressure is the lowest of any Louisiana landfall in HURDAT2.

### Deadliest hurricanes to hit Louisiana

  1. **Cheniere Caminada hurricane, 1893: 1,100 to 1,400 deaths** , and near 2,000 counting losses offshore (NHC).
  2. **Last Island hurricane, 1856: 400.**
  3. **Grand Isle hurricane, 1909: 350.**
  4. **Katrina, 2005: 341 direct deaths in Louisiana** , of 520 direct deaths in the US. Counting indirect deaths and those of undetermined cause, NHC's updated report puts Katrina's toll at nearly 1,400 across all states.
  5. **New Orleans hurricane, 1915: 275.**



_Not ranked, because NOAA gives only a total for several states: Audrey in 1957 (416, southwest Louisiana and north Texas), Camille in 1969 (256, Mississippi, southeast Louisiana and Virginia), Betsy in 1965 (75, with southeast Florida) and the September 1947 hurricane (51, with Florida and Mississippi)._

### Costliest hurricanes to hit Louisiana

  1. **Katrina, 2005: $212.6 billion** , the costliest US disaster in the database
  2. **Ida, 2021: $89.8 billion**
  3. **Rita, 2005: $31.1 billion**
  4. **Laura, 2020: $29.7 billion**
  5. **Gustav, 2008: $9.1 billion**



_Whole-storm US cost in 2026 dollars (Climate Central). Andrew (1992) made its second landfall in Louisiana and is counted under Florida._

## North Carolina

Seven of North Carolina's 60 hurricanes reached Category 3 or stronger there in AOML's table, and two of those seven never brought their centre ashore. Its deadliest made landfall in Florida.

### Strongest hurricanes to hit North Carolina

Rank| Hurricane| North Carolina landfall (UTC)| Category in NC| Wind| Pressure  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Hazel** 1954| Oct 15, 1954 (NC–SC border)| 4| 115 kt (130 mph)| 938 mb  
2| Helene 1958| Centre offshore| 3| 110 kt (125 mph) *| 938 mb *  
3| San Ciriaco hurricane 1899| Aug 18, 1899| 3| 105 kt (120 mph)| 945 mb *  
4| Fran 1996| Sep 6, 1996| 3| 100 kt (115 mph)| 954 mb  
5| Emily 1993| Centre offshore| 3| 100 kt (115 mph) *| 961 mb *  
6| Unnamed 1879| Aug 18, 1879| 3| 100 kt (115 mph)| 971 mb  
7| Gloria 1985| Sep 27, 1985| 3| 90 kt (105 mph)| 942 mb  
  
_Category: AOML. Wind and pressure: NHC HURDAT2 North Carolina landfall record; * AOML's coastal estimate where the centre stayed offshore or HURDAT2 has no pressure. Hazel's landfall point lies on the state line. AOML rates Gloria Category 3 in North Carolina although its HURDAT2 landfall wind, 90 kt, is Category 2 strength._

Hazel is the only Category 4 on record in North Carolina. It came ashore near Calabash at the time of the year's highest lunar tide, and the NWS reports a storm surge of up to 18 feet there. In Long Beach, only five of 357 buildings were left standing.

### Deadliest hurricanes to hit North Carolina

  1. **Helene, 2024: 85 direct deaths, 107 in all.** Freshwater flooding, including landslides and debris flows, caused 77 of the 85 direct deaths in western North Carolina, according to NHC. Helene's centre made landfall in Florida's Big Bend, not in North Carolina.
  2. **September 1883 hurricane: 53.**
  3. **Floyd, 1999: 35** of its 56 US deaths. Most of Floyd's deaths were drownings in freshwater flooding.
  4. **Fran, 1996: 26.**
  5. **(tie) Matthew, 2016: 25 direct deaths** , 24 of them in floods, and **Connie, 1955: 25.**



_Not ranked, because NOAA gives only a total for several states: the October 1898 hurricane (179, with Georgia and South Carolina; its centre came ashore in Georgia), the San Ciriaco hurricane of 1899 (at least 50, with South Carolina; the same storm killed 3,369 people in Puerto Rico) and the August 1940 hurricane (50, with Georgia and South Carolina). Hazel killed 19 people in North Carolina, according to NWS Newport/Morehead City, of 95 in the US (NWS Wilmington)._

### Costliest hurricanes to hit North Carolina

  1. **Florence, 2018: $31.7 billion**
  2. **Irene, 2011: $19.8 billion**
  3. **Floyd, 1999: $12.9 billion**
  4. **Fran, 1996: $10.6 billion**
  5. **Isabel, 2003: $9.9 billion**



_Whole-storm US cost in 2026 dollars (Climate Central), for hurricanes whose strongest US landfall was in North Carolina. Helene ($83.4 billion) is counted under Florida, where it came ashore, and Matthew under South Carolina._

## Peak Storm Surge Since 2017

NOAA found that large US hurricane death tolls were primarily the result of storm surge of 10 feet or more, and surge caused 41 of Ian's 66 direct deaths. These are the peak inundation heights in NHC's post-storm analyses, which combine tide gauges, USGS sensors and surveyed high-water marks (and, where observations were missing, storm-surge hindcasts), for every hurricane that came ashore in the four states at Category 3 or stronger from 2017 to 2024, plus Florence. Heights are above normally dry ground.

  * **Laura, 2020 (Louisiana): 17.1 ft** , a USGS still-water high-water mark in a home in Creole, the highest measurement without wave action; NHC estimates the maximum inundation at 18 ft.
  * **Helene, 2024 (Florida): 12 to 16 ft** from just west of Keaton Beach through Steinhatchee.
  * **Ian, 2022 (Florida): 10 to 15 ft** in Fort Myers Beach.
  * **Michael, 2018 (Florida): up to 14 ft** in Mexico Beach, where a USGS sensor on the pier recorded 14.7 ft above mean higher high water.
  * **Ida, 2021 (Louisiana): 9 to 14 ft** on the east bank of the Mississippi River in Plaquemines Parish.
  * **Idalia, 2023 (Florida): 8 to 12 ft** , partly from a hindcast, from Keaton Beach to Steinhatchee.
  * **Florence, 2018 (North Carolina): 8 to 11 ft** along the Neuse River and its tributaries; a USGS sensor across the river from New Bern recorded 10.4 ft above mean higher high water.
  * **Harvey, 2017 (Texas): 8 to 10 ft** on the western shores of San Antonio and Hynes bays.
  * **Milton, 2024 (Florida): up to 10 ft** near Manasota Key, an NHC estimate (no reliable high-water mark there).
  * **Zeta, 2020 (Louisiana): 6 to 10 ft** , from observations and a hindcast, in unprotected wetlands of Plaquemines Parish west of the Mississippi River levee, between Port Sulphur and Empire.
  * **Irma, 2017 (Florida): 5 to 8 ft** in the Lower Keys, from Cudjoe Key to Big Pine Key and Bahia Honda Key.

_Alert tier: the time from the storm's earliest DisasterAWARE record to landfall, rounded to the nearest hour. It measures how long the platform had been tracking the storm, not a specific warning's lead time. There were no US hurricane landfalls in 2025._

DisasterAWARE was carrying all 24 storms more than 38 hours before landfall, and 20 of them at least three days ahead. For the six landfalls since 2023, the archive also holds the NWS post-storm station maxima, all OBSERVED. Helene's record carries 1,410 rainfall stations, topped by 30.78 inches at Busick, North Carolina, and 87 water-level stations. Milton's peak rainfall, 20.4 inches, fell near St. Petersburg, and Beryl's, 14.99 inches, at Thompsons, Texas.

### For insurers and reinsurers

  * **The losses, state by state.** State insurance regulators collect claims from the insurers they oversee; none of the four figures includes policies written directly by the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation (OIR) puts Ian's estimated insured losses at $22.2 billion on 789,066 claims (as of March 4, 2025). The Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) reported that insurers expected to pay $19.6 billion on about 763,000 Harvey claims (through September 30, 2018), $6.7 billion of it federal flood insurance written by private insurers. The Louisiana Department of Insurance (LDI) reported $13.9 billion paid or reserved on 478,417 Ida claims through September 30, 2022. North Carolina's Department of Insurance (NC DOI) counted $3.49 billion of incurred losses on 125,658 Helene claims as of September 12, 2025.
  * **How these storms changed the view of the peril.** Category says little about loss. Harvey, a Category 4, did most of its damage with rain and became Texas's costliest hurricane. Helene's North Carolina deaths came from flooding far inland, in a state where it did not make landfall. Helene's insured losses in North Carolina ($3.49 billion, NC DOI) compare with its whole-storm cost of $83.4 billion (Climate Central).
  * **What event-level data exists.** For storms since 1998, DisasterAWARE's enhanced records hold the best track, with quadrant 34-, 50- and 64-knot wind radii where the agencies published them (generally from 2004), and the time the platform first carried the event. For 2023 onward they add NWS post-storm rainfall, water-level and wind-station maxima.
  * **What we do not hold.** DisasterAWARE's cyclone records carry no casualty or damage figures; every death and loss figure here is quoted from the named source.
  * **Where to go next.** [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>) delivers these storms as structured, location-queryable events. You can request a [sample dataset](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>) for your exposure along the Gulf and Carolina coasts.



## 2026 Status

  * **Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, at about 8:30 p.m. CDT on October 9, 2026 (01:30 UTC October 10),** as a Category 2 with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph and a central pressure of 971 mb, according to NHC's preliminary estimate. It was the season's first Atlantic hurricane; at noon CDT that day, NHC had given 120 mph and 959 mb.
  * This page will be updated when NHC publishes its final report on Isaias.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the worst hurricane to hit Florida?**  
By deaths, the 1928 Okeechobee hurricane, which killed at least 2,500 people around Lake Okeechobee. The strongest was the 1935 Labor Day hurricane (892 mb, 185 mph) in the Florida Keys, and the costliest was Ian in 2022, at $126.3 billion in 2026 dollars.

**What is the worst hurricane to hit Texas?**  
The Galveston hurricane of September 1900, a Category 4 that killed at least 8,000 people. The strongest Texas landfall was the 1886 Indianola hurricane, and the costliest Texas hurricane is Harvey (2017), at $168.8 billion in 2026 dollars. No Category 5 hurricane has ever hit Texas.

**What is the worst hurricane to hit Louisiana?**  
Katrina (2005) is the costliest, at $212.6 billion in 2026 dollars, and caused 341 direct deaths in Louisiana. The deadliest was the Cheniere Caminada hurricane of 1893, which killed 1,100 to 1,400 people. Camille (1969) brought Category 5 winds to Louisiana, and Ida (2021) came ashore with 150 mph winds and the lowest pressure of the state's Category 4 landfalls.

**What is the worst hurricane to hit North Carolina?**  
Helene (2024), which caused 85 direct deaths in North Carolina, 77 of them from flooding in the western mountains, and 107 deaths in all. The strongest was Hazel (1954), the only Category 4 on record in the state, and the costliest whose strongest landfall was in North Carolina is Florence (2018), at $31.7 billion.

**Which state is hit by the most hurricanes?**  
Florida. NOAA's table records hurricane impacts in Florida 128 times from 1851 through 2025, followed by Texas (67), Louisiana (65) and North Carolina (60).

# Biggest Snowstorms in NYC, Boston, Chicago and Buffalo History: The Top 10 in Each City (Mapped)

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/biggest-snowstorms-nyc-boston-chicago-buffalo-history  
**Summary**: The 10 biggest snowstorms in New York City, Boston, Chicago and Buffalo, ranked by storm total at each city's official station, with how storm totals are counted, the 2026 storms that made the lists, snowfall maps and what the storms cost.

_The 10 biggest snowstorms in each city, ranked by the storm total at its official weather station, with the storms of 2026 included._

**What was the biggest snowstorm in NYC history? The blizzard of January 22–24, 2016, which left 27.5 inches in Central Park, the official record since 1869.** The biggest snowstorm in Boston history is the Presidents' Day storm of February 17–18, 2003: 27.6 inches at the official station. Chicago's biggest is the Big Snow of January 26–27, 1967, with 23.0 inches. Buffalo's biggest is a lake-effect storm: 81.6 inches at the airport between December 24, 2001 and January 1, 2002. The winter of 2026 put two new storms on these lists: the February 22–23 blizzard is ninth in New York (19.7 inches), and the January 25–27 storm is eighth in Boston (23.2 inches). Below: the four lists, how storm totals are counted, the worst blizzards, a snowfall map, the warnings before recent storms, and the costs.

## How a Storm Total Is Counted

Official snowfall is recorded **per calendar day** at one station in each city. A storm total adds up the days a storm lasted, and nobody publishes those totals as an official statistic. The National Weather Service office in Chicago says so plainly: "calendar day snowfall records are part of the official climate database for major cities around the country. However, storm total snowfall records are considered 'unofficial' and are mainly developed and maintained by local NWS offices and weather historians." Deciding where an old storm began and ended, it adds, "is somewhat subjective."

That leaves two kinds of list:

  * **New York and Chicago** have lists published by their local NWS offices. We use them as published, and add the one 2026 storm that is newer than the New York list.
  * **Boston and Buffalo** have no published NWS storm list, so we compiled theirs from the official daily record (as served by NOAA's Applied Climate Information System, ACIS), with one mechanical rule applied identically in both cities. **A storm's dates come from the National Weather Service's own record of the event where one exists:** NWS Buffalo's lake-effect event summaries, then NWS Buffalo's weather-history pages, then NWS Storm Data entries for the station's zone (in NOAA's Storm Events Database since 1996). **Where no NWS event record exists, a storm is a run of consecutive days with measurable snow (0.1 inch or more).** The storm total is the sum of the official daily snowfall on those dates. Undocumented runs longer than five days usually hold several storms, so we list them rather than rank them.



Where the National Weather Service has published an airport total for a listed storm, the rule matches it: 81.6 inches for Buffalo's 2001 storm, 51.9 for 2022, 34.4 for 1985 and 28.3 for 1984; 25.4, 23.8 and 23.2 inches for Boston's 1997, 2022 and 2026 storms. Two differ: NWS Storm Data gave Boston's 2003 storm as 27.5 inches, while the official daily values add up to 27.6, and NWS Buffalo's summary of the November 20–23, 2000 storm gives 25 inches for "Buffalo NWS", against 26.4 in the daily values.

**Where the rule matters.** Boston has one undocumented run that the five-day rule leaves out: February 8–13, 1994, with 26.9 inches over six days, which the daily values suggest held two storms (18.7 inches on February 8–10, then 8.0 inches on February 11). Counted as one storm it would rank third. In Buffalo, 13 undocumented runs of six days or more would make the top 10 if counted whole, and three places (1936, 1958 and 1961) rest on undocumented runs of up to five days.

**Periods of record:** Central Park since 1869; Chicago since 1884; Buffalo since 1884; Boston since 1891. Every value in the tables below is OBSERVED: snow measured at the station.

## The Biggest Snowstorms in New York City History (Central Park)

_Official National Weather Service list (NWS New York), with the February 2026 storm added from the NWS storm total._

#| Storm total| Dates  
---|---|---  
1| **27.5 in**|  January 22–24, 2016  
2| **26.9 in**|  February 11–12, 2006  
3| **26.4 in**|  December 26–27, 1947  
4| **21.0 in**|  March 12–14, 1888  
5| **20.9 in**|  February 25–26, 2010  
6| **20.2 in**|  January 7–8, 1996  
7| **20.0 in**|  December 26–27, 2010  
8| **19.8 in**|  February 16–17, 2003  
9| **19.7 in**|  February 22–23, 2026  
10| **19.0 in**|  January 26–27, 2011  
  
_Source: NWS New York, "Biggest Snowstorms (One Foot or More) at Central Park (1869 to Present)", last updated January 1, 2026; February 2026 storm total from the NWS New York storm summary (19.7 inches)._

Seven of New York's ten biggest storms have come since 2000, and five since 2010. The 2016 record was a blizzard; the 1888 storm is the Great Blizzard of 1888, and the December 1947 storm dropped 26.1 inches on December 26 alone. Next on the list, at 18.1 inches, are January 22–24, 1935 and March 7–8, 1941. The **Blizzard of 2026** is the newest: 8.8 inches on February 22 and 10.9 inches on February 23, both record snowfalls for those dates, for a storm total of 19.7 inches, one-tenth of an inch behind Presidents' Day 2003.

## The Biggest Snowstorms in Boston History (Logan Airport)

_Compiled by DisasterAWARE from the official NWS daily record (rule above). NWS Boston publishes no storm-total list._

#| Storm total| Dates| Storm dates from| Notes  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| **27.6 in**|  February 17–18, 2003| NWS Storm Data| Presidents’ Day storm; Boston record  
2| **27.1 in**|  February 6–7, 1978| Daily record| Blizzard of ’78  
3| **26.3 in**|  February 24–27, 1969| Daily record| The “100-hour storm”  
4| **25.4 in**|  March 31 – April 1, 1997| NWS Storm Data| April Fools’ Day storm  
5| **24.9 in**|  February 8–9, 2013| NWS Storm Data|   
6| **24.6 in**|  January 26–28, 2015| NWS Storm Data| Blizzard; Boston’s record 110.6-in winter of 2014–15  
7| **23.8 in**|  January 28–29, 2022| NWS Storm Data| Blizzard  
8| **23.2 in**|  January 25–27, 2026| NWS Storm Data| Record daily snowfall Jan 25 (16.7 in)  
9| **22.9 in**|  February 8–10, 2015| NWS Storm Data| Also in the record 2014–15 winter  
10| **22.5 in**|  January 22–23, 2005| NWS Storm Data|   
  
_Storm totals from the official daily snowfall record for Boston (NOAA ACIS, threaded station record), with storm dates as shown. Next on the list: 21.5 inches, January 20–22, 1978._

Boston's top two are 25 years apart and only half an inch different: 27.6 inches in 2003 and 27.1 inches in the Blizzard of '78. Two of the ten fell in early 2015, the winter Boston set its seasonal snowfall record of 110.6 inches. The **January 25–27, 2026** storm brought 16.7 inches on the 25th, a record for the date, and 6.5 inches on the 26th, for 23.2 inches (NWS Storm Data gives the same figure for Logan) and eighth place. The **Blizzard of 2026** a month later, on February 23, dropped 17.1 inches at Logan, the date's record, but did not make the top 10.

## The Biggest Snowstorms in Chicago History (O'Hare and Midway)

_Official National Weather Service list (NWS Chicago)._

#| Storm total| Dates  
---|---|---  
1| **23.0 in**|  January 26–27, 1967  
2| **21.6 in**|  January 1–3, 1999  
3| **21.2 in**|  January 31 – February 2, 2011  
4| **20.3 in**|  January 12–14, 1979  
5| **19.3 in**|  January 31 – February 2, 2015  
6| **19.2 in**|  March 25–26, 1930  
7| **16.2 in**|  March 7–8, 1931  
8=| **14.9 in**|  January 6–7, 1918  
8=| **14.9 in**|  January 30, 1939  
10| **14.8 in**|  December 17–19, 1929  
  
_Source: NWS Chicago, "Chicago's Top 10 Largest Snowstorms" (list updated in 2015 and verified in 2025). Midway Airport was Chicago's official station for the 1967 and 1979 storms; O'Hare is the official station today._

No Chicago storm has broken into the top 10 since 2015. The biggest of the 2025–26 winter, around November 29–December 1, 2025, left about 10 inches at O'Hare.

**What was the worst blizzard in Chicago history?** On snow totals and on impact, the **January 26–27, 1967** storm. Snow began at 5:02 a.m. on January 26, and by 10:10 a.m. the next day 23 inches had fallen, with gusts to 53 mph at Midway. NWS Chicago records that 20,000 cars and 1,100 CTA buses were stranded in the city. About 60 people died, and business losses were an estimated $150 million at the time. NWS Chicago counts only the 1967 and 2011 storms as true blizzards among its top four, measured by the strength of the wind and how long visibility stayed near zero. In 2011 the visibility at O'Hare stayed at or below a quarter mile for 11 consecutive hours, and drivers were stranded on Lake Shore Drive. The January 1979 storm was not a blizzard by that measure, but it closed O'Hare for 46 hours, and roofs collapsed under the snow.

## The Biggest Snowstorms in Buffalo History (Buffalo Airport)

_Compiled by DisasterAWARE from the official NWS daily record (rule above). NWS Buffalo publishes no storm-total list._

#| Storm total| Dates| Storm dates from| Notes  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| **81.6 in**|  December 24, 2001 – January 1, 2002| NWS BUF event summary| Lake effect; 81.5 in fell Dec 24–28  
2| **51.9 in**|  December 23–27, 2022| NWS BUF event summary| Blizzard and lake effect  
3| **42.3 in**|  December 9–11, 1995| NWS BUF history page| Lake effect; 33.9 in on Dec 10  
4| **36.6 in**|  November 17–20, 2022| NWS BUF event summary| Lake effect; Bills game moved to Detroit  
5| **34.4 in**|  January 19–22, 1985| NWS BUF history page| Blizzard of ’85  
6| **30.3 in**|  March 17–21, 1936| Daily record|   
7| **28.5 in**|  February 15–19, 1958| Daily record|   
8| **28.3 in**|  February 27–29, 1984| NWS BUF history page| NWS: snow began 5:30 p.m. on the 27th  
9| **26.4 in**|  November 20–23, 2000| NWS BUF event summary| 24.9 in on November 20  
10| **25.7 in**|  December 27–31, 1961| Daily record|   
  
_Storm totals from the official daily snowfall record for Buffalo (NOAA ACIS, threaded station record), with storm dates as shown. Next on the list: 25.6 inches, December 31, 1944 – January 4, 1945._

Buffalo's top storms are mostly lake-effect: narrow bands of snow off Lake Erie that can bury the airport while nearby towns see far less. The **Christmas week storm of 2001** is in a class of its own: 20.5 inches on December 24, 21.9 inches on the 27th and 26.2 inches on the 28th, and 81.6 inches over the whole event as NWS Buffalo dates it. The **Blizzard of '85** (January 19–22, 1985) is fifth: NWS Buffalo records 34.4 inches in four days, with a driving ban across five western New York counties.

Thirteen undocumented runs of more than five days would make this top 10 if counted whole, so we name them rather than rank them. The largest are December 9, 1985 – January 1, 1986 (64.2 inches over 24 days), December 10–17, 1945 (40.7 inches), January 2–10, 1892 (34.3) and January 4–11, 1982 (32.5).

**What was the worst blizzard in Buffalo history?** Two storms, and neither won on snowfall alone.

  * **The Blizzard of '77 (January 28–February 1, 1977)** dropped only about 12 inches at the airport, much of it snow blown in off frozen Lake Erie. But it struck a city already holding a 37-inch snowpack. Winds averaged 46 mph and gusted to 69 mph at the airport, with wind chills of 55 to 60 below. NWS Buffalo records 29 deaths. President Carter declared a federal disaster area, the first ever for a snowstorm in the US.
  * **The Blizzard of 2022 (December 23–27)** brought both the wind and the snow: 51.9 inches at the airport, 22.3 inches of it on December 23 alone, a daily record. Blizzard conditions lasted 40 consecutive hours at the airport, with gusts to 72 mph. NWS Buffalo reports that the Thruway closed from Rochester to the Pennsylvania line, that travel bans in Erie and Niagara counties lasted a day or two beyond the blizzard, and that the Buffalo airport closed for several days. The storm was deadly in Buffalo; Climate Central's billion-dollar record attributes 87 deaths to the whole storm and cold wave, across the US.

Nine storms on the four lists have come since 2014. For each, the table shows the National Weather Service winter storm, blizzard or lake-effect snow warnings in force for the official station's forecast zone during the storm, when the first was issued, and when snow began at the station. These are NWS warnings (IEM): issued products, the ALERT tier, not measurements.

Storm (rank)| NWS warning(s) for the station's zone| First warning issued| Snow began at the station| Warning issued

"First warning issued" is the time of the product that first issued it, often an upgrade from a watch. "Snow began" is the first hourly or special observation (IEM ASOS archive) of the continuous run of snow reports that led into the storm. Standard time._

For every one of these storms a warning had been issued before steady snow began at the station, from about 4 hours ahead for Boston's February 2015 storm to almost two days ahead for its January 2026 storm. In three cases the warning changed type as the storm went on: Chicago's 2015 Winter Storm Warning was upgraded to a Blizzard Warning, and Boston's January 2015 and Buffalo's December 2022 Blizzard Warnings were followed by Winter Storm Warnings.

## For Insurers and Reinsurers: What Big City Snowstorms Cost

In big cities, snowstorm losses come through three channels.

  * **Roof collapse and snow load.** In early 2015, Boston's storms came one after another and roof snow compacted. 106 roofs caved in across Massachusetts in the two weeks to February 20, 2015, including a commercial plaza, a daycare centre and a lumber retailer (Insurance Journal, citing the Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency). Climate Central's record for the February 14–20, 2015 storm and cold wave notes "load-stress on buildings" in Boston and direct Massachusetts losses above $1.0 billion. Chicago's 1979 storm also collapsed roofs (NWS Chicago).
  * **Business interruption and transport.** The 1967 Chicago storm caused an estimated $150 million in business losses, in the money of the time, and O'Hare closed for 46 hours in 1979 (NWS Chicago). Buffalo's 2022 blizzard closed the airport for several days and the Thruway across western New York; Climate Central puts the whole December 21–26, 2022 storm and cold wave at $9.5 billion; it notes widespread frozen water pipes that led to extensive water damage.
  * **Regional loss.** The Groundhog Day Blizzard of February 1–3, 2011, Chicago's third-biggest storm, cost $2.7 billion and killed 36 people across the central and eastern US (Climate Central). The January 23–26, 2026 storm, Boston's eighth-biggest, is the costliest winter storm of 2026 so far in Climate Central's database: $4.5 billion and 171 deaths, with snow, ice and record cold from the Central US into the Deep South.



_Climate Central costs are CPI-adjusted and cover each event's whole footprint, not one city. Several storms on these lists, including New York's 2016 record, do not appear in the billion-dollar database at all._

**The data question.** A storm total at one airport is a poor proxy for a portfolio's loss. In November 2022, NWS Buffalo reported 81.2 inches at Hamburg, more than twice the airport's 36.6. In 2016, the NOHRSC analysis shows more than 30 inches southwest of New York City, where Central Park measured 27.5. An underwriter needs where the snow and wind actually fell, how long warnings were in force over each location, and what was exposed beneath them. ## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the biggest snowstorm in NYC history?**  
The blizzard of January 22–24, 2016: 27.5 inches in Central Park, according to the National Weather Service. It edged out the February 11–12, 2006 storm (26.9 inches) and the December 26–27, 1947 storm (26.4 inches). The most recent storm on the top-10 list is the Blizzard of February 22–23, 2026, ninth with 19.7 inches.

**What is the biggest snowstorm in Boston history?**  
The Presidents' Day storm of February 17–18, 2003, with 27.6 inches at Boston's official station, just ahead of the Blizzard of '78 (27.1 inches, February 6–7, 1978). The January 25–27, 2026 storm, with 23.2 inches, is eighth.

**What is the biggest snowstorm in Chicago history?**  
The Big Snow of January 26–27, 1967: 23.0 inches, measured at Midway Airport, which was then the official station. Second is the New Year's storm of January 1–3, 1999 (21.6 inches) and third the Groundhog Day Blizzard of 2011 (21.2 inches).

**What was the worst blizzard in Buffalo history?**  
By impact, the Blizzard of '77 (January 28–February 1, 1977): 29 deaths, and the first federal disaster declaration for a snowstorm in the US, although only about 12 inches of new snow was measured at the airport. The Blizzard of 2022 combined blizzard winds with 51.9 inches of snow at the airport, Buffalo's second-biggest storm total. The biggest storm by snowfall is the lake-effect storm of December 24, 2001 – January 1, 2002: 81.6 inches.

**Why do snowstorm totals differ between sources?**  
Official snowfall is recorded per calendar day; storm totals are an unofficial sum, and sources choose different start and end days. Some lists also use a rolling two-day window, which can count one storm twice. This article uses the National Weather Service's published lists for New York and Chicago, and for Boston and Buffalo the storm dates in the National Weather Service's own event records, summed from the official daily record.
