# Worst Winter Storms in US History: Blizzards, Ice Storms and Deep Freezes Ranked

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/worst-winter-storms-us-history  
**Summary**: The worst winter storms in US history, ranked four ways: costliest (Uri, the 1993 Superstorm, Elliott), every NOAA Category 5 snowstorm since 1900, the worst ice storms and costliest deep freezes. With snowfall maps and Uri's lessons for insurers.

_Four rankings, four rules: the costliest winter storms, every Category 5 snowstorm since 1900, the worst ice storms, and the costliest deep freezes, with snowfall maps for the storms since 2009._

**What was the worst winter storm in US history? By cost, the February 2021 storm and cold wave known as Winter Storm Uri: $28.8 billion in 2026 dollars and 262 deaths, more than twice the cost of any other winter storm in the billion-dollar disaster record that began in 1980.** By snowfall impact, the worst is the Great Blizzard of January 1978, whose score of 39.07 on NOAA's Regional Snowfall Index is the highest of any storm rated since 1900. By deaths, no federal list reaches back before 1980, but NOAA's account of the Great Blizzard of March 1888 puts its toll at more than 400, above the 270 of the 1993 "Storm of the Century", the deadliest winter storm in the billion-dollar record. Winter storms are not one hazard but three (snow, ice and cold), so below is a separate ranking for each, plus the costliest storms overall.

## How We Rank Winter Storms

No single official "worst winter storm" list exists, so each table uses one public source and states its rule: **cost** from Climate Central's billion-dollar disaster database (which took over the dataset from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information, NCEI, in 2025; total direct losses in 2026 dollars); **snowstorms** from NCEI's Regional Snowfall Index; **ice storms** from NOAA's Storm Events Database; **cold** from Climate Central's freeze and cold-wave events. Figures from DisasterAWARE's own archive are labelled as **alerts** (issued warnings and advisories), never as measurements.

## The Costliest Winter Storms in US History

Ranking rule: every Climate Central billion-dollar event of type "winter storm", 1980 to 2026, by cost in 2026 dollars.

#| Storm (Climate Central name)| Dates| Cost, 2026 dollars| Deaths  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Northwest, Central, Eastern Winter Storm and Cold Wave (**Uri**)| Feb 10–19, 2021| $28.8 billion| 262  
2| East Coast Blizzard and Severe Weather (**1993 Superstorm**)| Mar 11–14, 1993| $12.9 billion| 270  
3| Central and Eastern Winter Storm and Cold Wave (**Elliott**)| Dec 21–26, 2022| $9.5 billion| 87  
4| Southeast Ice Storm| Feb 8–13, 1994| $6.8 billion| 9  
5| Blizzard/Floods (**Blizzard of 1996** and the floods after it)| Jan 1–31, 1996| $6.5 billion| 187  
6| Northeast Winter Storm| Dec 10–13, 1992| $5.8 billion| 19  
7| Central and Eastern Winter Storm| Jan 23–26, 2026| $4.5 billion| 171  
8| Central and Eastern Winter Storm, Cold Wave| Feb 14–20, 2015| $4.2 billion| 30  
9| Midwest/Southeast/Northeast Winter Storm| Jan 5–8, 2014| $3.1 billion| 16  
10| Northeast Winter Storm| Mar 1–3, 2018| $2.9 billion| 9  
  
_Source: Climate Central, U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters (events list read October 9, 2026). Names in bold are the common names; Climate Central uses descriptive names._

Three of the ten have come since 2021, and the most recent, in January 2026, is already the seventh costliest and the fourth deadliest winter storm in the record. It is also the deadliest disaster of 2026 so far in Climate Central's record: a storm that brought snow and ice across the central and eastern states and into the Deep South, with daily record lows from Oklahoma and Texas to Alabama, and in parts of northern Mississippi power outages that lasted more than two weeks.

## The Worst Blizzards and Snowstorms: Every Category 5 Storm Since 1900

NCEI's Regional Snowfall Index scores a storm from the area it covered with snow, how deep the snow was and how many people lived under it, separately for each of six regions in the eastern two-thirds of the country. Category 5, "Extreme", is a score of 18 or more, which NCEI says about 1% of storms reach. NCEI has rated more than 500 storms back to 1900; only 26 reached Category 5 in any region. Ranking rule: each storm's highest regional score. The index measures a storm against what a region normally gets, so a Category 5 in the South can involve far less snow than one on the Northern Plains.

#| Storm (NCEI name, where it gives one)| Dates| Region(s) at Category 5| Highest RSI  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Great Blizzard of 1978 (Cleveland Superbomb)| Jan 23–28, 1978| Upper Midwest| 39.07  
2| Great Appalachian Storm of 1950| Nov 22–30, 1950| Ohio Valley| 34.69  
3| —| Apr 10–15, 1927| Northern Rockies & Plains| 34.20  
4| —| Feb 22–28, 1969| Northeast| 34.03  
5| —| Feb 18–22, 1921| South| 31.89  
6| —| Oct 31 – Nov 4, 1991| Upper Midwest| 30.18  
7| —| Feb 7–15, 1985| Upper Midwest| 27.06  
8| **High Plains to Great Lakes blizzard of 2026**|  Mar 14–17, 2026| Upper Midwest| 26.97  
9| Blizzard of 1996| Jan 6–9, 1996| Southeast (26.37); Northeast (21.71)| 26.37  
10| —| Apr 25–28, 1984| Northern Rockies & Plains| 25.95  
  
**Ranks 11 to 26:** 11\. Superstorm of 1993, Mar 12–15, 1993 (Ohio Valley 24.63, Southeast 24.43, Northeast 22.12); 12. Feb 27 – Mar 3, 1927 (Southeast, 24.42); 13. Jan 5–9, 1988 (South, 22.64); 14. Nov 28 – Dec 2, 1985 (Upper Midwest, 22.18); 15. Nov 21–29, 1993 (Northern Rockies & Plains, 22.00); 16. Groundhog Day Blizzard of 2011, Feb 1–4, 2011 (Ohio Valley, 21.99); 17. Jan 19–26, 1943 (Northern Rockies & Plains, 21.14); 18. Dec 19–24, 1929 (South, 21.13); 19. Apr 15–19, 1920 (Northern Rockies & Plains, 20.84); 20. Feb 28 – Mar 6, 1966 (Northern Rockies & Plains, 20.38); 21. Dec 22–29, 2009 (Northern Rockies & Plains, 19.62); 22. Feb 19–24, 1971 (South, 19.36); 23. Knickerbocker Storm, Jan 26–30, 1922 (Southeast, 18.53); 24. Blizzard of 1978, Feb 4–8, 1978 (Northeast, 18.42); 25. Jan 21–24, 1940 (Southeast, 18.14); 26. Chicago Blizzard of 1967, Jan 25–29, 1967 (Ohio Valley, 18.13).

_Source: NOAA NCEI Regional Snowfall Index, RSI and Societal Impacts tables for all six regions (read October 9, 2026). Storms rated Category 5 in more than one region are listed once. RSI uses 2000 Census population for every storm, so old and new storms are scored on the same population._

A few storms stand out:

  * **The 1993 Superstorm** is the only storm rated Category 5 in three regions at once, and the 1996 blizzard the only other one in two. Ranked by its highest single-region score, it comes 11th. NCEI's description says it hit more than 100 million people, buried Mount Le Conte in the Smokies under 5 feet of snow, and set Syracuse's 24-hour record of 35.4 inches.
  * **The Great Appalachian Storm of 1950** dropped 62 inches at Coburn Creek, West Virginia, brought a 108 mph gust to Newark, New Jersey, and 3°F to Atlanta, according to NCEI.
  * **The Knickerbocker Storm of 1922** dumped the heaviest snowfall in Washington, D.C.'s history, 24 to 38 inches across the area. The roof of the Knickerbocker Theater collapsed under it and killed about 100 people.
  * **The March 2026 High Plains to Great Lakes blizzard** is the newest Category 5. It was the first Category 5 in any region since the Groundhog Day Blizzard of 2011, and its 26.97 is the highest regional score since the Oct 31 – Nov 4, 1991 storm in the Upper Midwest. The Weather Prediction Center's final storm summary listed preliminary totals of 36.0 inches at Herman, Michigan, and 34.0 inches at Mountain, Wisconsin, with gusts to 69 mph at Grand Marais, Michigan.



**Before 1900.** The RSI starts in 1900, so it does not rate the two great blizzards of 1888. On March 12–14, 1888, the Great Blizzard buried the Northeast under as much as 58 inches of snow, with drifts over 50 feet, and more than 400 people died, according to NOAA's Physical Sciences Laboratory. Two months earlier, on January 12, 1888, the "Children's Blizzard" swept the northern Plains, with temperatures falling as low as -40°F; the National Weather Service's heritage project puts its toll at between 250 and 500.

For the biggest snowstorms on record in New York, Boston, Chicago and Buffalo, with the measured city totals, see our [city snowstorm records](<https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/biggest-snowstorms-nyc-boston-chicago-buffalo-history>).

## The Worst Ice Storms in US History

Ranking rule: NOAA Storm Events Database entries coded "Ice Storm", 1996–2025, joined into storms (an entry begins within 24 hours of the previous one), ranked by the property and crop damage reported to NOAA, in dollars of the year. We found 420 such storms; the top 10 are the same if entries are joined at 36 hours.

#| Dates| Hardest-hit states (reported damage)| Reported damage| Deaths recorded  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Jan 26–28, 2009| Arkansas $794M, Kentucky $307M, Missouri $50M| $1,156 million| 20  
2| Dec 8–12, 2007| Oklahoma $826M, Kansas $154M, Missouri $18M| $1,006 million| 17  
3| Dec 10–14, 2000| Arkansas $360M, Texas $124M, Louisiana $27M| $511 million| 2  
4| Jan 29–31, 2002| Oklahoma $302M, Kansas $37M, Missouri $32M| $382 million| 0  
5| Dec 24–28, 2000| Arkansas $165M, Louisiana $106M, Oklahoma $76M, Texas $32M| $378 million| 0  
6| Jan 3–10, 1998| Maine $304M, New Hampshire $28M, New York $23M| $362 million| 3  
7| Jan 12–20, 2007| Missouri $355M| $360 million| 6  
8| Dec 3–5, 2002| North Carolina $199M, South Carolina $100M, Arkansas $10M| $312 million| 1  
9| Apr 3–5, 2003| Michigan $166M, New York $66M| $232 million| 2  
10| Jan 1–6, 2005| Ohio $125M| $126 million| 0  
  
_Source: NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database, detail files for 1996–2025 (versions of March–August 2026). States listed where reported damage was $10 million or more. Deaths are those recorded in the ice-storm entries (direct and indirect)._

Reported damage understates the true cost. The January 1998 ice storm in the Northeast shows $362 million in Storm Events but **$2.9 billion** (2026 dollars) in Climate Central's total-cost record. The costliest ice storm of all predates the Storm Events coding: the **Southeast Ice Storm of February 8–13, 1994** , at $6.8 billion, fourth among all winter storms in the cost table above. Ice was also a large part of the January 2026 storm (NWS offices issued 16 ice storm warnings across 10 states, from Texas to the Carolinas, according to NWS warnings (IEM); see below), but NOAA's 2026 Storm Events file is still preliminary, so 2026 is not ranked here yet.

## The Worst Deep Freezes and Cold Waves

Ranking rule: every Climate Central event classed as a freeze or with "Cold Wave" in its name (20 events, 1980–2026), by cost in 2026 dollars.

#| Event (Climate Central name)| Dates| Cost, 2026 dollars| Deaths  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Northwest, Central, Eastern Winter Storm and Cold Wave (**Uri**)| Feb 10–19, 2021| $28.8 billion| 262  
2| Central and Eastern Winter Storm and Cold Wave (**Elliott**)| Dec 21–26, 2022| $9.5 billion| 87  
3| California Freeze| Dec 18–25, 1990| $8.9 billion| 0  
4| Freeze/Cold Wave| Dec 15–25, 1983| $6.8 billion| 151  
5| Florida Freeze| Dec 23–25, 1989| $5.5 billion| 10  
6| California Freeze| Dec 20–28, 1998| $5.2 billion| 0  
7| Central and Eastern Winter Storm, Cold Wave| Feb 14–20, 2015| $4.2 billion| 30  
8| Florida Freeze| Jan 20–22, 1985| $3.8 billion| 0  
9| Spring Freeze| Apr 4–10, 2007| $3.4 billion| 0  
10| Florida Freeze| Jan 23 – Feb 5, 2026| $3.2 billion| 0  
  
_Source: Climate Central billion-dollar disasters (read October 9, 2026)._

Two kinds of cold do the damage. Cold waves kill people and burst pipes: the December 1983 cold wave killed 151 and the January 1985 cold wave 150. Crop freezes cost billions with no deaths at all: the California freezes of 1990 and 1998 (citrus, avocados, fruit and vegetables in the San Joaquin Valley) and the Florida citrus freezes. The newest, Florida's freeze of late January into early February 2026, cost $3.2 billion, particularly to citrus, according to Climate Central, which notes that the first week of February ranked among the three coldest such weeks on record on the Florida Peninsula.

## From 1888 to Uri to Elliott: What Changed

The 1888 blizzard shut down transport and wrecked boats, and NOAA notes that it helped push New York to build its subway and put power and telegraph lines underground. Uri, 133 years later, was a story of systems failing.

**Uri, February 2021.** Much of Texas stayed below freezing until February 20. The joint report by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) found that more than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for as long as four days, and called the episode the largest firm load shed event in US history (23,418 MW). Over two consecutive days, ERCOT averaged 34,000 MW of generation outages, nearly half of its winter peak. Texas's Department of State Health Services counted 246 deaths in the state; Climate Central's national total is 262.

**Elliott, December 2022.** A historic winter storm and a powerful Arctic front brought rain, snow, ice and high winds, and temperatures plummeted. More than a million customers, from Texas to Maine, lost power (Climate Central). The FERC–NERC inquiry found 90,500 MW of generating units out at the same time at the storm's worst point. Grid operators in the Southeast shed more than 5,400 MW of firm load, the largest controlled firm load shed in the history of the Eastern Interconnection. In Buffalo, a blizzard with gusts of up to 79 mph (NWS Buffalo) killed at least 47 people in Erie and Niagara counties.

**January 2026.** The most recent entry in the top 10 is also the deadliest winter storm since Uri: 171 deaths (Climate Central), with snow, ice and record cold affecting 24 states.

## Map: Snowfall, Category 5 Regions and Ice Storms

The map shows NOAA NOHRSC snowfall analyses for seven storms since 2009, one at a time (switch in the layer menu). Each is the sum of the 24-hour snowfall grids over the storm's dates, so it also shows Western mountain snow from other systems. Click a coloured RSI region to list its Category 5 storms since 1900. Teal dots are the top 10 ice storms, placed at the damage-weighted centre of the hardest-hit states.

[Open map full screen ↗](<https://explore.disasteraware.com/maps/evergreen-worst-winter-storms-us-history.html>)

**Explore the map:** switch on more layers with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: the other six storms' **NOHRSC snowfall** ; NWS winter storm, blizzard and ice storm **warnings** (ALERT) for the nine storms in the warnings table (2014–2026); NWS **snow reports** for the seven snowfall storms (2009–2026); **ice-accretion reports** for ice storms #1, #2, #7 and #10 and January 2026 (none on file for 1998–2003); **Uri radar** , **1993 Superstorm satellite** imagery and Uri's Texas grid figures; and 17 **DisasterAWARE alert records**.

**What the map can show, by era.** Since late 2008, NOHRSC has published a gridded national snowfall analysis every day, so storms from 2009 on get a snowfall map built from that analysis. Earlier storms have RSI scores by region but no gridded snowfall layer here, so they appear through the region outlines. Ice storms are reported by forecast zone and county, not as measured swaths, so they appear as one marker per storm.

## Warnings for the Biggest Storms Since 2014

DisasterAWARE's historical hazard archive holds 3,074 US winter-storm records and 1,009 US extreme-temperature records (pulled October 9, 2026). They are **alerts** (warnings, watches and advisories), not measurements. From 2014 to 2024, the archive holds between 33 and 185 US winter-storm records a year, mostly one regional alert per storm. From 2025, it holds many more, finer-grained alerts, often one per forecast area: 844 in 2025 and 989 so far in 2026. Here is every storm since 2014 that NOAA rated Category 4 or 5 in any region, plus Uri and the January 2026 storm (both Category 3), with the NWS warnings issued for each:

Storm| NOAA RSI rating| NWS warnings (IEM)  
---|---|---  
Feb 11–14, 2014| Cat 4, Southeast| 58 in 35 states and DC: 52 winter storm, 3 blizzard, 3 ice storm  
Jan 22–24, 2016| Cat 4, Northeast and Southeast| 32 in 23 states and DC: 27 winter storm, 5 blizzard  
Mar 12–15, 2017| Cat 4, Northeast| 32 in 20 states and DC: 24 winter storm, 8 blizzard  
Apr 12–17, 2018| Cat 4, Upper Midwest| 39 in 15 states: 25 winter storm, 13 blizzard, 1 ice storm  
Feb 10–19, 2021 (Uri)| Cat 3, South| 151 in 36 states and DC: 123 winter storm, 3 blizzard, 25 ice storm  
Dec 13–20, 2022| Cat 4, Northern Rockies & Plains and Upper Midwest| 50 in 24 states: 33 winter storm, 13 blizzard, 4 ice storm  
Dec 21–26, 2022 (Elliott)| Cat 4, Upper Midwest| 71 in 26 states: 43 winter storm, 24 blizzard, 4 ice storm  
Jan 23–26, 2026| Cat 3, Ohio Valley and South| 69 in 32 states and DC: 53 winter storm, 16 ice storm  
Mar 14–17, 2026| **Cat 5** , Upper Midwest| 35 in 11 states: 18 winter storm, 16 blizzard, 1 ice storm  
  
_Counts: NWS winter storm, blizzard and ice storm warnings for the lower 48 states and DC that took effect within the storm's dates, one per NWS office warning. Source: NWS warnings (Iowa Environmental Mesonet VTEC archive), queried October 9, 2026; RSI ratings from NOAA NCEI._

**The March 2026 blizzard, warning by warning.** NWS offices across the Upper Midwest issued winter storm watches for the blizzard from the afternoon of March 12 (19:20 UTC), and the first blizzard warning followed on March 13 (NWS Aberdeen, South Dakota). From March 14 to 16, 16 blizzard warnings took effect across parts of eight states, from Montana and Nebraska to Illinois and Michigan, alongside 18 winter storm warnings (NWS warnings, IEM). In DisasterAWARE's archive, the regional winter storm watch record for the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains covered an alert area holding 11.7 million people. That is the population inside the alert area, not the number of people affected, so we do not rank storms by it.

Winter storm alerts, footprints and exposure, in one record

## For Insurers and Reinsurers: What Uri Changed

Reinsurers class winter storm as a secondary peril: Swiss Re Institute lists "secondary perils, such as winter storms, hail, floods or wildfires". Uri showed how large one can get, in four ways.

  * **The size of the loss.** The Texas Department of Insurance's data call (data as of December 31, 2021) counted 508,529 claims and an estimated ultimate insured loss of $11.2 billion in Texas alone, of which insurers expected about $3.4 billion (30%) to be covered by reinsurance. TDI's own comparison puts Uri at $11.15 billion against $19.74 billion for Hurricane Harvey at the same 10-month stage. A winter storm produced more than half Harvey's insured loss.
  * **Where it came from: pipes, not snow.** TDI lists the causes as freezing pipes, falling tree limbs, the weight of ice, sleet and snow, and power outages. About 85% of claims were on homes. Commercial property, other than business interruption, carried $4.57 billion of case-incurred losses on 44,201 claims, and 7,159 **business interruption** claims added $818 million. Losses depended on how long the cold lasted and the power stayed off, not on how much snow fell.
  * **The grid as the hazard multiplier.** FERC and NERC traced the outages to generating units and gas supply that failed in the cold. The Texas Comptroller cites estimates of $80 billion to $130 billion in financial losses across the state, far beyond the insured total. Elliott, 22 months later, showed that the same failure could happen in the Eastern Interconnection.
  * **Frequency.** Three of the ten costliest winter storms (Uri, Elliott and January 2026) have come since 2021.



**What event-level data exists.** For a winter portfolio, the useful record is footprint and duration: where the snow, ice and cold were, for how long, and which alerts were in force. NOAA publishes the RSI (back to 1900), NOHRSC snowfall grids (since late 2008) and Storm Events entries (since 1996). DisasterAWARE's archive adds its own alert records, each with its area and exposed population. [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>) licenses that archive across every hazard for back-testing, accumulation studies and event sets. The [sample datasets](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>) show the record format with no signup.

Decades of reconstructed, verified catastrophes -- browse the Historical Event Intelligence overview, or request sample data for your own portfolio.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What was the worst winter storm in US history?**  
By cost, the February 10–19, 2021 storm and cold wave known as Winter Storm Uri: $28.8 billion in 2026 dollars and 262 deaths, according to Climate Central's billion-dollar disaster record. By snowfall impact, the Great Blizzard of January 1978, with the highest score (39.07) on NOAA's Regional Snowfall Index since 1900.

**What was the deadliest winter storm in US history?**  
No federal database ranks winter-storm deaths before 1980. NOAA's account of the Great Blizzard of March 12–14, 1888 puts its toll at more than 400. Since 1980, in Climate Central's record, the deadliest winter storm is the March 1993 "Storm of the Century", with 270 deaths, just ahead of Uri (262).

**What was the worst blizzard in US history?**  
On NOAA's Regional Snowfall Index, the Great Blizzard of January 23–28, 1978 (the "Cleveland Superbomb") scores highest, at 39.07 in the Upper Midwest. The 1993 Superstorm is the only storm rated Category 5 in three regions at once.

**What was the worst ice storm in US history?**  
By total cost, the Southeast Ice Storm of February 8–13, 1994: $6.8 billion in 2026 dollars (Climate Central). Since 1996, the ice storm with the most damage reported to NOAA is that of January 26–28, 2009, in Arkansas, Kentucky and Missouri ($1.16 billion reported).

**How much did Winter Storm Uri cost?**  
$28.8 billion in 2026 dollars ($22.7 billion at the time) in total direct losses (Climate Central). Insured losses in Texas alone were estimated at $11.2 billion on 508,529 claims (Texas Department of Insurance).

# The Worst US Floods of the Last 20 Years, Ranked and Mapped

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/worst-us-floods-last-20-years  
**Summary**: The worst US floods of the last 20 years, ranked by deaths, flood-insurance payouts, total cost and record river crests: the 2025 Texas Hill Country flood, Harvey, Helene, Sandy, the 2008 Midwest floods and Irene, with a map of 1,047 record gauges.

_Four rankings, four rules: the deadliest floods, the biggest flood-insurance payouts, the costliest river and flash floods, and the floods that broke the most river records since 2006, with a map of every record-setting gauge._

**What were the worst US floods of the last 20 years? By deaths, the July 4, 2025 flash flood in the Texas Hill Country: NOAA's Storm Events Database records 124 flood deaths in Texas, 117 of them in Kerr County, more than any other US flood since 2006.** By flood-insurance losses, the worst is Hurricane Harvey in 2017: the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) paid $9.05 billion on 92,398 claims. By total cost of a flood that was not a hurricane, it is the 2008 Midwest floods, at $15.7 billion in 2026 dollars. And by river records, the remnants of Hurricane Irene in August 2011 pushed 68 long-record USGS gauges to the highest flows they had ever measured. Floods come as flash floods, river floods and storm surge, so each ranking below states its rule.

## How We Rank Floods

"Last 20 years" here means January 1, 2006 to October 9, 2026, so Hurricane Katrina (August 2005) falls just outside. No single official list ranks floods, so each table uses one public source:

  * **Deaths** from NOAA's Storm Events Database: deaths recorded in its flood entries (flash flood, flood, coastal flood and storm surge), joined into one flood when entries begin within 72 hours and 500 km of each other.
  * **Flood-insurance payouts** from FEMA's NFIP claims (the Redacted Claims v3 dataset), grouped by the flood event name FEMA assigns, in dollars of the time.
  * **Total cost** from Climate Central's billion-dollar disaster database (which took over the dataset from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information, NCEI, in 2025), for events it classes as flooding.
  * **River records** from the USGS annual peak-flow files.



DisasterAWARE archive figures are labelled **alerts** (issued warnings) or **observed** gauge readings.

## The Deadliest US Floods Since 2006

Ranking rule: deaths (direct and indirect) in Storm Events entries of type Flash Flood, Flood, Coastal Flood, Storm Surge/Tide and Lakeshore Flood, 2006 to June 2026, joined into floods as above. The top six are the same if entries are joined more tightly (48 hours, 300 km) or more loosely (96 hours, 800 km); places 7 to 10 change.

#| Flood| Dates| Deaths| Where (deaths)  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Texas Hill Country flash flood** (Guadalupe River)| Jul 4–5, 2025| 124| Texas 124  
2| **Hurricane Helene** , inland flooding| Sep 26–27, 2024| 87| North Carolina 67, Tennessee 17, South Carolina 2  
3| **Hurricane Harvey**|  Aug 26–29, 2017| 73| Texas 73  
4| Remnants of **Hurricane Ida**|  Aug 30 – Sep 2, 2021| 54| New Jersey 29, New York 18, Pennsylvania 4  
5| **Hurricane Sandy** , storm surge| Oct 28–29, 2012| 46| New York 39, New Jersey 7  
6| **Eastern Kentucky** flash floods| Jul 27–28, 2022| 40| Kentucky 40  
7| Midwest and South floods| Dec 23–31, 2015| 38| Missouri 17, Illinois 11, Tennessee 5  
8| **Tennessee floods** (Nashville)| Apr 30 – May 2, 2010| 32| Tennessee 22, Kentucky 4, Arkansas 2  
9| Texas–Oklahoma Memorial Day floods| May 23–25, 2015| 29| Texas 24, Oklahoma 4, Arkansas 1  
10=| **Hurricane Irene**|  Aug 27–28, 2011| 27| New York 10, New Jersey 9, Vermont 3  
10=| **Hurricane Matthew**|  Oct 8–13, 2016| 27| North Carolina 24, South Carolina 2, Virginia 1  
  
_Source: NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database, 2006–2026 detail files (2026 is preliminary, through June). Dates are when entries begin, local time. Places 10 and 11 are tied._

Two things stand out. Four of the six deadliest floods came from hurricanes or their remnants, but the deaths were mostly **inland** , in rain-fed flash floods far from the coast: Helene's 87 were almost all in the southern Appalachians of North Carolina and Tennessee (24 in Buncombe County alone), and 51 of Ida's 54 were in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania, far from where it came ashore in Louisiana. And the deadliest of all was not a hurricane: on July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River rose before dawn in Kerr County. Sandy is the exception: its 46 deaths are coastal-flood (storm surge) entries: 23 on Staten Island, the rest elsewhere in New York City, on Long Island and in New Jersey.

These counts are what NOAA's database attributes to flooding. Deaths that state and local officials count over the following months, or that Storm Events files under another event type (a hurricane, high wind), are not in them, so official tolls differ: by July 23, 2025, officials had confirmed 108 deaths in Kerr County, with two people still missing, and more than 130 across Texas.

## The Biggest Flood-Insurance Payouts Since 2006

Ranking rule: all NFIP claims with a date of loss from 2006 on, grouped by the flood event FEMA assigns, ranked by building, contents and increased-cost-of-compliance payments (dollars of the year paid, not adjusted for inflation). Claims without an event name never add up to more than $0.31 billion in any month, so no unnamed flood is missing from the top 10.

#| Event| NFIP paid| Claims| Largest states  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Hurricane Harvey** , 2017| $9.05 billion| 92,398| TX $9.03B, LA $15M  
2| **Hurricane Sandy** , 2012| $8.94 billion| 144,848| NJ $4.37B, NY $4.21B  
3| **Hurricane Helene** , 2024| $6.77 billion| 58,090| FL $6.49B, NC $220M  
4| **Hurricane Ian** , 2022| $4.91 billion| 48,824| FL $4.86B, SC $44M  
5| **Hurricane Ike** , 2008| $2.70 billion| 58,126| TX $2.23B, LA $334M  
6| **Louisiana floods** (NFIP: "Mid-summer severe storms"), 2016| $2.53 billion| 30,019| LA $2.53B  
7| **Hurricane Ida** , 2021| $1.35 billion| 28,318| LA $692M, NJ $354M  
8| **Hurricane Irene** , 2011| $1.34 billion| 52,493| NJ $598M, NY $347M  
9| **Hurricane Milton** , 2024| $1.21 billion| 21,675| FL $1.21B (nearly all)  
10| **Hurricane Irma** , 2017| $1.11 billion| 33,340| FL $984M, GA $65M  
  
_Source: FEMA OpenFEMA, NFIP Redacted Claims v3 (data as of September 7, 2026). Claims counts include claims closed without payment._

Hurricanes dominate this list because storm surge and hurricane rain flood thousands of insured homes at once. Katrina, just outside the 20-year window, is still the NFIP's largest flood: $16.21 billion paid on 208,348 claims. The only non-hurricane flood in the top 10 is **Louisiana's August 2016 flood** , when 20 to 30 inches of rain fell over several days (31.39 inches at Watson, according to Climate Central). The NFIP took 30,019 claims and paid $2.53 billion, 84% of it in East Baton Rouge, Livingston and Ascension parishes.

**Helene shows the gap.** Of its $6.77 billion in NFIP payouts, $6.49 billion went to Florida's Gulf Coast counties (Pinellas County alone: $3.23 billion). North Carolina, where 67 people died in the floods in the table above, accounts for $0.22 billion on 2,028 claims.

## The Costliest River and Flash Floods

Ranking rule: every Climate Central billion-dollar event of type "flooding" that began in 2006 or later (30 events), by total cost in 2026 dollars. Hurricanes are a separate type in this database, so their floods are not in this table; their flood-insurance losses are in the one above.

#| Flood| Dates| Total cost, 2026 dollars| Deaths  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Midwest floods (Iowa hardest hit)| Apr 1 – Jun 30, 2008| $15.7 billion| 24  
2| Missouri River and North Central floods| Mar 14–31, 2019| $14.3 billion| 3  
3| Louisiana floods (Baton Rouge)| Aug 12–15, 2016| $14.1 billion| 13  
4| Mississippi River, Midwest and Southern floods| Mar 15 – Jul 31, 2019| $8.1 billion| 4  
5| California atmospheric-river floods| Dec 26, 2022 – Mar 19, 2023| $5.0 billion| 22  
6| Mississippi River floods| Apr 1 – May 31, 2011| $4.5 billion| 7  
7| Arkansas River floods| May 20 – Jun 14, 2019| $3.9 billion| 5  
8| Houston floods| Apr 17–18, 2016| $3.8 billion| 8  
9| Texas and Oklahoma floods and severe weather| May 23–26, 2015| $3.6 billion| 31  
10| Tennessee–Kentucky floods and severe weather (Nashville)| Apr 30 – May 2, 2010| $3.5 billion| 32  
  
_Source: Climate Central billion-dollar disasters (read October 9, 2026). Total direct cost, insured and uninsured._

The 30 flooding events since 2006 cost $115.1 billion in 2026 dollars and killed 356 people, by Climate Central's count. Three of the seven costliest were in a single year, 2019. In March, a powerful storm sped up snowmelt and flooded the Missouri River basin, severely flooding Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska; high water then disrupted barge traffic on the Mississippi, and from May 20 into June levee failures and persistent rain flooded the Arkansas River basin, according to Climate Central's event summaries. The newest entry is the **Hawaii Kona-low floods of March 9–23, 2026** : back-to-back storms with rainfall totals above 20 inches on Oahu, Kauai and the Big Island and above 40 inches locally on Maui, at $1.0 billion. The deadliest flood of the 20 years, the Texas Hill Country flood of July 2025, is not in Climate Central's list at all.

## The Floods That Broke the Most River Records

How high did the water get? This is the measured view. USGS publishes annual peak flows for 5,695 stream gauges with at least 50 years of annual peaks. At 1,048 of them, the highest flow ever measured came in 2006 or later. Ranking rule: those record peaks, joined into one flood when they came within 7 days and 400 km of each other, ranked by the number of gauges that set an all-time record.

#| Flood| Record peaks| Gauges at all-time record| Biggest new record (peak flow)  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Remnants of **Hurricane Irene**|  Aug 28–29, 2011| 68| Schoharie Creek at Breakabeen, NY: 134,000 cfs (gage height 22.37 ft); old record 88,000 cfs (1996)  
2| **Midwest floods**|  May 30 – Jun 21, 2008| 37| Iowa River at Wapello, IA: 188,000 cfs (gage height 32.15 ft); old record 111,000 cfs (1993)  
3| **Hurricane Harvey**|  Aug 26 – Sep 2, 2017| 25| Village Creek near Kountze, TX: 182,000 cfs (gage height 35.96 ft); old record 67,200 cfs (1940)  
4| **Hurricane Helene**|  Sep 27 – Oct 2, 2024| 21| Nolichucky River below Nolichucky Dam, TN: 179,000 cfs (gage height 66.03 ft), a USGS estimate; old record 73,500 cfs (1906)  
5| Remnants of **Hurricane Ida**|  Sep 1–2, 2021| 19| Perkiomen Creek at Graterford, PA: 64,400 cfs, a USGS estimate; old record 45,600 cfs (2020)  
6=| Missouri–Arkansas floods| Apr 29 – May 2, 2017| 18| Gasconade River at Jerome, MO: 197,000 cfs (gage height 35.06 ft); old record 140,000 cfs (2015)  
6=| Midwest floods| Apr 18–21, 2013| 18| Spoon River at Seville, IL: 42,500 cfs (gage height 35.80 ft); old record 37,300 cfs (1924)  
8| **Hurricane Ian**|  Sep 29 – Oct 1, 2022| 16| Peace River at Arcadia, FL: 50,800 cfs (gage height 23.70 ft); old record 43,000 cfs (1912)  
  
_Source: USGS annual peak-flow files for all states and Puerto Rico (read October 9, 2026). Peaks coded as daily averages, dam failures, minimum values or opportunistic readings are excluded. Places 6 and 7 are tied. The file holds peaks for most gauges through September 2025 but almost none since; the July 2025 peaks at Hunt and Kerrville on the Guadalupe River and the March 2026 Hawaii peaks are not in it yet._

**Irene ranks first under every joining rule we tried.** On August 28–29, 2011, its rain set all-time records at gauges in nine states from Maryland and Delaware to Maine. In New York's Schoharie Valley, Schoharie Creek at Breakabeen ran at 134,000 cubic feet per second (cfs), half as much again as its 1996 record. **The 2008 Midwest floods** come second: the Cedar River at Cedar Rapids, Iowa peaked at 140,000 cfs on June 13, 2008, nearly double its 1961 record of 73,000 cfs, with a gage height of 31.12 feet. Ranks 9 to 12 are tied at 15 record gauges each: the Louisiana–Texas floods of March 2016, the Midwest floods of September 2008 (NFIP files their Illinois claims under Hurricane Ike), the New England floods of March 2010 and high runoff at Western mountain gauges in June 2010 (likely snowmelt).

## The Worst US Floods by Type

  * **Flash flood (not tropical):** the Texas Hill Country flood of July 2025 (124 deaths) is the deadliest, ahead of eastern Kentucky in July 2022 (40). Flash flood entries hold 70% of all flood deaths in Storm Events since 2006 (1,592 of 2,284).
  * **River flood:** the 2008 Midwest floods are both the costliest ($15.7 billion) and the second-largest record-breaker (37 gauges), ahead of the 2019 Missouri River floods ($14.3 billion).
  * **Storm surge:** Sandy in 2012 ($8.94 billion in NFIP payouts, $4.37 billion in New Jersey and $4.21 billion in New York) and Ian in 2022 ($4.91 billion, nearly all in Florida).
  * **Hurricane rain inland:** Harvey (the top NFIP payout, 25 record gauges) and Helene (87 deaths, 21 record gauges).

The map shows the 11 deadliest floods (dark red, at the county with the most deaths, or one of the tied counties), the 10 largest NFIP payouts (blue, at the county paid most), and 1,047 of the 1,048 USGS gauges that set an all-time record peak since 2006 (teal for the 12 floods that broke the most records, grey for the rest; one gauge has no location in the USGS site service). Click any gauge for its record flow, the old record and how long it has been measured. Orange outlines are the 82 flash flood warnings the National Weather Service issued for Texas on July 3–6, 2025 (IEM VTEC archive).

**Explore the map:** switch on more layers with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: the 105 **record crests** (NWS crest history) on DisasterAWARE flood alerts for the eight floods in the archive table below; NWS **flash and river flood warnings** (ALERT) for five more floods (2016–2024); NWS **river crests** and **storm reports** for 12 floods (2010–2025); **USGS high-water marks** (2011–2025); **FEMA declared counties** for 12 floods (REPORTED); and **Stage IV rainfall** estimates for four floods (MODELED).

**What the map can show.** Gauge records cover every flood that reaches a river; storm surge shows up in claims and deaths instead. The warning polygons are where the National Weather Service told people to act, not the flooded area.

## In the DisasterAWARE Archive Since 2014

DisasterAWARE's historical hazard archive holds 128,945 flood records worldwide, 85,445 of them in the US. They are **alerts** (warnings and advisories). Of its 60,893 US flood warning records since 2014, 59,549 (98%) also carry a flood enhancement block: the river gauges inside the warning area with their measured crests (**observed** readings, labelled as such), storm reports, and the matching NOAA Storm Events and FEMA claims summaries. Here is what the archive holds for the floods above since 2014:

---|---|---|---|---

Texas Hill Country flash flood, Jul 2025| 72 Texas records, Jul 3–6| 10| 1| Guadalupe River at Hunt: 37.52 ft, a preliminary record (36.6 ft in 1932)

**The Texas Hill Country flood, in the archive.** The National Weather Service's first flash flood warning for Kerr County (with Bandera County) was issued at 1:14 a.m. CDT on July 4, 2025. The Guadalupe River at Hunt crested at 37.52 feet at 5:10 a.m., a preliminary record above its 36.6 feet of July 1932, and at Kerrville it reached 37.51 feet at 6:45 a.m., 28.51 feet above flood stage and just short of the 39.0-foot record set in 1932. Downstream at Comfort, USGS measured a peak flow of 177,000 cfs, the third highest in its record, after 1978 and 1900.

Every flood, every alert, one record

DisasterAWARE Historical Event Intelligence links flood warnings to the gauges, crests and footprints behind them -- event by event, since 2014.

## For Insurers and Reinsurers: The Uninsured Gap

For flood, the gap between insured and total losses is wide, and the public data shows where it opens.

  * **Take-up is low, and lower still where the recent killers struck.** FEMA's residential penetration rates (as of August 2026) put about 2.9% of US residential structures under an NFIP policy: 3.16 million contracts for 109 million structures, summed over the counties FEMA reports. Inside the high-risk Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), where flood insurance is often required, the rate is 47.9%. Outside it, 1.3%. In the counties hit hardest by the deadliest floods it is lower still: 2.4% in Kerr County, Texas; 1.0% in Buncombe County, North Carolina (Asheville); 1.1% in Knott County and 1.5% in Breathitt County, Kentucky.
  * **The losses fall outside the map.** Of all NFIP claims with a date of loss since 2006, 28% were rated outside the SFHA. In Harvey, it was more than half: 48,472 of 92,398 claims, and $4.59 billion of the $9.05 billion paid. For Tropical Storm Imelda, two years later in southeast Texas, it was 68%.
  * **Insured flood is a sliver of total cost.** Harvey's NFIP payouts were about 7% of Climate Central's total cost estimate for the hurricane ($125 billion at the time). For the Louisiana flood of August 2016, it was about 25% ($2.53 billion of $10.0 billion). As of September 7, 2026, with claims still open, NFIP had paid $17.6 million on 125 claims in Kerr County for the July 2025 flood, and $23.1 million on 422 claims for the March 2026 Hawaii floods, a $1.0 billion event.
  * **Most homeowners policies exclude flood.** FEMA's FloodSmart puts it plainly: "Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage." What is not on an NFIP or private flood policy falls on households, businesses, governments and disaster aid.



**What event-level data exists.** For a flood portfolio, the useful record joins the hazard to the exposure: which warnings were in force where and when, which gauges crested and how high relative to flood stage and to their records, and which claims followed. NOAA, USGS and FEMA publish the pieces separately. DisasterAWARE's archive adds the alerts themselves, each with its area, gauge readings, crest-history ranks and exposed population. [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>) licenses that archive across every hazard for back-testing, accumulation studies and event sets. The [sample datasets](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>) show the record format with no signup, and the [flood data page](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/flood-data>) lists what each flood record carries.

Decades of reconstructed, verified catastrophes -- browse the Historical Event Intelligence overview, or request sample data for your own portfolio.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What were the worst floods in the last 20 years in the US?**  
By deaths, the July 4, 2025 Texas Hill Country flash flood (124 deaths in NOAA's Storm Events Database). By flood-insurance payouts, Hurricane Harvey in 2017 ($9.05 billion paid by the NFIP). By total cost of a non-hurricane flood, the 2008 Midwest floods ($15.7 billion in 2026 dollars, Climate Central). By river records, the remnants of Hurricane Irene in 2011, which set all-time peak flows at 68 long-record USGS gauges.

**What was the deadliest flood in US history?**  
If storm surge counts, the Galveston hurricane of September 1900: the National Hurricane Center says storm tides of 8 to 15 feet were largely responsible for its 8,000 deaths (estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000), the deadliest weather disaster in US history. The Johnstown Flood of May 31, 1889, when the South Fork Dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, killed 2,209 people, according to the National Park Service. Since 2006, the deadliest is the July 2025 Texas Hill Country flood.

**What was the costliest flood in US history?**  
Among events Climate Central classes as flooding, the Midwest floods of June to August 1993: $49.1 billion in 2026 dollars. By flood-insurance payouts, Hurricane Katrina in 2005: $16.21 billion paid by the NFIP.

**Does homeowners insurance cover floods?**  
Usually not. FEMA's FloodSmart says most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood needs a separate NFIP or private flood policy. About 2.9% of US residential structures have NFIP cover, and since 2006, 28% of NFIP claims have come from outside the high-risk flood zone.

# Worst Derechos in US History: 2020 Iowa, 2012 Mid-Atlantic and More (Mapped)

**Published**: 2026-10-13  
**URL**: https://www.disasteraware.com/news-event/worst-derechos-us-history  
**Summary**: The worst derechos in US history, ranked three ways: costliest (Iowa 2020, $14.2 billion in 2026 dollars), deadliest (June 2012, 22 killed) and strongest measured gusts. Plus 2026's derechos, with every wind report mapped.

_The costliest, deadliest and strongest derechos on record, ranked from the Storm Prediction Center's derecho archive and the US billion-dollar disaster database, with every wind report mapped._

**What was the worst derecho in US history? The Iowa derecho of August 10, 2020.** It cost $11.0 billion at the time, or $14.2 billion in 2026 dollars, which makes it the costliest derecho in the US billion-dollar disaster database by a factor of three. It flattened crops across central Iowa and tore through Cedar Rapids, where the National Weather Service estimated winds near 140 mph from the damage. The **deadliest** derecho is the June 29–30, 2012 storm that ran from Indiana to the Atlantic coast near Washington, D.C.: 22 people killed, according to the Storm Prediction Center (SPC). The **most recent** derecho came on August 11, 2026, from eastern Iowa through Chicago into Ohio; SPC has preliminarily confirmed it, along with one on June 10, 2026.

Below are three rankings (cost, deaths and the strongest measured gust), the longest derecho paths, the 2026 derechos, and a map of every wind report SPC assigns to each storm, measured and estimated.

## What Counts as a Derecho

A derecho is a widespread, long-lived windstorm produced by a fast-moving line or cluster of thunderstorms. SPC's current definition requires a swath of wind damage **at least 250 miles (about 400 km) long** , with gusts of at least 58 mph along its length and **several well-separated gusts of 75 mph or more** , from a storm system that moves faster than the mean wind. These requirements come from revisions published in 2016 (Corfidi and colleagues) and 2025 (Squitieri and colleagues).

In 2026, SPC and its partners published the first archive built on the revised definition: 173 cases from 1955 to 2025, each with its quality-checked wind reports. It splits them into 96 **definitive** and 13 **likely** derechos in the radar era (1996–2025), and 48 likely and 16 **possible** derechos from 1955 to 1995. Every ranking below starts from that archive, and the tables say when a storm commonly called a derecho is not in it. Five of the ten costliest are in it; four are not (among them December 2021), and one (2026) postdates it. Nor is the 2024 Houston derecho.

Two kinds of wind numbers appear in derecho records, and they are not interchangeable:

  * **A measured gust** is a reading from an instrument: an airport weather station, a state road-weather or mesonet station, or sometimes a home weather station. It is an **observation** , though home stations are not calibrated to official standards.
  * **An estimated gust or a damage-survey wind** is a judgment: a spotter's estimate, or the wind speed an NWS survey team infers from what was destroyed. Damage-survey estimates are how the highest derecho winds are usually known (Cedar Rapids, about 140 mph), but **they are not gust readings** , and this article never calls them gusts.



## The Costliest Derechos

Ranking rule: every event in the US billion-dollar disaster database (now maintained by Climate Central, continuing NOAA's) whose name or summary identifies a derecho, ranked by total cost in 2026 dollars. These are whole-event totals: several include tornadoes and other storms on the same dates, not split out.

#| Event (database name)| Dates| Cost, 2026 dollars| Cost at the time| Deaths (whole event)| In SPC's archive?  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
1| **Central Severe Weather – Derecho** (Iowa)| Aug 10, 2020| **$14.22 billion**|  $11.03 billion| 4| Yes, definitive  
2| **Plains/East/Northeast Derecho**|  Jun 29–Jul 2, 2012| $4.22 billion| $2.89 billion| 28| Yes, definitive (Jun 29–30)  
3| Midwest/Southeast Tornadoes and Derecho| Apr 4–5, 2011| $4.11 billion| $2.78 billion| 9| No  
4| Central Derecho| Jun 13, 2022| $3.61 billion| $3.20 billion| 1| No  
5| **Midwest Derecho and Severe Storms**|  Aug 9–12, 2026| $3.02 billion| $3.02 billion| 7| Preliminary (Aug 11); archive ends in 2025  
6| Northern Plains and Great Lakes Derecho, Tornadoes| May 30–Jun 2, 1998| $2.33 billion| $1.14 billion| 20| Yes, definitive (May 31)  
7| Midwest Derecho and Tornado Outbreak| Dec 15, 2021| $2.14 billion| $1.78 billion| 1| No  
8| Midwest, South and East Severe Weather| Jun 9–12, 2009| $2.06 billion| $1.33 billion| 0| Yes, two (Jun 10–11 and Jun 12)  
9| Southern Derecho and Eastern Severe Weather| Jul 21–23, 2003| $1.84 billion| $1.01 billion| 7| No  
10| Rockies and Midwest Derecho| Jul 10–11, 2011| $1.83 billion| $1.24 billion| 2| Yes, two (Jul 10–11 and Jul 11)  
  
_Source: US billion-dollar disaster database, Climate Central (continuing NOAA NCEI's), events page fetched 2026-10-09; total direct costs, insured and uninsured, CPI-adjusted to 2026 dollars. Archive status: SPC Derecho Archive (Squitieri et al. 2026)._

Six more derecho events in the database fall below $1.83 billion: the May 2018 Northeast derecho (inside a $1.82 billion event), the 2024 Houston derecho ($1.64 billion), April 19–20, 2011 ($1.54 billion), the May 1989 Texas derecho ($1.49 billion), May 2009 ($1.34 billion) and the April 29, 2025 Ohio Valley–Northeast derecho ($1.29 billion).

Iowa 2020 stands apart. In 2026 dollars it is the second-costliest severe-storm event of any kind in the database, behind only the April 2011 tornado outbreak ($15.13 billion), out of 238 severe-storm events since 1980.

## The Deadliest Derechos

Ranking rule: all US deaths that NOAA attributes to the derecho's winds, direct and indirect, taken from SPC's own case write-up where SPC has one, and otherwise from NWS Storm Data (NCEI Storm Events, direct plus indirect thunderstorm-wind deaths). These counts differ from source to source, so the table shows the other NOAA counts where they disagree.

#| Derecho| Deaths| Source of the count| Notes  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| **June 29–30, 2012** , Indiana to New Jersey and Washington, D.C.| **22**|  SPC case write-up| Mostly falling trees; 5 million lost power. Storm Data on the reports in SPC's archive: 15; the billion-dollar event (Jun 29–Jul 2): 28  
2| **July 4, 1969** , Ohio and Lake Erie| 18| SPC case write-up (in Ohio)| Falling trees and capsized boats during holiday fireworks; SPC's archive lists it only as a "possible" derecho  
3| **July 19, 2018** , Kansas to Arkansas| 17| NCEI Storm Events: 17 direct| A tour boat sank on Table Rock Lake, Missouri; NWS's service assessment calls the storm a derecho. Not in SPC's 2026 archive  
4=| **May 16, 2024** , Houston| 8| NCEI Storm Events: 4 direct, 4 indirect| A ninth death, from a lightning fire, is listed separately. Not in SPC's archive table  
4=| **April 4–5, 2011** , Southeast| 8| NCEI Storm Events: 4 direct, 4 indirect| SPC's write-up says only "several wind-related deaths". Not in SPC's 2026 archive  
6=| **July 12–13, 1995** , "Right Turn" derecho, North Dakota to Ohio| 7| SPC case write-up| NCEI Storm Events: 6 (Ohio 3, Michigan 3). Longest path in SPC's archive (below)  
6=| **March 12–13, 1993** , Florida| 7| SPC case write-up| Florida only; SPC adds 10 deaths in Cuba. Includes embedded tornadoes; not in SPC's 2026 archive  
8=| **July 14–15, 1995** , "Ontario–Adirondacks" derecho, Michigan to New England| 6| SPC case write-up| New York 5, Massachusetts 1 (NCEI the same); SPC adds one in Ontario. SPC's archive: likely  
8=| **August 10, 2020** , Iowa to Indiana| 6| NCEI Storm Events: 4 direct, 2 indirect| No SPC case write-up. Storm Data on the reports in SPC's archive: 4  
8=| **May 17, 1986** , southeast Texas| 6| SPC case write-up| Six boaters drowned, five of them on Lake Livingston; NCEI Storm Events: 9 (Polk and Tyler counties). Not in SPC's 2026 archive  
8=| **July 4–5, 1980** , "More Trees Down" derecho| 6| SPC case write-up| Four of the six died when boats overturned; Storm Data on the reports in SPC's archive: 3  
  
_Sources: SPC "About Derechos" case pages; SPC Derecho Archive; NCEI Storm Events Database (1980–2020 files of 2026-03-23; 2024 file of 2026-07-28); NWS Table Rock Lake service assessment._

Death counts before the mid-1990s are incomplete: NOAA's Storm Data often did not record wind deaths, and SPC has written up only selected older derechos, so older storms may be missing from this list.

The pattern is consistent: derecho deaths come from **trees falling on people** , in homes, cars and tents, and from **boats capsized** on lakes. May 31, 1998 killed five in the US (SPC; a sixth in Ontario). The two Labor Day derechos of September 7, 1998 killed seven between them (SPC's case write-up; neither is in SPC's 2026 archive). The billion-dollar database gives higher multi-day tolls (21 for May 1–6, 1989; 20 for May 30–June 2, 1998), but they include tornado deaths: the violent Spencer, South Dakota tornado of May 30, 1998 alone killed six.

## The Strongest Measured Derecho Gusts

Ranking rule: for every case in SPC's archive, the highest wind report coded **"Measured"** , ranked by the archive's value in knots. The archive codes a report as measured when Storm Data does; before 2000 reports are assumed estimated unless the record says otherwise. The table gives what each report says about the instrument, because "measured" ranges from an Air Force base to a farmer's wind gauge.

#| Derecho| Measured gust| Where| What the report says  
---|---|---|---|---  
1| Apr 22, 1997, Ark-La-Tex| 125 kt (144 mph)| Barksdale AFB, Bossier City, LA| The base's weather observation: peak wind 125 kt from the west-northwest at 13:08 UTC (METAR "PK WND 300125/08"); Storm Data: "clocked at 144 mph". Shreveport's airport, 16 km away, peaked at 41 mph: a very localized macroburst  
2=| **May 31, 1998** , southern Great Lakes| 111 kt (128 mph)| Near Lebanon, Dodge Co., WI| "Peak gust of 128 mph measured"; also cited by SPC  
2=| May 17, 1996, Northern Plains (SPC: likely)| 111 kt in the archive (128 mph); the report says 126 mph| South of Heil, ND| A farmer's recording equipment, before it was destroyed  
4| Jul 10, 2011, North Dakota–Minnesota| 110 kt (121–127 mph)| Near Straubville, ND| Six sensors on a temporary wind-energy tower, 130–200 ft above ground (the WMO standard height for wind sensors is 10 m)  
5=| Jun 29, 1998, Corn Belt| 109 kt (126 mph stated)| Washington, IA| "Unofficial wind speed measured at 126 mph"  
5=| **Aug 10, 2020, Iowa**|  109 kt (126 mph stated)| Atkins, Benton Co., IA| "maximum measured unofficial wind gust"; a home weather station  
7| Jun 22, 2015, South Dakota–Wisconsin| 106 kt ("over 120 mph")| Hayes, SD| A home wind system  
8| Jul 8–9, 1993, Nebraska (SPC: likely)| 105 kt in the archive (121 mph); the report says 125 mph| York, NE| "Thunderstorm winds measured at 125 mph"  
9| Jul 31, 2008, Dakotas–Minnesota| 100 kt (115 mph)| Hiland, SD| "measured with a wind meter"  
10| Jun 7–8, 2005, Dakotas| 98 kt ("over 110 mph")| Onida, SD| Two planes flipped at the airport  
  
_Source: SPC Derecho Archive per-case report files (Squitieri et al. 2026), all 173 cases. Knots as stored in the archive; mph in brackets is the converted value unless the report states its own figure ("stated"). Where the report's own figure and the archive's knots disagree (Heil 1996, York 1993), both are shown; ranked by the archive's value. Storm Data also codes a 98-kt report at Shallow Water, Kansas (July 22, 2000) as measured, but the report names no instrument ("Irrigation sprinkler destroyed"), so it is left out._

Two lessons from this table. First, **most of the very highest readings come from unofficial instruments.** The top of the list is a single Air Force base observation in a macroburst; then come a farmer's gauge, a tall wind-energy tower and home weather stations. Below Barksdale, airport sensors in the same archive top out lower: 106 mph at the Bemidji, Minnesota airport (June 21, 2025), 100 mph at Salina, Kansas (May 19, 2024) and 96 mph at Omaha's Eppley Airfield (July 10, 2021). Second, **the strongest winds are usually not measured at all.** The Iowa derecho's most famous number, about 140 mph in Cedar Rapids, is an NWS damage-survey estimate, and so is the "100 to 110 mph" in northwest Indiana in 2026.

## The Longest Derecho Paths

By the archive's track length, the distance between the first and last wind report:

  1. **July 12–13, 1995, the "Right Turn" derecho** (likely): 2,414 km (about 1,500 miles) in 30 hours, from Montana and North Dakota across Minnesota and Michigan to Ohio and Pennsylvania.
  2. **July 4–5, 1999, the Boundary Waters derecho** (definitive): 2,210 km (about 1,370 miles) in 22 hours, from North Dakota to Maine. It flattened forest in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area of Minnesota.
  3. **July 11, 2011** (definitive): 1,975 km (about 1,230 miles) in 23 hours, from northeast Colorado to western Pennsylvania.



The Iowa derecho of 2020 covered 1,111 km in 13 hours by the same measure, and the June 2012 derecho 1,124 km in 12 hours.

## The 2026 Derechos

SPC confirms each year's derechos once that year's Storm Data is final, so 2026's official list will come in 2027. Two 2026 storms have already been **preliminarily confirmed** by SPC, according to the NWS offices that covered them, and NWS Norman has described a third as a derecho:

  * **June 10, 2026.** A line of storms formed in eastern Iowa and moved east across northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin toward the western Great Lakes (NWS Quad Cities), bringing multiple 80+ mph gusts to southern Wisconsin (NWS Milwaukee). The strongest measured gust among NWS reports was 94 mph at the Oshkosh, Wisconsin airport weather station.
  * **June 22, 2026.** NWS Norman described the overnight line of storms across Oklahoma as a derecho; an Oklahoma Mesonet station west of Hinton measured a 102 mph gust at 1:15 a.m. CDT. We found no published SPC classification for it.
  * **August 11, 2026.** The most destructive derecho of the year moved from eastern Iowa through the Chicago area and northwest Indiana, then on toward Ohio and eastern Kentucky. SPC's preliminary note recorded a maximum measured gust of 86 kt (99 mph) at Gary/Chicago International Airport. An NWS Chicago damage survey estimated peak winds of 100 to 110 mph in northern Lake and Porter counties, Indiana, where some forested areas near Portage lost more than 80% of their tree canopy. NWS Chicago reports one death from its straight-line winds, a woman struck by debris in Gary. The billion-dollar database puts the August 9–12 event, the derecho plus the storms before and after it, at $3.02 billion and 7 deaths.



## Map: Every Wind Report, Measured vs Estimated

The map plots the wind reports SPC assigns to each ranked derecho: **blue dots are measured gusts** , **orange dots are observers' estimates** of 75 mph or more (beneath measured). Red outlines are drawn 20 km around every report: derived, not surveyed damage swaths. Purple dots are the June 10 and August 11, 2026 reports (preliminary); dark-red markers are every ranked derecho plus other SPC-archive and 2026 derechos. A radar snapshot shows the 2020 storm over Cedar Rapids.

**Explore the map:** switch on more layers with the layers icon at the bottom right of the map: **NEXRAD radar** frames from 1995; **SPC watches** (from 1997) and **discussions** (from 2003) and **NWS severe thunderstorm warnings** (from 2003), all ALERT; **NWS damage-survey points** (survey estimates, not gusts) where logged, from 2011, at zoom 7 and closer; and the **other wind reports** in SPC's archive, from 1969.

## In the DisasterAWARE Archive

In the DisasterAWARE historical hazard archive, severe thunderstorm alert records are enriched with the storm reports and NWS damage-survey points inside them. That makes it possible to separate what was measured from what was estimated, which is exactly where derecho data goes wrong.

A fresh pull (October 9, 2026) found **147 US severe thunderstorm alert records** (144 warnings, 3 watches) with a wind value of 100 mph or more. Checked one by one against their own reports, **only 44 of those values are measured gusts.** **96 are NWS damage-survey wind estimates** , and the other 7 are estimated gusts in storm reports that also come from NWS damage surveys. The highest value, 131 mph near Highmore, South Dakota (June 29, 2026), is a measured gust from a state mesonet station, held on a severe thunderstorm watch record; the next highest, 130 mph in Lea County, New Mexico (May 31, 2023) and Jones County, South Dakota (June 12, 2022), are both survey estimates. After merging duplicates, the 44 measured values are 37 distinct readings. Eleven of them came during derechos in SPC's archive, among them:

  * **Iowa, August 10, 2020:** 112 mph near Midway in Linn County and 106 mph from a personal weather station near Le Grand. The archive's Davenport warning record for Cedar Rapids alone holds 111 storm reports, including the 126 mph Atkins reading and estimated gusts of 130 mph, plus NWS survey points up to an estimated 140 mph.
  * **South Dakota, May 12, 2022:** 107 mph at a state road-weather station near Tripp. The severe thunderstorm warning covering that spot was issued 26 minutes before the gust (NWS Sioux Falls warning #75; NWS warning times, IEM VTEC).
  * **Illinois, July 15–16, 2024:** 101 mph on an anemometer west of Davis Junction, 60 minutes after NWS Chicago's severe thunderstorm warning #116 was issued for the area (NWS warning times, IEM VTEC).



For the August 11, 2026 derecho, the archive's Chicago alert, which summarizes three NWS severe thunderstorm warnings, carries 138 storm reports (32 of them measured, peaking at the 99 mph Gary airport gust) and 342 NWS damage-survey points, the highest estimated at 110 mph. Every number here is labelled by tier: the warnings are **alerts** , the gust reports are **observations** , and the survey winds are **estimates**.

Every gust, warning and damage survey in one record

## For Insurers and Reinsurers: Why Derechos Are a Blind Spot

Derechos are a severe convective storm (SCS) peril, part of what the industry calls "secondary perils". The label is misleading: at $14.2 billion in 2026 dollars, the August 2020 derecho cost more than 46 of the 68 tropical cyclones in the billion-dollar database. Three features make them hard to price.

**The losses are wide, shallow and mixed.** In Iowa alone, insurers reported **200,597 claims and $1.61 billion paid** by November 2, 2020, with more than $1 billion still held in reserve (Iowa Insurance Division). Farm losses then go on through a second channel: federal crop insurance paid **$325.8 million** in Iowa for "Wind/Excess Wind" losses in August 2020, $316.3 million of it on corn, across 1.38 million acres and 9,021 policies (USDA Risk Management Agency, cause-of-loss data).

**The hazard data is mostly estimates.** A derecho's record is hundreds of reports along a path of 1,000 km or more, mostly estimates, with a minority of instrument readings and damage surveys of the worst spots. The Iowa derecho has 569 reports in SPC's archive: 85 measured, 484 estimated. A model or a parametric trigger built on "the gust" will often be built on a spotter's estimate or a survey judgment without knowing it. Separating measured from estimated, and both from survey winds, changes the event: in our own archive it removes more than two-thirds of the "100 mph gusts".

**Event boundaries are inconsistent.** The billion-dollar database bundles derechos with tornado outbreaks and multi-day storms (2011, 2026); SPC's new archive leaves out storms that most people call derechos (Houston 2024, December 2021); and death and loss counts differ between sources by a factor of two (22, 15 or 28 deaths for June 2012). A portfolio's event set for this peril depends on which definition was used to build it.

DisasterAWARE's [severe convective storm data](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/severe-convective-storm-data>) links severe thunderstorm alert records to the storm reports and NWS damage-survey points inside them, with every value flagged as measured, estimated or surveyed. That is the event-level detail behind calibrating a wind vulnerability curve, back-testing a parametric SCS trigger, or reconstructing a derecho footprint over a portfolio. [Historical Event Intelligence](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data>) licenses the archive, and the [sample datasets](<https://www.disasteraware.com/products/historical-catastrophe-data/sample-datasets>) show the record format.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What was the worst derecho in US history?**  
By cost, the Iowa derecho of August 10, 2020: $11.0 billion at the time, $14.2 billion in 2026 dollars, according to the US billion-dollar disaster database. By deaths, the June 29–30, 2012 derecho, which killed 22 people from the Midwest to the Mid-Atlantic, according to SPC.

**When was the last derecho in the US?**  
August 11, 2026, from eastern Iowa through Chicago and northwest Indiana toward Ohio and Kentucky. SPC preliminarily confirmed it (SPC statement quoted by NWS Northern Indiana), with a 99 mph gust measured at Gary/Chicago International Airport. SPC also preliminarily confirmed a derecho on June 10, 2026, and NWS Norman called the June 22, 2026 Oklahoma storms a derecho. Official 2026 derechos are confirmed once Storm Data is final, in 2027.

**What is the strongest derecho wind ever recorded?**  
The highest report coded as measured in SPC's derecho archive is 144 mph at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana, on April 22, 1997: the peak wind in the base's own weather observation (125 kt) during a macroburst. SPC also cites 128 mph measured in eastern Wisconsin on May 31, 1998. Damage surveys have estimated winds of about 140 mph (Cedar Rapids, 2020), but those are estimates from the damage, not gust readings.

**What was the worst derecho in Iowa history?**  
August 10, 2020. In SPC's archive its Iowa wind reports run from 8:16 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. CDT. It flattened corn across central Iowa and hit Cedar Rapids hardest. Iowa insurers had paid $1.61 billion on 200,597 claims by November 2020, and federal crop insurance paid $325.8 million in Iowa for wind losses that August.
